nytimes.com.title: Macron Dreamed of Reviving France, but His Term Is Ending in Crisis
nytimes.com.text:
As thousands of high school students took to the streets last week in a collective cry of youthful anger, President Emmanuel Macron of France traveled to a navy ship off the coast of Brittany. From the deck, he watched the firing of a new ballistic missile from a French nuclear-powered submarine.
It was a telling display of Mr. Macron’s priorities in a country where the president, by tradition, rises above the messy scrum of domestic politics. Mr. Macron left it to his prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to try to reassure the French people that the government was handling the proliferating unrest.
It also reflected how Mr. Macron, after nearly a decade in power, has failed to solve the manifold problems afflicting France’s economy and welfare system — problems he promised to address when he was elected in 2017, at 39, as an ambitious reformer, and which have now coalesced into a systemic crisis.
“Remember, Macron published a book before the 2017 election, called ‘Révolution,’” said Jérôme Fourquet, a political analyst at the polling institute IFOP. “We told ourselves: he will relaunch the machine, he will lead a revolution.”
With just seven months before he leaves office, the president “hasn’t been able to bring about this revolution,” Mr. Fourquet said. Instead, the analyst said, he may be remembered as “the last captain of the boat.”

nytimes.com.title: FIFA Pays Millions for Trump Tower Office Said to Be Rarely Used
nytimes.com.text:
About a year before the World Cup, FIFA held a splashy opening for its latest office, a 17th-floor suite in Trump Tower. President Trump’s son Eric Trump said his family’s organization was “honored” to host the global soccer body.
FIFA signed a more than seven-year lease, worth about $4 million, according to two officials directly involved in the deal and documents reviewed by The New York Times. The suite mostly sits empty.
The terms of the deal, which have not been previously reported, raised concern among some senior FIFA officials about renting space in a Trump-linked building, in a high-tax state, without a clear need.
The deal offers another example of how FIFA and its president, Gianni Infantino, sought closer ties to President Trump ahead of the 2026 World Cup, despite pushback from senior soccer officials.
Mr. Infantino has lavished praise on the American president, even creating a special peace prize in his honor. During the World Cup, FIFA rescinded the suspension of Folarin Balogun, a star striker for the U.S. team, after a call between Mr. Trump and Mr. Infantino, prompting accusations of bias and political interference.
Since the tournament, Mr. Infantino has faced intense scrutiny over his conduct, including for engaging in secret talks to sell a portion of future tournaments to a private fund run by the brother of Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. The plan prompted European soccer’s governing body to threaten to bring a complaint to criminal court. Mr. Infantino has accused his critics of a harassment campaign.

nytimes.com.title: Why Chinese College Grads Are Becoming Farmers
nytimes.com.text:
new video loaded: Why Chinese College Grads Are Becoming Farmers
transcript
Why Chinese College Grads Are Becoming Farmers
Facing a competitive job market, college graduates in China are trading corporate jobs for farming, equipped with smartphones and tech skills.
- On Chinese social media, recent college grads are calling themselves xinnonren, or new farmer in English. They are among the 15 million people who’ve moved to the countryside in the past few years to farm or start small businesses. Most of them have given up on the job hunt in big cities, where unemployment has stayed stubbornly high. Local governments are also jumping on the new farmer trend by offering tax breaks and loans to entice young people. We spoke to a recent college graduate who filmed his daily life for us and shared his social media posts, which give a glimpse into why some are rethinking their life goals. Wang Hongbo grew up in Inner Mongolia on a sunflower farm that has been in his family for generations, and he was the first to go to university. As a lover of movies, Wang majored in filmmaking and landed a dream internship at a production company in Beijing. But the grueling work while making only $500 a month, made him feel burnt out. Wang graduated and moved home. He applied to dozens of corporate jobs but had no luck. Then one day, while with his dad in the fields, he posted this video of himself dressed like an office worker. The video got millions of views. These days, Wang wakes up at 6 in the morning and works alongside his parents. To reduce a lot of the manual labor, Wang is modernizing the way they work. He has deployed drones that spray pesticides. He’s also convinced his dad to try a machine with A.I. that figures out when it’s best to water and fertilize the crops. But Wang said the most valuable tool is his smartphone, which he uses to livestream about products. Some local farmers are now paying Wang a 20 percent commission to sell their produce, earning him up to $400 per livestream. And that money goes much further in the countryside. But the life of a new farmer can be physically exhausting. And he’s had to learn how to deal with bad weather. Unlike some new farmers who had to start from scratch, Wang has had his family’s support. But he said there’s still a lot to learn for someone who’s never done agriculture before. So Wang attends conferences for new farmers, where they can learn from each other and share new ideas. For now, Wang said being a new farmer beats being unemployed.

nytimes.com.title: After Lockdown, Sea of Protesters Flows Through India’s Capital
nytimes.com.text:
Thousands of opposition political party supporters marched along a busy thoroughfare in central Delhi to challenge sweeping revisions of the nation’s voter roll.
In a contrast to a week of lockdowns and detentions by the authorities, the demonstrators on Monday far outnumbered security forces stationed on the road. They stood atop orange buses, waving the flags of the opposition Indian National Congress party. Columns of police and other security officials, dressed in riot gear, watched.
The turnout signaled a show of strength for the long-beleaguered Congress party leader, Rahul Gandhi. He marched with a rambunctious crowd, at times flanked by his sister, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra. In an effort to portray a unified front against the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, Mr. Gandhi was also joined by Neha Bora, a leftist student activist, along with regional politicians from North India.
Mr. Gandhi’s lawyer filed a petition on his behalf in the Supreme Court, calling for an inquiry into the proceedings of the election commission. Its chief, Gyanesh Kumar, has been the target of more than a week of protests across India, by youth groups, opposition politicians, and ordinary citizens who say the election commission’s revision of the voter roll is a politically motivated purge of critics of the ruling party. Since it began last summer, the revision has expunged over 130 million names.
Together, months of protests over a wide range of frustrations about poor education and a lack of job opportunities represent the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his 12 years in office.
The government’s tactics on Monday, allowing the march to proceed mostly unimpeded, were a stark contrast to the intense crackdown on protests over the course of the last week, when would-be demonstrators were grabbed and stuffed into police vans.

nytimes.com.title: Dozens Killed in Airstrikes Near Sudan-Egypt Border
nytimes.com.text:
Dozens of gold workers in northern Sudan were killed over the weekend after warplanes bombed an open air mine near the Egyptian border, according to Sudanese rights groups, graphic video and eyewitnesses interviewed by The New York Times.
Footage from the aftermath of the bombing showed badly mutilated bodies of young men scattered amid sacks of mineral ore at a remote site in Red Sea State, roughly 25 miles from Sudan’s border with Egypt.
“We were overcome with terror,” said Saif Eldin Adam, 26, a university student who worked at the mine for the past three months. Mr. Adam said he helped rescue the wounded and recover the dead after the strikes.
“There are no words for what we saw,” he said.
Emergency Lawyers, a rights group, estimated the death toll at 72. Two eyewitnesses said it was at least 65, with another 120 or more wounded.
The attack occurred hundreds of miles from the front lines of Sudan’s devastating civil war. Sudanese media reports and several rights groups blamed the strike on Egypt. Last June, miners accused Egyptian forces of carrying out a drone attack on another gold mine in the same region.
Sudan mines billions of dollars in gold every year, with the two warring sides using the profits to bankroll their fight. Sudan’s military has bombed mines controlled by its enemy, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, in the far south of the country, in an effort to curtail a valuable source of finance.

cnn.com.title: The US is fighting over data centers. China is building them fast
cnn.com.text: The area appears like a high-tech mirage. Block after block of hulking data centers – both new and under construction – rise up seemingly out of nowhere from rolling plains and fields of sunflowers and sorghum. On their sides are some of the biggest names in Chinese tech – hardware giant Huawei, social media platform Kuaishou, service provider VNET – all packed into a zone thrumming with bustle and movement. This is Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, a Chinese city on the edge of the Gobi desert. It’s fast becoming one of the data hubs fueling a massive AI boom in China that’s made the country the only serious rival to the US’ ambitions to dominate the technology. Nearly 90 data centers are slated to be built in this city of fewer than two million people. As of last year, the US had roughly 10 times more AI data centers than China, according to Stanford University research – and vastly more computing power, other estimates show. American tech firms have something China’s don’t: access to the most advanced chips, the single most important ingredient for developing AI. But Ulanqab – with its growing number of AI and big-data centers – showcases the advantages on China’s side in the race for the technology that could define the 21st century. The towering units here were constructed at breakneck speed, with most of the densely packed Bayin Big Data Industrial Park taking shape in just two years, testament to China’s capacity to build fast. Heavy winds, beating sun and wide, open spaces give the area plentiful access to cheap green energy and land. And, crucially, throughout the Communist Party-run country, public opposition to the mass construction of data centers – the kind that is making headlines in the US – is non-existent. ‘With open arms’ At Ulanqab’s Bayin industrial park on a recent weekday, a steady stream of construction workers had their faces scanned as they filed past guards to enter building sites, while trucks rumbled along, feeding supplies to the facilities taking shape within. Outside their perimeters, vendors hawked noodles and cigarettes from makeshift stalls. The din of construction didn’t appear unwelcome to locals living nearby. Some who spoke to CNN said they were benefiting from the projects – and the influx of migrant construction workers that came with them to an area whose economy was otherwise largely reliant on agriculture. “Before, we’d just sit there and wait for customers. Now we’re constantly busy – picking up orders, doing this and that. We barely get a break,” said Ma Rong, 56, who has run a grocery store and guest house in the area for the past 30 years. “Our business has gotten much better than before,” he said. Some have been uprooted by changes sweeping the region, like restaurant owner Liu Baoping, 58, who said he had to leave his original business location due to the demolition of a highway. But he describes his daily clientele as doubling alongside the data-center buildout. “The environment isn’t as clean as before, but people’s incomes and the economy – it’s way better,” he said. Ulanqab is part of Beijing’s vision to rapidly scale up data infrastructure – a key priority for a government that sees AI as a crucial engine of growth for the country’s slowing economy with its shrinking population. “China has embraced AI with open arms,” Chinese leader Xi Jinping told a global artificial intelligence conference in Shanghai this past July. He pointed to China’s initiative to inject AI into sectors from health to home goods and hailed its push to embed AI in manufacturing as a “shining hallmark of Chinese modernization.” Already more than 700 million people use AI in China, according to official statistics. And the plan to weave AI across manufacturing, industry and daily life also requires massive amounts of compute. Beijing last month announced a $560 billion plan to rapidly scale up information infrastructure, including computing facilities, over the next five years. Private tech companies are also ramping up investment in AI infrastructure, though they still trail their Silicon Valley peers by a longshot. Such investment from listed Chinese companies will double this year to around $139 billion, according to research firm Rhodium Group. But that is still less than one-fifth of the $800 billion in AI data center investment from their US peers. And that’s not the only bottleneck. Chinese firms face another critical challenge: limits on the amount of high-end hardware available to fill these centers. Washington’s export bans restrict their access to the best AI chips, like certain models from Nvidia and AMD, while Beijing has restricted imports of some less powerful options. Domestic chipmakers are racing to catch up, but their tech still lags the US – and supplies of their cutting-edge models are tight. “If you look at the overall production cost of building a data center, chips are the most important factor, and they just don’t have enough,” said Nick Corvino, a researcher at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. But what China lacks in chips and capital, it’s trying make up for with an advantage: ample, affordable power, much of it green. Excess energy While energy-hungry data centers are straining an aging US grid that’s not expanded significantly in decades, China between 2022 and 2025 added capacity equivalent to that of industrial power sources across the entire US as of the end of 2025. And it has more green power than it can use: the country wasted enough excess green energy in the first six months of 2026 to power the entire country of Mexico for a year, findings from independent research organizations the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air and Global Energy Monitor suggest. Beijing wants data centers to sop up that excess – much of it in western, rural areas where sun, wind and land are plentiful – while boosting business for its green tech sector, under a plan known as “Eastern data, Western compute.” Under that strategy, first launched in 2022, China has designated eight national computing hubs – including several in its west – and 10 national data center clusters. Its latest five-year national economic blueprint elevated the linkage further, calling for pairing the build-out of computing infrastructure and green energy. “China’s trying to take advantage of the fact that it has this muscle memory for building energy (infrastructure) quickly,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Whereas for the US, we haven’t done this kind of grid buildout in a long time and so we are struggling on the power generation and grid connection front.” Abundant power can also help China make up for its less powerful domestic chips. Chinese chip designers like Huawei are combining clusters of chips to create the computing power of superior tech. The fix can be effective for some tasks, analysts say, but uses significantly more electricity. Observers say that even with ample power, Beijing’s vision has its limits. Some computing hubs in the west are too far away to handle certain tasks at the speeds needed for urban hubs in the densely-populated east. There’s also concern about so-called “ghost data centers” or ill-conceived projects in rural areas, built to fit a topline government initiative, yet lacking the hardware or users to justify the investment. But in hubs in Inner Mongolia, where optical cables can transmit data to Beijing – some 200 miles away – faster than the blink of an eye, and top players are pouring major resources, China’s vision appears to be taking shape. ‘Get prepared’ Long one of China’s top coal producers, the wind-swept region bordering Russia and Mongolia has more recently become a hub for green energy. Fields of solar panels blanket parts of Inner Mongolia, while the slender silhouettes of wind turbines spin above grazing sheep. Along some stretches of highway unused turbine blades line the roadsides like giant, fiberglass elephant tusks. In Ulanqab, which falls within one of China’s 10 national data center clusters, nearly half the grid draws from wind and solar – and some data center providers are finding ways to rely even more heavily on clean sources. Several miles from the thrumming construction of Ulanqab’s Bayin industrial park, the Envision “Galaxy Campus” is running one such model. Spanning more than 20 football fields and slated to be among the world’s largest by area when completed, this data center will be home to servers and chips from tech companies, used to handle queries users input into AI apps in places like Beijing. Upwards of 80% of the power for the facility will come directly from wind farms operated by the company, bypassing the grid completely, Envision says. Battery systems then store wind power, while a cutting-edge solid-state transformer can rapidly adjust how much power is feeding the servers, based on demand, according to Ricky Zheng, the facility’s general manager, who showed CNN around the under-construction campus on a recent day. Water is another key resource that’s sparked backlash against data centers in America, but Zheng says it’s not an issue here. The chilly climate in Ulanqab reduces the need for cooling overall, while the facility is running a so-called “zero-water” system that uses industrial alcohol as coolant, he says. Zheng also seemed optimistic when it comes to demand from tech companies for their facilities – and those clients’ ability to kit out server racks with needed hardware. The first phase of the planned total 2GW facility was already fully booked, he said, and the company was building additional phases, both for AI and cloud services. AI chips and servers “are owned by our off-takers,” he said. “When they give us the order to build such a big data center … they were confident to have enough infrastructure to be installed in these (server) racks.” And this company, like Ulanqab itself, is planning to be ready for an expected surge in AI demand in the coming years. “We designed this for the next 10 years,” said Zheng. “You need to get prepared for the future.”

cnn.com.title: Democrats are feeling America’s pain. Whether they can fix it is another question
cnn.com.text: Democrats may win the midterm election simply by exposing an unpopular president’s mirage of an economic “golden age.” But that won’t bring the price of groceries and gasoline down. On the campaign trail, Democratic candidates have effectively voiced the pain of families in the grip of the affordability crisis. They’re less good at nailing down specifics on how they plan to make life cheaper. And with the House looking increasingly likely to go blue and with Republicans sweating on the Senate, the question of whether Democrats could take tangible, fast action to ease Americans’ financial burden deserves more scrutiny. There’s some truth to President Donald Trump’s complaint that Democrats just turned the buzzword of “affordability” against him — especially since the Biden presidency saw inflation spike to its highest levels since the 1980s before falling back. “It’s fake,” Trump said at the GOP midterm convention. “They are so fake, because it was them that caused the affordability, to use their word, crisis.” Those are the breaks for an incumbent president — particularly one who called out the high price of groceries when he was running in 2024 and then failed to bring them down. Trump has been his own worst enemy, drowning out his own affordability plays — such as limiting taxes on tips and taking action to lower the prices of some prescription drugs — by choosing to wage Iran and tariff wars that sent costs soaring. But if Democrats were to win a share of Washington power on November 3, they’d also assume the burden of action — though their ability to reshape the economy would be constrained, in part by a president willing to wield his veto. That means a new Democratic Congress would have a greater capacity to thwart the most aggressive wielder of presidential power in modern history than to enact its own solutions. This could be a trap. Recent elections in the US and elsewhere in the democratic world show that voters quickly lose patience with parties that are elected to forge change but fail to deliver it. A Democratic honeymoon could therefore quickly fade. WWDD: What would Democrats do? As the midterms race into the final three weeks, Democrats contemplating the possibility of a restoration in Congress face three questions: In a midterm showdown dominated by Trump’s cacophony and controversy, there’s been less attention on detailed Democratic proposals for a potential House or Senate majority in the 120th Congress. It’s not that there are no plans — there are scores of them. Candidates, interest groups and think tanks are churning out ways to bring down the cost of housing, raise wages, restore benefits, overhaul healthcare, protect workers from AI, introduce universal child care, launch a house-building boom, and slash the cost of groceries and gasoline. Roy Cooper, the Democratic Senate nominee in North Carolina, touts his “Make Stuff Cost Less” plan. Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, who will appear at a CNN & Jubilee Town Hall on Wednesday, has a “New American Dream” agenda. Sen. Ruben Gallego has unveiled an expansive plan that includes a New Deal-style public service jobs program. Sen. Chuck Schumer could dust off a deeply detailed policy blueprint he futilely rolled out in a GOP Senate in January if Democrats win back the majority. But ideas won’t count for much without an actionable roadmap in what will be a fractured Washington if voters decide to deliver a rebuke to Trump next month. The country already intuits that turning to the Democrats won’t alone end an affordability crisis years in the making. In a CNN/SSRS poll in September, Democrats had a 7-point lead as the party Americans saw as closest to their views on the economy. But only 35% thought the party would have a mainly positive effect on the cost of living and a meager 27% said the same regarding their personal financial situation. Brainstorming does not equal actionable plans Democrats would need to move fast. There’s two things they think they could do. “If we don’t stop this war, if we don’t stop it now, we are going to continue to watch as the Iranian regime chokeholds the Strait of Hormuz, making our energy prices higher,” Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said at a debate this month. “And you are going to pay for it both at the gas tank and at the grocery store.” And Cooper told voters in July that “we need to roll back these chaotic tariffs, and Congress needs to take back its constitutional authority on that — because that’s ending up costing everyday people and small businesses.” In theory, a new Congress could end the war and overturn Trump’s tariffs. But it would be almost impossibly difficult. Democrats could try to block new supplemental spending for military operations in Iran and pass laws to restrict how broader military funds are spent. But it would be a high-risk move since Trump could accuse them of deserting American troops in a war zone and could use his veto to block legislation. The failure of a Democratic House to stop the Iraq war after the party’s 2006 midterm victory is a daunting omen. And a war powers showdown with Trump over the dubious legality of the war seems as likely to produce a constitutional morass as to end the conflict. Congress could overturn the remnants of Trump’s tariffs that survived the Supreme Court’s rescinding of duties built on emergency powers. But a veto-proof two-thirds majority against the president might be a stretch in the Senate even if Democrats had overall control. If Democrats can’t immediately change the nation’s course, their political messaging will be even more critical. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters in June that the first bill if the party wins the majority, HR.1, would be on affordability. “It will be hyper-focused on driving down the high cost of living and of course fixing our broken health care system as a part of that,” he said. His challenge would be in unifying the Democratic caucus behind proposed legislation given the ideological chasms between democratic socialists, progressives and moderates that were highlighted during this year’s primaries. Jeffries must hope for a larger majority than the minuscule one that has plagued GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson. But even if Democrats gain a healthy majority in the House, a Senate victory is unlikely to deliver anything but a narrowly divided chamber. Republicans will almost certainly still enjoy the capacity to block legislation if Democrats can’t amass 60 votes. Democratic priorities could be packaged into the kind of filibuster-proof reconciliation bills often used by the GOP. But presidents retain the veto — a power used, for example, by President Barack Obama to send back a GOP reconciliation bill in January 2016 that aimed to overturn the Affordable Care Act. How high hopes might be dashed It’s a quaint thought, but the US system of divided federal power does envisage compromise. Maybe Democrats could find an accommodation with Trump on housing affordability, prescription drug prices, child tax credits or infrastructure — issues that have interested the president in the past. But a promised Democratic onslaught of investigation targeting the Trump White House would surely precipitate a political cold war, making cooperation elusive. The most ambitious Democratic priorities — such as restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies — might only emerge from a show of strength in budget negotiations or potential government shutdowns. Such clashes are gambles for both parties. Elections perpetually conjure hope, promises and expectation. Divided government, however, usually results in bitter inertia. So an inevitable sequel may already be looming: yet another election, in 2028, on the same issue of affordability, as voters wait and wait for answers.

cnn.com.title: Trump holds raucous Ohio rally as he tries to shore up base voters for GOP
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump on Monday kicked off a week of red-state campaigning with a raucous rally in Ohio, where Republicans are fighting to hold onto a Senate seat that could be key to the majority. He spent portions of his nearly 90-minute remarks railing against Somali and Haitian communities, delivering red meat political attacks and catering to his base. He at times conjured two out-of-state Democrats — Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar and Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed — as bigger threats than former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who’s giving GOP Sen. Jon Husted a run for his money in a state that Trump had turned into a reliably red bastion. After Ohio, Trump’s scheduled to hit Alaska and Montana — states he won by 13 and 20 points in 2024 — as his team banks on him juicing base turnout in conservative areas. But on Monday night — as Trump returned to the same arena where he held a packed 2017 ‘thank you’ tour — large sections of seating on the left and right of the press riser, which came with prime views of the president, were empty. Still, it was a much livelier affair than some recent rallies, with two significant interruptions. At one point, a brawl appeared to break out between a protester wearing a “Release The Epstein Files” t-shirt and a rally-goer in the stands. Another interruption came from a young woman holding a Mexican flag. A big part of Trump’s pitch was about immigration, returning to a theme he hit hard in 2024, when he repeated his false claim that Haitian migrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating their neighbors’ pets. “Just look at what’s happening in the once great state of Minnesota,” he said, teeing up his attacks on Omar — a frequent target of his ire. Federal officers executed a search warrant early Monday at the Washington, DC-area home of the congresswoman, according to a Justice Department spokesperson and a source familiar with the matter. And while Trump insisted he was not involved in that search, he went on to call Omar — who’s a US citizen — a “disaster” and attack the country where she was born. “[Rep. Omar] comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, without — all they do is shoot each other — and she comes into our country, and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right,’” Trump said. “She’s got a constitutional right? She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.” As he launched into into a tirade against Somalis in the US, supporters in the audience began chanting “Deport!” “They think they’re in Somalia, where they don’t have pants to wear,” Trump said at one point, going on to repeat his insult about “low IQ people.” He made blue-state Minnesota the foil. “If you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked, and destroyed like Minnesota’s being destroyed, we’re going to stop it. Just like we did with Springfield, we’re going to stop it,” Trump said. When the president turned to Brown — who holds a 6-point lead over Husted in CNN polling released last week — he tried to link the former three-term incumbent to national Democrats in more generic terms. “Sherrod Brown is the candidate of the Marxists, the communists, the anti-American radicals, who want to tear down America’s heritage,” Trump said, arguing that he also wants the Midwest “turned into Mogadishu.” Brown, a progressive populist first elected to the Senate in 2006, held onto his seat in 2018, during Trump’s first term, but lost reelection while on the ballot with Trump in 2024. “So, what happens is every time I run, we do great,” Trump said, repeating his call for voters to “pretend” he’s on the ballot this year. The first days of early voting in Ohio showed signs Democrats are more enthusiastic to vote, with affiliated Democrats making up larger shares of pre-election voters than they did two years ago, even in the most Republican parts of the state, according to data from the secretary of state’s office last week. (But Republicans in recent years have much been much more likely to vote early in person or on Election Day.) Trump seemed to tacitly acknowledge Ohioans’ previous tendency to back Brown, arguing that a vote for the former senator could have much wider ramifications. “It’s one vote, but that one vote can steer Congress into a direction that you’re not going to be happy with. And it’s not Ohio values.”

cnn.com.title: Trump is playing to his base in red-state campaign swing. But he’s often been dismissive of those voters
cnn.com.text: It’s been more than 10 years since President Donald Trump quipped, “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose voters.” His base isn’t nearly so devoted to him these days. But he still returned to the theme this weekend during one of his many recent stops in deep-red territory where Republicans hope he’ll turn out the base for the November midterms. “When you stand up here, it’s just like the love,” Trump said at a rally in Tennessee. “I could say the stupidest things, and you clap. ‘Oh, I love you so.’” Both comments were couched as jokes, but both also pointed to a perception that Trump is happy to feed: that his base is almost cultishly devoted to him — as if they are unthinking automatons. A number of former Trump associates and advisers have said these kinds of comments betray a certain contempt that Trump has for his voters. And over the years, he has assembled a lengthy volume of comments that could be understood to be similarly dismissive of the base voters who Republicans are pinning their midterm hopes on. Let’s recap. January 2016: ‘I could be the worst person in the world’ Before Trump’s “Fifth Avenue” comment, he tried out a different version. “One of the things that came out in the one poll — nobody’s ever leaving me,” he said in New Hampshire in 2016, according to NBC News. “I could be the worst person in the world, they’re not leaving.” Trump said that even if he did “some really inappropriate things, my people stay.” January 2016: The ‘Fifth Avenue’ quote “I have the most loyal people — did you ever see that?” Trump said in Sioux Center, Iowa, adding: “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose voters.” He added: “It’s, like, incredible.” February 2016: He could get away with ‘anything’ “Even the really dishonest press says Trump’s people are the most incredible,” he said in Sparks, Nevada, just before the state’s caucuses. “I mean I had already 68% would not leave under any circumstances,” he added. “I think that means murder. I think it means anything.” February 2016: ‘I love the poorly educated’ After winning the caucuses, Trump pointed to his superior polling numbers among voters with less formal education, which has been one of his most loyal demographics over the years. But he rather provocatively called them the “poorly educated” — repeatedly. “We won with young. We won with old. We won with highly educated. We won with poorly educated,” Trump said, adding: “I love the poorly educated.” August 2016: Asking Black voters: ‘What the hell do you have to lose?’ In making an appeal to Black voters, Trump offered a pretty dismal review of their conditions. “Look, what do you have to lose?” he said in Michigan. “You live in your poverty, your schools are no good, you have no jobs, 58% of your youth is unemployed. What the hell do you have to lose?” 2020: Complaining about having to visit certain places As CNN’s Kevin Liptak noted late in the 2020 campaign, Trump’s pitch to voters often included saying he wouldn’t have visited their locales if he didn’t have to. He often pointed to the freezing weather. “Before the plague [Covid] came in, I had it made. I wasn’t coming to Erie,” Trump said in Pennsylvania. “I mean, I have to be honest: There’s no way I was coming.” June 2024: ‘I don’t care about you; I just want your vote’ In another jokey comment, Trump told people assembled in stifling heat in Las Vegas that he needed them to live so they could deliver for him at the ballot box. “Do you feel the breeze? ’Cause I don’t want anybody going on me,” Trump said. “We need every voter. I don’t care about you; I just want your vote. I don’t care.” A joke, sure. The crowd laughed. But six rallygoers were hospitalized for heat-related illness. July 2025: Calling Epstein-focused supporters ‘weaklings’ “Their new SCAM is what we will forever call the Jeffrey Epstein Hoax, and my PAST supporters have bought into this ‘bullshit,’ hook, line, and sinker,” Trump wrote on social media about the push to release more documents related to Jeffrey Epstein. “They haven’t learned their lesson, and probably never will, even after being conned by the Lunatic Left for 8 long years.” Trump called these people “weaklings” who “do the Democrats work.” (Left unsaid: The fact that many of those who had pushed this story before he returned to office were his own high-profile supporters. That included some who went on to serve in major roles, such as FBI Director Kash Patel.) Saturday: ‘I could say the stupidest things, and you clap’ “When you stand up here, it’s just like the love,” Trump said in Tennessee. “I could say the stupidest things, and you clap. ‘Oh, I love you so.’ It’s true.” After some laughter, the president assured that isn’t what he actually does. “But we don’t say the stupidest things,” he said. “We say things of common sense.”

cnn.com.title: Hackers heat French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and spoiling food
cnn.com.text: Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers ​at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), causing fires and spoiling food. The Paris prosecutor’s office said on Monday ‌that a “large-scale” attack was “affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France,” leading to food losses and fires. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a person in his office said. France was coordinating with European counterparts because other countries could also be affected, the person said, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk. Felix Aime, a senior cyber threat intelligence analyst ​at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected. Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were hit, while Monoprix, which operates about 490 ​stores in France, said 5 per cent of its stores were affected. Les Mousquetaires, owner of retailer Intermarche, said fridges at around 150 of its ⁠stores were heated up to 50 C for six hours overnight. A spokesperson said all affected food had been discarded to eliminate health risks. Paris resident Geert de Clercq witnessed staff ​at an Intermarche in central Paris throwing cartfuls of defrosted frozen foods into a giant trash container, with molten ice cream sloshing out of broken tubs on the street. Cooperative U CEO ​Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket group had also been targeted. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he wrote on X. Food retailers E.Leclerc and Auchan did not respond to requests for comment. There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV the “unprecedented” attack would represent losses amounting to “tens ​of millions of euros nationwide in a single day.” Christel Delberghe, director general at European retail association Eurocommerce, said, “This incident underlines the importance of resilience across the entire supply chain.” Cold aisles controlled over internet Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store’s fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere. The source ‌close to ⁠Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss. Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”. The affected units “were running outdated firmware,” Danfoss said, adding that it had “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions.” On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty’s Team82 published research detailing vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller. According to the report, software updates issued by Danfoss addressed issues that could have allowed attackers to bypass ​authentication controls and execute code on compromised devices. The ​attacks resemble disruptions reported at about a ⁠dozen US military commissaries in late August that led to food losses after fridges were affected. In a statement, French retail association Fédération du Commerce et de la Distribution called for “full transparency” from Danfoss about the incident. It said supermarkets aimed to protect consumers and return to ​normal operations as soon as possible. The FCD said some impacted stores were already back up and running. Dutch security issue Dutch retailer ​Ahold Delhaize, which operates the ⁠Netherlands’ largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has major operations in the US, said it was dealing with a “security issue” on its network and had taken several systems offline as a precaution. A message on the retailer’s smartphone app said it was unable to deliver groceries because of a “cybersecurity incident”. Online orders account for about 10 per cent of Albert Heijn sales. Physical stores remained open, while Dutch news ⁠agency ANP ​reported that rival retailers had seen a surge in delivery orders. Ahold Delhaize said there was no reason to ​see a link between the incidents in France and its supermarkets. Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US. Websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion chains displayed notices saying “site temporarily down”.

cnn.com.title: New White House press secretary has a history of conspiracy-laced social media posts
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump’s incoming White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, repeatedly made baseless accusations of pedophilia against prominent Democrats and shared conspiracy-related content, including claims that echoed the debunked “Pizzagate” theory and that Hollywood elites were pedophilic cannibals, according to a CNN KFile review of her social media posts. The posts, many from 2022, reveal a history of inflammatory rhetoric and conspiracy-related content from a woman now poised to become one of the administration’s most visible spokespeople. Zacharia also has a record of since-deleted social media activity that shows her advocating for hardline policies and criticizing the administration she is now poised to represent. She pushed for more aggressive action on immigration, suggesting in a series of now-deleted posts from June 2025 that the administration should suspend habeas corpus for migrants because the circumstances justified invoking the Constitution’s exception for cases of rebellion or invasion. The fundamental legal protection allows people to challenge their detention in court. Zacharia also publicly criticized the direction of Trump’s second administration, warning Republicans of a potential midterm “bloodbath” in a now-deleted tweet. In another deleted tweet, she shared a post accusing the Justice Department of covering up for people implicated in the Jeffrey Epstein scandal. She also promoted on Truth Social a repost that claimed that comedian Joan Rivers died mysteriously after saying that former President Barack Obama was gay and that former first lady Michelle Obama had a penis. In response to questions about her previous social media activity, Zacharia said in a statement to CNN, “I am grateful to serve President Trump as Press Secretary, and I will diligently and effectively amplify his successful agenda.” In another statement, Steven Cheung, White House communications director, told CNN, “Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team. She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.” Neither the White House nor Zacharia addressed the content of the posts. Some of Zacharia’s since-deleted posts on X were first reported by The Bulwark. Her posts on Truth Social, the social media platform founded by Trump where she worked as communications adviser, remain publicly available on her account. In posts on Truth Social in 2022, Zacharia repeatedly accused prominent political figures and Hollywood elites of pedophilia, at times invoking conspiracy theories about powerful people sexually abusing children. “Pedo Podesta. #pedoPodesta,” Zacharia wrote in a September 2022 post about John Podesta, a longtime Democratic political operative and former White House chief of staff who had been a central target of the debunked Pizzagate conspiracy theory. The false theory emerged during the 2016 presidential election after Russian-linked hackers released emails belonging to Podesta, then Hillary Clinton’s campaign chairman. Conspiracy theorists falsely claimed the emails contained coded references to child sex trafficking and that Clinton and other prominent Democrats were operating a child sex abuse ring out of the basement of Comet Ping Pong, a pizzeria in Washington, DC. The restaurant did not even have a basement, and the baseless claims had real-world consequences when in December 2016, a North Carolina man armed with a rifle entered the restaurant and fired shots while attempting to investigate the supposed trafficking ring. Days after her first post on Podesta, Zacharia tagged Fox News host Sean Hannity and Trump in another post, asking why Fox News didn’t do a “feature” on “what a pedophile Podesta is.” In another post, Zacharia wrote, “The radical left Hollywood elitists are sick pedo cannibals. Change my mind,” responding to a September 2022 Variety article about actor Timothée Chalamet receiving a standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival for his role in “Bones and All,” a film about two young cannibals in love. Just weeks after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Zacharia also posted seemingly in support of Vladimir Putin, reposting a post that the Russian president was fighting a secret network of powerful elites. “Putin is at war with the CABAL - and the Ukraine is in bed with them,” read the post from an account named Richard Tomas, which included an image featuring prominent political figures, including Hillary Clinton, Barack Obama, Joe Biden and billionaire George Soros. Zacharia also reposted a baseless claim from Ali Alexander, a far-right activist who helped organize the “Stop the Steal” movement that promoted false claims of widespread election fraud following Trump’s 2020 defeat. “Democrats want to mask and rape your children. That’s their satanic platform,” Alexander wrote in an April 2022 post that Zacharia shared. Zacharia also reposted a September 2022 post from a Truth Social account called “Oinker” that compared then-President Joe Biden and anti-fascist protesters to Nazis, using the hashtags “#Antifa,” “#PedoHitler” and “#WrongSideOfHistory.” Zacharia also reposted the baseless conspiracy theory about former first lady Michelle Obama and the death of Joan Rivers. “Remember that time Joan Rivers said Obama was gay and Michelle had a dick then suddenly died?” read the July 2022 post that Zacharia shared. In another since-deleted tweet, Zacharia expressed frustration with the direction of Trump’s second administration, warning that the GOP could face devastating losses in the 2026 midterm elections if they didn’t shift course. In a December 2025 post, Zacharia responded to far-right commentator Mike Cernovich, who had criticized figures in the administration for focusing on media appearances, podcasts and cryptocurrency schemes rather than delivering on their promises. “We had our chance to save our country,” Cernovich wrote, lamenting that prominent figures were instead pursuing “vanity fair interviews, podcasts, and meme coins.” “2026 Midterms will be a bloodbath if we don’t shift course now,” Zacharia replied. Zacharia also amplified an accusation that the Trump administration’s Justice Department was covering up for people involved in Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual abuse of minors. On July 8, 2025, Zacharia retweeted a post from right-wing commentator Rogan O’Handley, known online as DC Draino, that questioned whether the Justice Department could be trusted. “I wish I could get excited about this,” the post read, discussing Trump plans to investigate former FBI Director James Comey and other officials involved in the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. “But if the DOJ will cover up for Epstein pedos, how can we trust them to go after these guys?” The repost came just a day after the Justice Department and FBI released a memo concluding that investigators had found no evidence of an Epstein “client list,” and no credible evidence that Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals. The memo had sparked backlash from prominent Trump supporters, many of whom accused then-Attorney General Pam Bondi and other administration officials of concealing information about Epstein after years of promises to release additional records. In June 2025, Zacharia also called for suspending the constitutional right to challenge one’s detention in court. “Suspend habeas corpus,” she wrote in one post, first reported by The Bulwark. In two replies to White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, she urged suspending it “for reasons of Invasion,” citing the Constitution’s clause allowing suspension “in Cases of Rebellion or Invasion.” Miller had said weeks earlier that the administration was “actively looking at” the option.

cnn.com.title: Fact check: Trump posts fake quote of Denzel Washington supposedly praising him
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump has shared another fake quote on social media, this time a fabricated comment in which “Denzel Washington” supposedly heaps praise upon him. The phony quote that Trump’s Monday post wrongly attributed to the legendary actor has previously been wrongly attributed to fellow celebrities Mick Jagger and Matthew McConaughey, the fact-checking website Snopes reported. Fictitious claims about Washington publicly declaring himself a Trump supporter have circulated online for years. Washington has generally kept a low political profile, but federal records show he made donations to support Democratic presidential candidates Barack Obama in 2008 and Hillary Clinton, who ran against Trump, in 2016. Trump has long used his social media accounts to both make his own false claims and amplify false claims from others, including conspiracy theories and imaginary quotes. In 2019, he shared a glowing but fake quote about himself that an obscure account had wrongly attributed to former President Ronald Reagan. This spring, he shared a fake quote attacking Obama that a pro-Trump commentator had wrongly attributed to Republican Sen. John Kennedy. Trump posted the fake praise wrongly attributed to Washington on Monday morning. The president’s post, on his Truth Social platform, was an image of a Saturday post made by a pro-Trump X account called “Red Eagle Updates.” That post said “BOOM,” and then quoted Washington as supposedly saying this: “I’ve worked with a lot of people in my life, and I’ve never met anyone braver, smarter, or who cares more about America than Donald Trump. He’s a great friend and an even better president. I’m proud to be a steadfast supporter, and I’ll never apologize for it.” Media outlets including MeidasTouch and Mediaite noted Monday morning that the supposed quote was fake. Alan Nierob, a representative for Washington, confirmed to The Washington Post that the quote was “not real” and said he had “no idea where it came from.”

cnn.com.title: Do you have questions about AI safety risks? We want to hear from you
cnn.com.text: The past several weeks have brought a rash of dire warnings about artificial intelligence posing existential risks to humanity. A string of workers have resigned from leading AI labs over concerns around AI potentially causing human extinction. Some AI leaders have called to slow down its development. Yet others say these fears are overblown and no new regulations are needed to keep AI safe. CNN wants to better understand your big questions around these extreme AI safety risks. What feels unclear to you? What would you like to hear from the experts or AI leaders?

cnn.com.title: MAGA watches another conspiracy theory blow up in its face
cnn.com.text: Two weeks ago, GOP Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri saw his conspiracy theory about former special counsel Jack Smith implode spectacularly at a congressional hearing for all to see. Rather than seemingly learning a lesson from that episode, the MAGA movement in recent days embraced another sketchy theory that quickly fell apart — that Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico was missing from the campaign trail because of a mental health episode. There have been plenty of such episodes this year. And it’s hardly just random social media accounts. The Talarico example is especially astounding for its reach. The idea that Talarico’s lengthy absence from the campaign trail was not due to the flu (as his campaign said), but rather a mental health episode quickly spread far and wide. Over just a few days, it went from an admitted rumor; to some like former Los Angeles GOP mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt claiming they had actual sources; to winks and nods from Talarico’s GOP opponent Ken Paxton and President Donald Trump; to right-wing sites covering the still-baseless claims; to some attempted independent journalism that has been repeatedly promoted by Elon Musk. By Sunday afternoon, a pair of right-wing influencers shared audio of what they said was a call with a mental health center in Ohio seemingly confirming that Talarico had just been released from its facility. “Looks like he was just discharged this evening,” a voice is heard saying. “That’s why I don’t have it.” The story then exploded on the right. But it just as quickly fell apart: Some on the right are now deleting their posts about the false claim. Others like former Trump adviser Caroline Wren are walking back the significance of the claim. One of the two right-wing influencers who shared the audio, Nick Sortor, appeared at the White House last year during a roundtable on antifa. For what it’s worth, as CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski has noted, Talarico did a virtual event on September 30 where he said he had the flu and looked physically unwell. He was then off the campaign trail for nine days — not the two weeks that many on the right have claimed — before reemerging publicly on October 9. Talarico also has type 1 diabetes, which can make flu symptoms worse. But for the MAGA movement, this is merely the latest conspiratorial episode. Two weeks ago, it was Schmitt presenting what he seemed to view as smoking-gun evidence that Smith had been at an Atlanta Hawks game in February 2024 and — the theory seemed to go — might have been coordinating with local prosecutors who had indicted Trump in Fulton County, Georgia. Except it turned out Smith was actually at a basketball game in Maryland that night. And even if he was in Atlanta, it would have proven basically nothing. Back in July, MAGA figures led the charge in embracing rumors and even flat-out claiming that GOP Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky — an unpopular figure among Trump supporters since he declared the president lost the 2020 election — was brain dead, amid his much-longer absence from public view. GOP Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin even cited a claim that a photo of McConnell was AI-generated, before later backing off. A GOP House member even said he didn’t know whether McConnell was alive. McConnell later returned to the Senate. Over the summer, many on the right embraced Trump’s baseless conspiracy theory that vandals had sabotaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. A conservative reporter posted supposed video proof. Trump’s Justice Department even indicted a former Olympian. But the Justice Department later acknowledged that the damage “was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism.” In June, Republicans far and wide — including elected officials — suddenly promoted theories suggesting voter fraud was to blame for Pratt failing to make the runoff in the Los Angeles mayor’s race. Except the theory rested on a complete misreading of the data and was debunked even by Trump’s DOJ and a top local GOP official. Pratt’s showing was also very much in line with how Republicans usually perform there. And, strategically, it would have made no sense for incumbent Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass to rig the system to promote a fellow Democrat, who would have a better chance at beating her in the runoff than Pratt. And in February, many on the right shared supposedly damning evidence from right-wing influencer Nick Shirley citing 30 allegedly illegal voter registrations at a UPS Store in San Diego. Those promoting the story included Donald Trump Jr., who accused the media of ignoring it. But fact-checkers noted that the UPS Store was actually on the ground floor of a mixed-use building with residential units above it. California elections officials said none of the registrations used the UPS Store’s suite number. Of course, it’s entirely possible that the people promoting these theories don’t necessarily believe them — and that they just see value in promoting them, regardless of how true they are. Some MAGA influencers, after all, continued to promote Schmitt’s theory even after it fell apart. It would seem especially expedient to promote such rumors about Talarico, given he has continued to lead Paxton in some Texas Senate polls and could give Democrats a crucial win in their quest for a Senate majority. Or, as one participant on an X Spaces event about the Talarico story put it on Sunday: “Whether it’s true or not, people deserve to know the potential of this.” Regardless of whether these people have a gullibility problem, the MAGA echo chamber now has a well-established credibility problem. This story has been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: Judge ‘furious’ as 430 trees are chopped down from golf course Trump wants to renovate
cnn.com.text: A federal judge on Monday said she was “furious” with the Trump administration’s move over the weekend to cut down at least 430 trees from a Washington, DC, public golf course that President Donald Trump is seeking to renovate. US District Judge Ana Reyes, who is overseeing a legal challenge to Trump’s plans to overhaul the East Potomac Golf Course, put a tentative hold on any further tree removal through Tuesday afternoon after an emergency hearing Monday. “I actually don’t think courts should be playing ‘Parks and Rec,” Reyes said, but she believed that, without any order from the court, the administration would move forward with chopping down hundreds of more trees. “So now we are all going to have a massive fire drill because the government can’t be trusted,” she said. Reyes began the hearing by telling Justice Department attorneys they had lost “credibility” with her because they gave less than a day’s notice before cutting down the trees. “More than just being upset and furious right now, I am just beyond disappointed with the government,” Reyes said. When a DOJ attorney said they had done their “best” to give her and the plaintiffs a heads-up, the judge said, her voice raised, “No, you did your absolute worst.” “I am thoroughly unamused right now,” Reyes also said. She demanded that two National Park Service officials appear at the virtual hearing, which lasted more than three hours, to testify about how the plans to remove the trees came to be. The project came out of an October 5 meeting, one of the officials testified, during which the official was told to carry out a seven-year-old proposal seeking to restore the course’s “cultural” heritage. Reyes said the officials failed to provide any reason for why hundreds of trees needed to be removed so suddenly. She will hold another hearing next week with an order that a top Trump appointee at the Interior Department, as well as the acting head of the National Parks Service, be prepared to testify. After a Justice Department questioned the relevance of the testimony, the judge said it appeared the court had been misled about the administration’s plans for the course. “The question goes to whether or not I have been lied to, whether I have been lied to in declarations about the plans, whether I have been lied to about the timing of things,” Reyes, who was appointed to the bench by President Joe Biden, said. The park is one of several renovation projects Trump is working on in Washington, DC. The administration’s desire to turn the public course into a professional course — a renovation that could cost between $20 million and $49 million — has been wrapped up in litigation and angered those who fear it may take away a public and affordable place to play golf in the nation’s capital. The Interior Department first gave notice of the tree removal plans on Friday evening in a filing describing the tree-chopping as part of a long-standing maintenance plan that was not connected to “renovation or redesign of the Golf Course.” Crews were at the park by Saturday morning chopping down the trees. Kevin Griess, the superintendent of the National Mall and Memorial Parks, testified Monday that his office came up with the plan last week that identified the specific trees that were to be cut down. His office had planned to remove another 100-plus trees from other areas of the park. He said the removal plan was moving forward now because resources and NPS workforce that had been surged for the America 250 events over the summer had recently become available. He said the only awareness he had of Trump’s own plan to redo the golf course was from social media. Griess’ office was carrying out a directive from a top National Park Service official, who had told them last week to carry out a 2019 plan known as the Cultural Landscapes Report. The report proposed making East Potomac and other golf courses look more in line with how they looked when they first opened. That official, Frank Lands, the NPS deputy director of operations, said he was given the instruction to implement 2019 recommendations at an October 5 meeting with Greg Wischer, a political appointee, who is the Interior Department’s deputy chief of staff. Lands said he was told to execute the plan as soon as “practicable,” while doing so in a way that was safe, didn’t disrupt golf play and that completed the appropriate environmental reviews. Neither official could answer the judge’s questions about how much the tree removal project will ultimately cost taxpayers. Lands said that before last week, he had been involved in some discussions the 2019 cultural recommendations and that some of those discussions also touched how those recommendations would fit with Trump’s plans for remaking the golf course, but Lands wasn’t “privy” to those details. Lands revealed that two or three months ago, he met with premiere golf course architect Tom Fazio and showed him the course, but the official testified he had not spoken to Fazio or the White House about Trump’s proposed renovation since then. At the conclusion of the hearing, Reyes noted that some of the same agency officials who were involved in carrying out the recent tree removal had submitted court declarations asserting that there were no concrete plans to implement Trump’s proposed overhaul for the golf course. Reyes accused the administration of “double speak” and said it was “preposterous” for the officials to think that they didn’t have to include the tree removal plans in their court declarations. She will also issue an order requiring the administration to give 72 hours notice of any plans for the golf course, tree removal or otherwise, while the case plays out. This story has been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: One teen killed, others wounded, after explosion on Israeli school trip near Lebanon border
cnn.com.text: One teenager was killed and others were wounded, according to Israeli emergency response services, after an explosion on an Israeli school trip near the Lebanon border. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said an initial review by soldiers at the scene indicated that explosion was caused by an unexploded Hezbollah munition that had fallen in the area. It’s unclear when the projectile was fired. Pictures released by the IDF showed a military helicopter evacuating patients for medical treatment. “Apparently, the suspicion is that an unexploded munition of some kind exploded in the hands of one of the students,” said Deputy Police Commissioner Meir Eliyahu, a commander in Israel’s northern district, according to Reuters. According to United Hatzalah, an Israeli emergency response service, three people sustained serious injuries in the explosion, while at least 10 others suffered light-to-moderate injuries. The wounded were evacuated to three hospitals in the area, police said. In a statement, the Ma’alot-Tarshiha municipality in northern Israel said students and staff were on the local school’s annual trip when the explosion happened. The country’s Ministry of Education said it was an “extremely difficult incident, and our thoughts are with the victims and their families.” Commissioner Daniel Levy told Reuters it was a “very serious incident, in which children who went on a field trip were hurt, to our sorrow.” On Monday evening, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, along with Israel’s education minister, visited the wounded and their families at Rambam Hospital in Haifa. Netanyahu instructed the IDF to reinforce the prohibitions against touching unexploded ordinance. Shortly after the explosion occurred on Monday afternoon, Israel Police said the initial suspicion was that the explosion was a result of an unexploded munition along the border near the villages of Yiftah and Manara. Bomb disposal experts were dispatched to examine the cause of the explosion, police said. MDA said it was a “complex incident” as they sent numerous teams to the site. “We quickly dispatched substantial forces to the scene, including ambulances, mobile intensive care units (MICUs), and an MDA helicopter, which was also scrambled to the incident,” said regional director Itzik Shushan. A US-brokered ceasefire in late-June was supposed to end months of conflict in southern Lebanon as it paved the way for the deployment of the Lebanese military and the gradual withdrawal of the IDF. Israel pulled back from two small areas along the so-called yellow line that demarcates the zone occupied by the Israeli military, but further progress on the agreement has largely stalled. Israel has razed entire villages in southern Lebanon and has continued to carry out regular strikes there as it tries to remove Hezbollah from the territory.

cnn.com.title: Inside the Kenyan manufacturer betting on Africa’s industrial future
cnn.com.text: In a central Nairobi factory, a steady stream of household, hair and skincare products rolls off the production line. HACO Industries makes around 90 products designed for African consumers. Its brands reach more than 3 million families across the continent, while raw materials are sourced from more than 500 farmers in Africa. For Mary-Ann Musangi, whose family launched HACO more than 50 years ago, the opportunity lies in making products on the continent for people whose needs the business recognizes. “How do we reach African consumers with products that they want and need, manufactured by a company that understands them — understands African skin, African hair and African needs?” she said. HACO currently exports to eight African countries. Kenya is its largest market, but it also has a presence in Uganda, Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia. “Distances can be a challenge and African logistics is one of the key challenges in terms of penetrating across the continent,” Musangi said. The company’s plastics plant, which produces the packaging for its products, has the capacity to produce 5 million components a month, according to its manufacturing director, Peter Ndichu. A separate plant has the capacity to process and pack 1,365 metric tons of products monthly. HACO is trying to strengthen its supply chain by buying more ingredients within Africa. The company works with small and medium-sized suppliers of natural oils, offering technical support to help them meet its quality standards. Shea butter is now sourced from Uganda or Ghana. Ndichu said HACO previously imported it from the United States for 5,000 Kenyan shillings ($38.50) per kilogram, compared with 1,000 shillings ($7.70) per kilogram from Uganda. HACO is now looking to automate more of its operations. “In terms of packing, we are currently achieving 3,000 pieces in an hour,” said Ndichu. Automated machinery could quadruple that to roughly 12,000 items an hour, he said, adding that HACO plans to build a new factory to accommodate the upgrades. Hubs and partnerships To support its goal of exporting to 30 African countries by 2030, HACO plans to establish five regional hubs across Africa. Ghana is set to become its West African manufacturing base, from which products can be exported to neighboring markets. Musangi said collaborating with local companies will be essential for expansion. “Africa is so fragmented in many ways: the countries, the boundaries, our taxation laws, our policies, our culture, our language, our money, currency. We’ve got to see, how do we reduce these points of fragmentation?” she explained. “The only way I see we can do it is through these partnerships, working with local people.” In Ghana, HACO is partnering with Ayewa Labs, a product development and manufacturing firm specializing in making goods from African ingredients. Founder Nanayaa Bates said the African Continental Free Trade Area — which came into effect in 2019 and is the world’s largest free-trade area by number of countries — is helping the company attract clients from other African countries. HACO supplies raw materials for Ayewa, which then manufactures products for other companies beyond Ghana. Bates said the partnership had increased Ayewa’s manufacturing output tenfold. Making more in Africa Manufacturing is seen as an important route to economic growth and job creation across Africa, yet in many countries it accounted for less than 15% of gross domestic product in 2023. Musangi argues that African countries should retain more of the value generated by their raw materials. “It is unacceptable that we continue to simply extract raw materials from Africa and send them out to the West for them to manufacture and send us the finished product to consume at much higher prices,” she said. “We have the technical skills,” Musangi added. “Our youth are highly skilled and highly educated. We need to make sure that we develop and continue developing the manufacturing sector so that we can add value to these raw materials.”

cnn.com.title: Elon Musk emerges as the top booster for Republicans with $276 million in donations
cnn.com.text: Elon Musk has poured at least $276 million into the midterms since the summer, re-emerging as the top known donor to the Republican Party. A spokesperson for Musk’s main political group, America PAC, confirmed the figure on Monday, three days before a key campaign finance disclosure deadline. A majority of Musk’s latest giving — $158 million — went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the top Republican super PAC in Senate races, according to the spokesperson. The group is currently spending big to retain a Senate seat in Texas, a state that is hugely important to Musk’s business empire. The figure, which covers Musk’s giving from July onward, was first reported by The New York Times. Musk, the world’s richest person, donated nearly $300 million during the 2024 campaign to help Donald Trump win the presidential election. The financial support made him a top target of Democrats, especially as he returned to Washington with Trump to lead the Department of Government Efficiency, a government cost-cutting project. Musk said in May 2025 that he would “do a lot less” political spending in the future, and he later fell out with Trump over his signature tax and domestic policy law. But their relationship has appeared to improve since then, and Trump last week honored Musk with the National Medal of Science. Musk’s apparent interest in Texas comes as the state’s GOP attorney general, Ken Paxton, is in a tight Senate race against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico. Texas has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994. The Senate Leadership Fund has poured well over $100 million into the Texas contest. The group has said the massive red-state outlay is coming from a “dedicated” fund and not diverting resources away from other competitive Senate races. Thursday is the deadline for campaigns and certain political action committees, including America PAC, to report their finances to the Federal Election Commission for the past three months.

cnn.com.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar responds after federal officers search her home
cnn.com.text: Federal officers executed a search warrant early Monday at the Washington, DC-area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, the Minnesota Democrat who has been the persistent target of ire from President Donald Trump’s administration, according to a Justice Department spokesperson and a source familiar with the matter. The congresswoman is running for reelection and the search warrant was executed only weeks before the midterms. It is unusual for the Justice Department to take such an aggressive investigative step toward a candidate so close to an election. Voting is well underway in Minnesota, with more than 127,000 people having already voted, according to data from the secretary of state. The Department of Justice said in a statement Monday that investigators from Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of the Department of Homeland Security that handles criminal investigations, “executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice.” “This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” a DOJ spokesperson said. The statement did not indicate what the investigation entailed. Omar called the search “the latest escalation” in Trump’s “campaign of political intimidation.” “I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” she wrote on X. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.” Later on Monday, Trump called Omar “a terrible person,” but insisted he was not involved in the search of her home. “I understand they’re looking at her very carefully – I’ve always found her to be a totally crooked person,” the president told reporters at the White House, adding the search on Monday “has nothing to do with me.” “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ, I have nothing to do with it,” he said. House Democratic leaders called the search “deeply disturbing” and said it “raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries.” “For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Whip Katherine Clark and caucus Chair Pete Aguilar said in a statement, adding that it comes with “less than 30 days until the midterm election.” A spokesperson for the congresswoman said in a statement to CNN, “For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back … The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong.” While authorities have not said what prompted the search, administration officials have previously indicated that Omar was facing an investigation. White House border czar Tom Homan said on Fox News last month that “things are going on” in relation to Omar, before adding: “But I can’t give the specifics of what’s happening.” Speaking to Fox on Monday morning, Homan confirmed the search warrant was executed, but provided no other information. “The specifics of the investigation, I think I need to turn that over to Todd Blanche or Markwayne Mullin,” he said, referring to the attorney general and DHS secretary. “I don’t want to get ahead of them commenting on an ongoing investigation.” One of Omar’s neighbors told CNN they were awoken around 4:30 a.m. Monday to the sounds of banging on doors. Later that morning, CNN observed that the home was surrounded by Homeland Security Investigations officers and that investigators were removing boxes from the home. Before leaving the scene, officials used a camera to document the condition of the house. Omar was born in Somalia and grew up at the peak of that country’s civil war. She fled to the US as a teenager and later became a US citizen. She was first elected to Congress in 2018 and became part of “The Squad,” a group of congresswomen of color known for pushing for progressive causes. Since joining Congress, she has been the target of racist vitriol, including from Trump, who called Omar “garbage” last year and said Somalis should “go back to where they came from.” Omar’s home district in Minnesota was the target of an expansive immigration-enforcement campaign earlier this year that led to violent clashes between protesters and immigration authorities and the fatal shootings of two US citizens. Top administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Mullin, have accused Omar of marrying her brother to help bring him into the United States. They have provided no proof of this claim. Homan said on Fox News last month, referencing Omar, that if “someone committed immigration violation, someone committed marriage fraud, or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law.” Asked specifically whether that means there was an open investigation into Omar, Homan responded: “I’m confirming that ICE is — yeah, like I said months ago, that is something that’s been reported and needs to be looked at.” In prior years, the department has treaded cautiously for the 60-day period before an Election Day to not make searches or levy charges that would disadvantage a candidate. Department policy also bars prosecutors and investigative agents from selecting timing in an investigation so that it would influence an election. Top Justice Department leadership signed off on the search after thorough deliberations given the proximity to the election, and a federal judge ultimately approved it, a source familiar with the investigation told CNN on Monday. The Justice Department also has special policies requiring additional approvals when investigations involve a member of Congress, and the Constitution provides additional protections for members around papers and communications that relate to their legislative work. This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: NASA may already have proof life once existed on another planet. Scientists might never get to find out
cnn.com.text: A leopard-spotted rock that could prove whether life ever existed beyond Earth is sitting in a tube on Mars. NASA’s Perseverance rover grabbed up the sample, called Sapphire Canyon, from rocky outcrops on the edges of the Neretva Vallis, a valley sculpted by rivers that once flowed into an ancient lake in Jezero Crater more than 3 billion years ago.
