The rover landed at the dried lakebed in February 2021 for expressly this purpose, hunting for rocks created or modified by water in the past, which would have had the best chance of preserving evidence of life. Members of the Perseverance science team have said the Sapphire Canyon sample, about the size of a chalk stick, is exactly the type of rock they hoped the rover would discover. “This is the first time I think we’ve found something that qualifies as a ‘potential biosignature’” on Mars, said Adrian Broz, a member of Perseverance’s science team and a postdoctoral researcher in the Planetary Surface Processes Lab at Purdue University in Indiana. “It’s currently sealed inside of Perseverance rover’s chassis, and it sits there quietly and awaits return to Earth.” But the sample might not make it to our planet, at least not anytime soon. The Mars Sample Return program, a joint venture by NASA and the European Space Agency to ferry the promising cache back to Earth, attracted intense scrutiny for its high price tag and complex design. After sinking billions of dollars into the endeavor, NASA paused and began reassessing the program in 2024 before canceling it entirely — with no clear alternative in sight. “While Perseverance’s samples remain safely stored on Mars, NASA is exploring a range of potential return options that could offer simpler and more affordable approaches than the original Mars Sample Return plan, including possible commercial or international contributions,” the agency said in a statement shared with CNN in July. NASA’s leaders still haven’t revealed a path forward. And while the discovery of the Sapphire Canyon sample is building a strong case for the existence of ancient microbial life on Mars, there’s only so much scientists can learn from afar, said Dr. Briony Horgan, professor of Earth, atmospheric and planetary sciences at Purdue University. The rover, which cost NASA about $2.4 billion to build and launch, doesn’t have the instrument suite to answer such lofty questions by itself on the red planet. “We can keep doing these studies and coming up with these hints, but we’re never going to know for sure until we get those samples back,” said Horgan, also a coinvestigator and planner on the Perseverance team. “These samples are our best current chance for really understanding is life abundant and common, or is Earth truly unique?” Now, it’s possible one of NASA’s biggest competitors in the new space race will be the first to achieve Mars sample retrieval: China is looking to pick up its own souvenir from the red planet in 2031, and it has taken steps to ensure success by designing a mission that’s similar to one it pulled off two years ago. But the rocks returned by the country’s Tianwen-3 mission, expected to launch in 2028, could look very different — and perhaps offer different insights — from Perseverance’s samples, depending on how plans evolve. ‘Scientific holy grail’ Scientists consider Sapphire Canyon such a promising find because of its spotted appearance. On Earth, the tiny dots, called reaction fronts or reduction spots, form in soils and sediments due to the presence of microbial activity. “When there’s organic matter that’s lodged in sediment or soil that’s buried and microbes start to digest some of that organic matter, they form these bleached halos and spots that are quite resemblant to the ones that Perseverance found in this ancient river valley,” said Broz, coauthor of a study about the rock sample published in September 2025. Perseverance drilled the Sapphire Canyon sample from an arrowhead-shaped rock called Cheyava Falls in July 2024. The mudstones surrounding the rock were also covered in hundreds of thousands of promising reduction spots potentially made by ancient microscopic life. Still, returning the samples to Earth is the only way to determine whether these distinctive features were formed by the presence of life, or abiotically — through chemical or geological processes that did not require life, Broz said. It’s a lesson planetary scientists learned from studying the famed Allan Hills 84001 Martian meteorite, uncovered in the Antarctic in 1984 and originally thought to contain the remnants of ancient life. Multiple groups of scientists analyzed samples from the meteorite, discovering that nonbiological, geological processes left behind signatures that could be misinterpreted as organic carbon compounds attributed to life. “Even when you have all the labs all over the world looking at a rock that has putative evidence of ancient life, it is a really difficult thing to do, and so you want to just be able to apply every technique you can think of in all the best labs,” said Ashwin Vasavada, project scientist for the Curiosity rover at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California. The rover’s onboard tools can offer some data, but they weren’t designed to do the kind of analysis necessary to make definitive answers because that wasn’t part of the original plan. “The science instruments had been selected with the assumption that they would be doing reconnaissance for sample selection and providing the geologic context on Mars for samples that were always expected to be returned to Earth,” said Dr. Melissa Rice, a professor of planetary science at Western Washington University who has worked on NASA rover missions for over two decades. The first entry in NASA’s budget request to Congress for initial studies of a Mars sample return program occurred in the fiscal year 1978, according to Casey Dreier, chief of space policy at The Planetary Society. The request was made on the heels of the agency’s Viking missions to Mars, considered NASA’s first attempt to search for evidence of life on the red planet. “It tells you how long it has remained this kind of scientific holy grail for Mars,” Dreier said. A 2003 survey identifying top scientific objectives for future space missions — and several subsequent reports — highlighted retrieving red planet samples as a key priority, which led to Mars Sample Return becoming intertwined with the Perseverance rover’s mission. The two projects were developed hand in hand. A complicated path The original concept for Mars Sample Return, shared in 2020, included a succession of multiple missions launching from Earth to Mars: a lander containing a Mars fetch rover to collect the samples and an ascent vehicle to return the samples to Earth by 2031 at the earliest. The ascent vehicle was intended to shoot out a football-size container holding the samples that would be captured by a separately launched ESA spacecraft orbiting Mars. Then, the ESA orbiter would head back to Earth, transferring the sample container into yet another vehicle that could deploy from the orbiter and safely land the samples on our planet. By 2022, the plan shifted: Perseverance would deliver the sample suite to the Mars Ascent Vehicle that would launch on a return journey. The lander would carry two small recovery helicopters, which could grab samples from the rover if Perseverance wasn’t in good enough condition to make the drive to a landing site. This nudged the return date to 2033. As things progressed, assessments from independent review boards pointed out how unwieldy and complex the retrieval process had become. The program’s budget ballooned to an eye-popping maximum of $11 billion and the estimated return date for the samples pushed to 2040. NASA also faced budget cuts for the 2024 and 2025 fiscal years, and the excessive costs of the mission led to waning political support for the program. The agency put out a call for cheaper, quicker and less complex proposals and, in January 2025, identified two strategies that relied on commercial partnerships or leaned on previously used Mars landing technology so as to not reinvent the wheel. That assessment came out just weeks before President Donald Trump took office and began the search for a new NASA administrator. The next sample return update, revealed with NASA’s fiscal year 2026 budget request, was an abrupt blow: “NASA plans to terminate the Mars Sample Return Program given that current architecture options remain unaffordable. It is anticipated that future missions to Mars will return samples for study on Earth.” The agency’s 2027 budget request didn’t mention the program at all. NASA spent about $2.5 billion on the Mars Sample Return through its cancellation, Dreier said. However, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman has mentioned that he’s interested in getting Perseverance’s samples delivered to Earth. “As I’ve said many times, I think retrieving the samples from Mars can lead to the most significant scientific breakthrough in human history,” Isaacman said at a news conference on August 30 after the successful launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. “There’s no question we’re going to go get samples, whether it’s robotic or whether it’s astronauts picking it up will be the question, and certainly the time frame associated with it.” Speaking at the All-In Summit in September, Isaacman blamed his predecessors for the program’s failures, noting “the prior administration canceled the Mars Sample Return mission that was on track to cost more than an aircraft carrier.” While the finger-pointing about the fate of the original program appears to continue, no additional details about next steps have emerged. China’s challenge China’s plan to fetch Mars samples is also complex, though arguably less so than NASA’s original design. Called Tianwen-3, the approach China is using draws on the success of Chang’e-6, a 2024 mission that retrieved the first samples from the moon’s far side. Tianwen-3 will include two launches: one for a lander, ascent vehicle and helicopter, and another for an orbiter and return vehicle to shuttle the samples to Earth, according to a study published by the mission team in 2025. The lander is equipped with a drill that can reach 2 meters (6.5 feet) beneath the Martian surface, the ideal place to search for signs of past or present life. The helicopter can also gather rock samples. Mission scientists plan for the lander to operate on Mars’ surface for about 70 days during sample collection, according to Yiliang Li, a core member of Tianwen-3’s science team who is aiding in the selection of landing sites. The Tianwen-3 team is narrowing down a list of 86 potential landing sites to identify regions where liquid water once existed on Mars, mineral-enriched regions and areas where ancient microbial activity could still be preserved, according to a 2024 study. Jezero Crater does not appear to be on the list. Ideally, the mission will retrieve two types of samples from ancient lake beds, said Li, a coauthor on both studies. The team is aiming to find one sample with iron oxides, which might have preserved cell shapes for billions of years, and a second sample that contains thick aquatic clays because they could contain ancient organic molecules created by living organisms, said Li, who is also a professor of astrobiology in the department of Earth and planetary sciences at the University of Hong Kong. Zengqian Hou, Tianwen-3’s chief scientist and economic geologist of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, announced in September at the International Deep Space Exploration Conference that engineers are currently building a prototype of Tianwen-3. China also plans to build a planetary protection laboratory to house the samples, Hou said during the announcement. In recent years, NASA has focused increasingly on America-first messaging to position the US as leading the charge on marking milestones in space, including of beating China at being the first to land humans on Mars. A sample return win for China would certainly undermine that message. “American exceptionalism is being challenged in the high ground of space,” NASA Administrator Isaacman said while testifying on the 2027 NASA budget proposal in April. “To win, we cannot establish programs designed to be ‘too big to fail,’ but at the same time ‘too costly to succeed.’ Nor should it be throwing more money at the problem, but rather fixing the problems, concentrating resources on the mission and delivering outcomes.” Even as it ramps up the “space race” rhetoric in its efforts to return humans to the moon, the agency has made no mention of the fact that China may be the first to retrieve Martian samples — despite NASA already having a leg up with collected samples that just need to hitch a ride to Earth. “It’s remarkable that the US has advocated its leadership in this area of space exploration and just handed China the win in that one sector of the space race,” Rice said. Glimmer of hope Scientists remain hopeful that the Perseverance samples will be returned in some way, Horgan said. The ongoing work of industry partners is part of what’s keeping researchers optimistic. Lockheed Martin, for example, has worked with NASA on Mars missions and other sample return efforts in the past, which enabled the company to develop a streamlined concept to pick up the abandoned Perseverance samples, said Whitley Poyser, director of Lockheed Martin’s exploration mission area. The proposal included a fixed-price mission under $3 billion to return 30 of the rover’s samples to Earth no later than 2037. The concept revolved around using a lightweight Mars Ascent Vehicle, a small lander inspired by Lockheed Martin’s involvement in the InSight mission to Mars, and a compact Earth delivery system derived from lessons the company learned by assisting with the OSIRIS-Rex asteroid sample return mission, Poyser said. The company remains committed to their plan for retrieving samples from Mars and is prepared if the opportunity comes their way, she said. “The big area from a technical perspective that needs to mature is Mars ascent, especially if we are going to send someone there and send them back,” Poyser said. “We want to know how it’s going to work. All of those technologies are critical and they can be demonstrated through Mars Sample Return.” Even if the samples don’t contain signs of life, scientists say that knowledge could present intriguing possibilities, including the idea the spots may have been the work of prebiotic chemistry — the soup of elements, metals and organic carbon that could have formed a cell or living entity but didn’t reach its full potential. And if it turns out that life never existed on Mars, one of our planet’s closest neighbors, then why did it arise on Earth and not a world with similar conditions during the same time frame? Martian samples could tell the tale in a way that Earth’s rocks, shaped and lost over time due to erosion and other processes, can’t — and it’s up to the scientific community to share that message, Rice said. “I think there’s going to be a lot of advocacy for years to come, making sure that the general public is aware of how close we are to answering those big questions,” she said. “The rocks are there, they’re in their tubes, they’re ready. All we got to do is go get them.”

cnn.com.title: Nikon revokes first prize in Small World in Motion video competition over AI use
cnn.com.text: The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified after organizers concluded that his use of generative AI broke the rules. Ning Xu was named the winner of the annual Nikon Small World in Motion competition in September, but his video received a number of critical comments from experts who questioned its use of AI. Nikon launched an investigation, and announced its conclusion in a statement Friday. “After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI,” the statement reads, adding that the competition rankings have been adjusted. “This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent,” it said. Nikon also said it would revisit its rules and evaluation procedures for the annual competition in future. The new winner is a video showing a tiny roundworm and a single-celled Dileptus, a kind of single-celled microorganism, by Vietnamese researcher Nguyen Nam Nhat. Xu’s video captures the abnormal beating of airway cilia — hairlike structures that protrude from cells within the human body — in a child living with primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), a rare genetic disorder. When Nikon posted the video on LinkedIn, it attracted criticism from scientists such as Edward Phelps, an associate professor at the University of Florida, who said there were “many serious problems with this video.” Phelps said that some of the biological structures shown in the footage do not behave as expected. “The microscopy community deserves an explanation from Nikon,” Phelps added. In response, in a series of comments on LinkedIn, Xu acknowledged that he had used AI. “AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion,” he wrote. “It was applied afterwards to the reconstructed grayscale data to distinguish and color structures with similar morphology,” he added. CNN has reached out to Xu, who now works at the National University of Singapore as a research fellow, for further comment.

cnn.com.title: When AI goes rogue, who should get sued?
cnn.com.text: The AI industry has been buzzing with concern about potentially catastrophic risks to humanity — a hum of anxiety that’s grown louder as Anthropic prepares to make its stock market debut next month. But companies building AI models like Claude and ChatGPT face a more immediate and prosaic risk: They’re likely to get sued. A lot. AI companies have so far avoided major lawsuits over recent incidents in which they’ve failed to keep AI agents — systems capable of working autonomously with little oversight — contained to their testing environments. But some legal experts and policymakers say it’s pretty clear: The companies can and should be held responsible “The question of ‘how is the law going to apply to this?’ is a lot easier to answer if you see (AI) as it is, and not as this hypothetical thing that many in the industry are proposing it might someday be,” said Kristen Thomasen, associate professor at University of Windsor and an expert in robotics law. “The law has dealt with new technologies for as long as it has existed.” The AI industry often refers to the breakout incidents as the technology going “rogue” — language that some critics say is designed to amplify the companies’ claims that their technology is so powerful that even its creators struggle to contain it. It may also be a tactic to try to shield themselves from responsibility and future legal claims, Thomasen said. Still, she said, the liability questions around AI models have a simple answer: “It’s a thing that this company is putting out into the world. If it does harm, there are laws that regulate that.” The cost of ‘rogue’ meddling So far, the real-world harms done by rogue bots have been far from calamitous but nonetheless costly for the organizations they’ve infiltrated. Last week, the nonprofit that operates Wikipedia said it had found evidence of unauthorized OpenAI agents attempting to make “potentially malicious edits” to some pages and pummeling it with so much traffic that they may have triggered a partial outage. The investigation “stopped work inside key parts of the organization for us to focus on this,” Eric Mill, product manager for safety and security at Wikimedia, told CNN. “We put our very best people on it… and it’s a pretty messy process.” Wikimedia launched its investigation this summer as global alarm grew over the Hugging Face attack and dozens of other instances of internal AI models breaking out of their testing environments to hack other computer systems. Meta and Anthropic also disclosed that their test models have hacked into other systems without authorization. The Wikimedia probe is significant in part because of what didn’t happen: There was no catastrophic, existential threat to humanity of the sort that AI executives often allude to. But the cost — more than two weeks of work carried out by the leading engineers at a global, $200 million-plus organization — was real. Wikimedia isn’t pushing any one policy or technological solution, and Mill said the organization is in communication with OpenAI about its findings. (OpenAI didn’t respond to CNN’s request for comment.) But the nonprofit hopes these incidents are a wake-up call for AI developers. “AI companies are not doing enough to secure their systems and protect the public from the harm they cause,” Wikimedia said in its blog post last week. “That burden is falling onto everyone else, including smaller organizations.” ‘Long overdue accountability’ Anthropic, which is preparing to go public next month in one of the largest IPOs in history, disclosed in a regulatory filing that because the legal framework around AI is “unsettled,” those agents’ actions could expose the company to “significant and unpredictable” lawsuits, according to a copy of the document viewed by Reuters. The potential litigation onslaught isn’t just a headache for company lawyers or a quandary for academics — it could also become a major drag on Anthropic’s bottom line. Litigation costs are a financial drain for any company, but it could become especially problematic for Anthropic, which is burning through cash faster than it can bring it in. The company tore through $42 billion last year while bringing in just $4.6 billion in revenue, according to the document seen by Reuters. The CEOs of both Anthropic and OpenAI have argued for new regulations tailored to the industry. Dario Amodei recently penned an essay arguing that companies “pace the frontier” and foster international cooperation on safety protocols. But the rival AI firms have diverged slightly on the liability question. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman earlier this year favored an Illinois bill that would limit when AI labs can be held liable, even when their products cause “critical harm.” (Anthropic came out against it.) And while Altman endorsed Amodei’s “pace the frontier” proposal, he also told POLITICO earlier week that his worldview isn’t perfectly aligned with his rival’s: OpenAI believes “the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” he said. Altman also told the news site that “if something goes wrong with our models during training, there’s gonna be some version of that we need to be responsible for.” An Anthropic spokesperson told CNN the company sees liability laws as a backstop, rather than a substitute, for safety regulations. Anthropic has never proposed exemptions from existing liability laws, the spokesperson added. Policymakers on the left and the right have sought to cut through some of the more nuanced questions of future regulation and underscore the legal liabilities AI is already subject to. Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair under President Joe Biden, has become a prominent challenger to AI executives, arguing on X that “we shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books.” Meanwhile, Republican Senator Josh Hawley, alongside Democratic counterpart Chris Murphy, introduced a bill last week that seeks to ensure “AI agent operators and developers are held liable for hacking incidents.” “What these companies need is not more power… but some long-overdue accountability,” Hawley wrote in a Washington Post op-ed. “One way to give that to them is to let the people they harm sue them in court.” A design question Legal experts who spoke to CNN said that while product liability and consumer protection issues aren’t new, there will inevitably be some nuanced aspects of the technology that will ultimately fall on the courts to rule on. “We’ve seen these sorts of issues with gun safety or with cigarettes or other issues, and it’s really interesting — what analogy will the courts seize onto?” said Frank Pasquale, a Cornell law professor and an expert on AI law. One of the bigger questions Pasquale expect courts to grapple with is design. For example, he said, imagine if a manufacturer made a car with sharp swords at the end of it, and then someone drove that car into a pedestrian. The logical response is pretty simple: Don’t design something with swords attached to it. It’s similar with AI products, he said: Don’t design something that tries a password 50 times or more. Make sure it contains high level instructions that would override any user’s effort to misuse it. “I think it’s very hard for (AI companies) to say, ‘Oh, it can do a billion different things but we can’t control it.’” Pasquale said. “That doesn’t make sense to me because if it can do all these things, then you can also have meta-rules, or rules for the for the rules, that would that would prevent it from doing certain bad things.” —CNN’s Hadas Gold contributed reporting.

cnn.com.title: Robert Price was sitting on a $1 trillion frozen goldmine. Then Dr. Phil got involved
cnn.com.text:
Robert Price hadn’t noticed the 10-foot-tall wartime photo of his dad behind him.
“That’s him, yeah. He was stationed…”
The Texas wildcatter stopped, his eyes welling up with tears. He gave a cautious laugh and looked back up at the photo.
“Um,” Price started again, his voice wavering. “He was stationed in Greenland for three years at a weather station.”
Price was sitting in the middle of a decked-out studio, recording a podcast hosted by Phil McGraw, aka Dr. Phil, the frequent “Oprah Winfrey Show” guest turned TV host turned vocal surrogate for President Donald Trump.
The veteran oilman had gained exclusive drilling rights in Jameson Land, a remote part of Greenland right at the Arctic Circle – and what he believes is the world’s last frontier oil project.
As many as 13 billion barrels of crude, worth more than $1 trillion at today’s prices, were frozen deep within the very same stretch of frozen land that Price’s weatherman father was deployed to monitor during World War II. It was oil that the world desperately needed, with war raging in the Middle East and global crude stockpiles plunging by 2 billion barrels to reach critical lows over the past seven months.
Price wanted to tell the world all about it, and Dr. Phil was going to help him do it. “My dad would be really proud,” he said on the podcast.
The emotional interview may have undone Price’s dream.
Greenlanders, already on edge about Trump’s ambition to control Greenland, were furious. Local regulators withdrew their backing for the project. Price cut ties with Dr. Phil and is trying to make peace. In an interview with CNN, he said politics aren’t at play here. This is about helping Greenland benefit from its natural riches.
“This is about bringing capital to Greenland. It has nothing to do with the Trump administration,” Price told CNN. “Politics will come and go, but our project will be there for a long period of time.”
Price hopes he can salvage the massive and expensive project by doing some serious damage control. His company, Greenland Energy, said in a recent press release it would take no shortcuts, and it would continue the painstaking regulatory process “one day and one step at a time.” Another misstep could keep all that potential oil locked under the frozen surface forever.
Promise of riches
Price has oil in his blood. His grandfather died in an oil rig fire. His father was raised in Cushing, Oklahoma, the pipeline crossroads of the world. And Price spent his decades-long career getting land for oil majors to drill.
But he had never seen an opportunity like this.
Price knows it sounds nutty. His wells are hidden miles under an ice sheet in a remote part of Greenland with no way in or out, all winter long. Price remembers his father telling him stories about dogsleds, skiing, fishing, eating seal, hunting and the like. He still has 50 letters that his father wrote home to Price’s grandmother from his remote station in the arctic.
But he says the gamble is worth it: This isn’t a complicated extraction project like the tar sands of Canada, Brazilian pre-salt oil or even Texas Permian Basin horizontal fracking. It’s old-fashioned, drill-straight-down-until-you-strike-oil stuff, which means if he strikes oil (Price says “when” he strikes oil), he can drill considerably more profitably than those projects.
“Greenland is a beautiful, extraordinary place,” Price told CNN. “And to tell the story, not only of Greenland, but of the Greenlandic people and what our potential discovery might be, is important to me.”
Price argues that Greenland’s potential oil riches would become a boon for its inhabitants. But convincing Greenlanders – who endured threats this year by President Donald Trump to annex or buy their land – of the wisdom of allowing an American oil company to profit from their natural resources may be difficult.
So when an opportunity arose more than 10 years ago to get a license to drill there, Price jumped at the chance.
Arco, a company that had surveyed the basin starting in the 1970s, put its Greenland drilling licenses and seismic surveys up for auction. The company had spent three decades and $250 million preparing to exploit the oil in two gigantic wells below Jameson Land, a remote part of Greenland right at the Arctic Circle. Arco built an airstrip nearby. But the economics never made sense for Arco, and in 1990, the company gave up on the project. It never drilled there.
Now, the economics have changed entirely: Oil is around $100 a barrel, and drilling technology has vastly improved over the past several decades. Price sniffed an opportunity.
Except a British company, 80 Mile, beat him to the punch. So Price reached out with an offer: 80 Mile would work with the Greenland government to nail down the drilling rights, and Price would bring in all the financing, drilling equipment and workers. Price would enter a joint venture with 80 Mile and take up to a 70% interest in the wells.
That meant Price got an opportunity to follow in his father’s footsteps and go to Greenland – a dream he says he had long held since hearing those stories of how his father secretively helped deliver critical weather information to the Allied Forces in their fight against the Nazis.
Price set up the financing, getting some big-named backers, including mega hedge fund Citadel and its CEO Ken Griffin. Greenland Energy went public in March through a SPAC.
As recently as this past spring, it seemed all systems go: 80 Mile had completed its permitting paperwork in May 2025. The Greenland government asked the company to drill in the winter to reduce the potential environmental impact and to drill only one of its wells. An Albertan rig was ready to set sail from Montreal to Nuuk.
And then Dr. Phil shared the news about his Greenland Energy documentary.
The Dr. Phil Podcast
To tell his story, Price chose Dr. Phil. Throughout the 44-minute episode, McGraw interviewed Price about the project and previewed future episodes of the adventure, which he titled “Frozen Gold: Oil’s Final Frontier.”
Trump’s “less-than-sensitive language” wasn’t helpful to Greenland Energy’s specific project, but his comments shone a light on Greenland’s importance to the Western world, to the United States and to NATO, said Greenland Energy Chair Larry Swets. That helped increase investor awareness and, with it, capital, he told CNN.
Still, Greenlanders got riled up over Greenland Energy’s connection to Griffin (a well-heeled Trump supporter), Carol Craig (who runs a company working on Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense project that Trump wants stationed in Greenland), and the splashy adventure documentary from McGraw.
The Greenland government, which had been working closely with 80 Mile for years, slammed the brakes. The government said Greenland Energy had attempted to set sail under an expired permit. The company decided to air-lift equipment instead, which really got Greenland authorities upset – they viewed the gambit as an effort to bypass regulations.
In August, Greenland Energy announced it would delay its operations until October. A week later, the company said it was suspending all drilling until 2027.
The company also paused its relationship with McGraw. Representatives for McGraw did not respond to a request for comment.
Choosing Dr. Phil may have been a mistake. But Price doesn’t see it that way.
“Regardless of what his political affiliations are, he is a compelling storyteller,” Price said.
The whole premise of the documentary was that “there is an amazing story to tell,” added Swets. “Not just about energy and oil, but about the geopolitics and the people that are in the middle of that,” he told CNN. “It’s regrettable that maybe we didn’t take enough time to have Greenlanders come alongside (the documentary), rather than feel like it was pushed on them.”
Why Greenland matters
Drilling in the Arctic Circle is not for the faint-hearted.
Between 40 and 50 workers would need to be helicoptered in for the winter with an on-staff nurse, a blood bank and two chefs – because once temperatures plummet and the ice sheet moves in, there’s no easy way out. Every onsite worker will be required to carry a gun to protect themselves from polar bears.
Those are the risks that wildcatters like Price are willing to take on.
“This is about shoring up a potential supply of oil on into the future,” Price said.
The war in Iran made clear that the world needs alternative energy sources – including renewable energy but also easily drillable oil projects outside the Middle East. The shale revolution has made the United States the world’s largest energy producer, but some oil industry analysts fear Texas’ Permian Basin is close to exhausting its supply of tier 1 oil – the most easily accessible and profitably extracted crude.
No one knows exactly when that might happen; many think the Permian has another few years or even a decade of tier 1 oil left. But oil majors aren’t waiting. ExxonMobil’s massive oil well discovery off the coast of Guyana is already nearing 1 million barrels of production a day. Chevron and the United States are placing massive bets on Venezuela.
Price’s expectation of achieving profitability at around $20 means there’s enormous potential reward in Greenland. Even though Arco confirmed the presence of the massive subterranean wells decades ago, drilling doesn’t always yield anything.
“There’s clearly risk in doing exploration,” acknowledged Swets. “We know the oil is there, but we don’t know if we can get it out… The only way to get new information is to drill a well.”
Greenland has a long history of failed attempts to extract its oil, including from big companies like BP and Shell and many smaller companies who weren’t able to get much of anything out of the ground. In 2021, Greenland stopped offering drilling licenses – only allowing grandfathered licenses, such as Greenland Energy’s, to exploit the resources.
If they’re available.
“After we get the first well drilled, then we can decide how to move forward after that,” Price said.
He’ll have to wait until next year to find out. At least.

cnn.com.title: ‘Just start shooting’: Death threats over data centers are tearing American towns apart
cnn.com.text: The handwritten warning was left at an Amazon data center construction site in suburban Virginia: A dozen pipe bombs scattered throughout the building would explode in the next half hour. Officers rushed to the scene as workers dropped their tools and fled. Bomb-sniffing dogs prowled every corner of the site. That April 22 message in the city of Manassas, authorities soon confirmed, was an empty threat – the latest in a string this year that has rattled the state and communities across the nation. As thousands of new data centers have been built to fuel the booming artificial intelligence industry, escalating public resentment against both the energy-sucking infrastructure and AI itself is roiling small towns and suburban communities from coast to coast, a CNN investigation has found. Police have been called into action to investigate dozens of threats to data centers, from bomb claims etched on bathroom walls to online incitements to “use bullets on city council members” to suggestions that protesters should “unalive” pro-development officials, according to a CNN review of more than 100 police reports filed since last year. Aside from rare cases like an Indianapolis council member whose home was sprayed with gunfire, those threats have rarely led to actual violence – but they’ve eaten up hundreds of hours of police time, alarmed workers and inflamed communities already on edge over the projects. That rising outrage has also inspired a growing police crackdown, including federal agencies tracking data center protests and local cops questioning vocal activists, and even filing criminal charges against critics that have later fallen apart in court. The police records as a whole paint a vivid picture of a national backlash against the rise of data centers and AI reaching a boiling point at a moment when the debate has become a key issue threading party lines ahead of the midterm elections. They also show growing concern among law enforcement agencies about extremist groups at opposite ends of the political spectrum hopping on the anti-data-center bandwagon. “Anti-technology extremist narratives appeal to a broad array of ideological movements – including anarchists, environmental extremists, and white supremacists – creating a common target between otherwise opposing movements,” Colorado state officials warned in an April bulletin for police agencies. A similar California memo warned in June of “a broad range of threat actors… mobilized by AI-related grievances.” Still, some people who have been charged with making threatening comments insist they’re not extremists and do not actually wish violence upon anyone. Rather, they say they were driven to take dramatic action by rising electricity bills, environmental worries or fears of AI. “I’m not really political,” Anthony Hinojosa, an Illinois man arrested in February over an alleged data center threat, told an investigator who interrogated him, according to police recordings. “I feel like we don’t have a vote.” But elected officials say the reports show how the battle over data centers and AI is entering dangerous territory, where they’re fearing for their lives just for doing their jobs. Minneapolis council member Michael Rainville was left pleading in an August letter to his constituents for a more peaceful dialogue over the issue. “Please stop the threats against me and my family,” he wrote. ‘Terroristic threats’ In early February, police in Troy, Illinois fielded multiple calls about ominous statements on a community Facebook page. At the time, the city had been debating whether to clear the way for a roughly 200-acre data center that backers said could create hundreds of jobs. Like similar proposals around America, the once-anodyne pitch had become hugely contentious. Views of data centers have soured significantly this year. Nearly nine in 10 Americans say they’re more concerned than excited about the rise of these facilities, a CNN poll conducted by SSRS found in September. Amid that debate, Troy officials confronted a tirade on Facebook: “My hypothesis is no one would want to be shot at so just start shooting the people involved and it’ll never be built,” Hinojosa, a 33-year-old lawn-care businessman, commented beneath a post about the proposed data center. When a user asked if he was really suggesting violence, Hinojosa responded, “for sure,” screenshots of his posts show. Later that day, officers knocked on his door. “You’re being placed under arrest for making terroristic threats,” an officer said. “I think people are taking things out of context,” Hinojosa told the authorities. He said he had been upset about the proposed data center’s potential strain on electricity and water supply, but he insisted he would not hurt anyone and his words had been misconstrued. “Over a misunderstanding you are literally going to ruin my life,” he said. “It just feels like the mayor of Troy and the city council, they’re just not really listening to the public.” Hinojosa, who described himself in police recordings as a moderate Republican, now faces felony charges for intimidation and harassment through electronic communication. He has pleaded not guilty. His lawyer declined comment, citing an upcoming trial. Hinojosa’s case is one of about 70 among the police reports CNN reviewed that include allegations of threats, intimidation or planned attacks – a collection showing a striking range of anger at AI infrastructure that at times has spilled into serious claims of potential violence. Dozens of additional police reports detail other security concerns, including scuffles at county meetings, calls for police patrols at local officials’ homes and confrontations with data center staff. Some even describe explicit calls for assassinations. “Time to use bullets on city council members. Nothing is going to change until some of them are dead,” stated a post in August after officials green-lit site plans for a major data development in Westlake, Texas. “I’ll just shoot you in the face,” read another message described in a Salt Lake County, Utah case. In the Utah case, the alleged sender was charged in June with stalking and making multiple threats of violence along with other charges. His target, someone apparently linked to the project but not identified in court records, told police the ordeal led him to temporarily relocate his family and spend about $14,000 on home security. The case is pending. In Bell County, Texas, authorities arrested a man who allegedly threatened officials in an online screed that referenced the murder of a UnitedHealthcare CEO by Luigi Mangione. “We can always unalive them. Luigis Unite!” the comment stated beneath a post about local data center construction. His case is also ongoing. Police did not charge anyone in many of the incidents that clearly crossed the line into violent rhetoric. In some cases, threat recipients declined to press charges, such as in Archbald, Pennsylvania, where police heard about a voicemail in which a man threatened to “grab” the skull of a staffer for a data center development company and “smash it.” The man later apologized for “being an a**hole,” according to a police report. Other cases appear to have no suspects. That includes more than a dozen bomb threats at data center construction sites in multiple states including Iowa, Maryland, Utah and Virginia. In April, thousands of workers evacuated one of those sites in Eagle Mountain, Utah after someone wrote inside a portable toilet that a bomb had been set in a nearby building. One month later, authorities were called to the same site for the same reason and again found nothing, according to incident reports. The messages are often simple. “Bomb a data center,” read graffiti found at a Maryland construction site in June. “The bomb is ticking you better find it,” read another found at a Virginia site. The sheriff’s office in Loudoun County, Virginia – dubbed the data center capital of the world – has received reports of at least nine such bomb threats in less than a year, records show. A representative for an electrician business even complained to deputies that the frequency of bomb scares angered his colleagues because they were losing wages with the regular closures. “While each of these is handled with great urgency, the sheriff’s office is fortunate to have methods that enable us to quickly determine if it is a hoax,” Thomas Julia, spokesperson for the Loudoun County Sheriff, told CNN, adding that the expected prominence of data centers in upcoming elections “will likely mean more calls for service.” Growing police crackdown The flood of angry and at times frightening blowback to data centers has left police and lawmakers on edge around the country, CNN’s investigation found. Authorities have issued sweeping warnings of the potential for attacks, monitored activists and at times even arrested citizens for seemingly innocuous comments against data centers and those who support them. A West Virginia agency that analyzes threats, for example, shared a report about “potential risks” associated with a website that maps data center projects across the country. An office within the Department of Homeland Security forwarded the report to other agencies, records show. In June, US Capitol Police alerted law enforcement in an email about protests by Humans First, a group chaired by Amy Kremer, a conservative activist who helped organize the rally that preceded the January 6 Capitol riot. Kremer condemned the violence of the riot and was not accused of any criminal wrongdoing. The Capitol Police email in June noted her new group had coordinated “several demonstrations… targeting AI Data Centers.” Asked about that email, Kremer said, “That is unbelievable,” noting that her group is peaceful. “It is our right as Americans to protest, and we don’t condone violence.” Kremer argued the real threats authorities should scrutinize are AI and the companies behind it. “We do not have to give Big Tech a blank check and let them cram their technology and their infrastructure down our throat,” she said. Separately, among the incident reports obtained by CNN are more than a dozen that describe situations with no specific calls for violence by suspects that still triggered investigations or arrests. Police in El Paso, Texas questioned at least three data center opponents, including a woman who wrote to the city council, “we need to clear you out lol.” She later told investigators she simply wanted the officials voted out of office. In another case, a special unit looked into a woman who called a city representative and left a voicemail saying, “I hope you rot in hell and die.” She told investigators she had been repeatedly denied the opportunity to speak to the official about a local data center. “She feels threatened because I said ‘I hope’ – that is ridiculous. I’m threatened by the data centers,” the woman told El Paso police officers, according to body camera video. “We have to take everything serious,” an officer said. Separately, authorities in Cumberland County, Pennsylvania charged a man with making “terroristic threats” after he reportedly said he wanted local officials who supported a data center dead. A judge dismissed the case. Harley DeLander, a 28-year-old from Dixon, Illinois – a quaint community best known as the hometown of former President Ronald Reagan – learned while scrolling social media in May that a nearby plot of land had been promoted as a potential data-center site. Fearing what such infrastructure could do to the region’s water and electricity costs, DeLander lashed out at the head of a county association that had touted the land for development. “If he cared about his kids, he wouldn’t be actively trying to ruin the world they are being raised in,” DeLander posted on Facebook, along with a call for a protest at the man’s house and a statement that he “needs to have someone put the fear of god in him and his family. Make him scared to close his eyes at night.” The man, a former state representative, alerted Dixon’s police chief to DeLander’s comments, according to a police report. Authorities then charged DeLander with multiple felonies, including intimidation and cyberstalking. DeLander told CNN he then lost his job and was forced to wear an ankle monitor. Shocked and confused by the case, he retained an attorney and crowdsourced funds for his defense. After legal negotiations, he pleaded guilty to one petty charge lower than a misdemeanor and agreed to complete a court-ordered program to get the more serious charges dismissed. “I don’t regret my position toward data centers,” DeLander told CNN in an interview, noting that he received an outpouring of support from other data center opponents after his arrest and used the notoriety to further publicize his concerns. Officials in his city and county have stated there are currently no data center proposals under consideration for development, though DeLander fears that could still change. “I was an idiot for saying those things online but sometimes you have to be an idiot for someone to hear you. Sometimes you’ve got to do something foolish to get the word out,” DeLander said. The state’s attorney on the case, Charles Boonstra, declined to discuss specifics since the matter technically remains pending. Boonstra said DeLander was not prosecuted “because of his data center opposition; it was because of his incitement to violence and threats of violence.” ‘Jumped too far down the deep end’ Many Republican and Democratic politicians have pivoted away from backing data centers ahead of the midterms, but others – namely President Trump – have doubled down on their development. Amid these political debates, some extremism researchers warn that the risk of violence may be growing. They point to multiple would-be attacks that have already been disrupted. Last year, police in Ashland City, Tennessee arrested a man who said he purchased materials to burn down an xAI facility in Memphis; he told police he had gotten “wrapped up in politics” and “jumped too far down the deep end,” according to an incident report. In June, authorities charged multiple people in connection to an alleged plot to attack a UFC event at the White House. The mother of one of them told law enforcement the group held grievances including “data centers taking up all the water in communities,” and some of them also discussed attacking data centers in California, according to court records. Future attackers may not belong to any groups or even have exposure to the type of extremist content typically associated with threats, said Yannick Veilleux-Lepage, an associate professor at the Royal Military College of Canada who has studied AI-grievances and political violence. “You don’t need to be reading Ted Kaczynski to be radicalized against AI. You can simply listen to Sam Altman and Elon Musk talk for a couple minutes and that’s probably enough to radicalize some people,” Veilleux-Lepage said. Rainville, the Minneapolis council member who asked constituents to stop threatening him, told CNN he had not even taken a public stance on a proposed data center when he received intimidating messages. Those notes suggested they knew where he lives and what kind of car he drives. He said much of the opposition has falsely lumped all data centers together and presumed any development will inevitably drive up electricity costs and strain water supply. “You’re comparing apples and oranges, but that shows you the emotion, not only here in Minneapolis but around the country,” Rainville said.

cnn.com.title: Two Americans win Nobel prize for models to tackle economic downturns
cnn.com.text: American professors Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford have won the 2026 Nobel prize in economics for developing new economic models that help governments and central banks stabilize their economies to minimize the impact of external shocks. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the prize in Stockholm on Monday. “The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the academy said in a statement, adding that their models have been “extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.” Hall, born in Palo Alto, California in 1943, is a professor at Stanford University. Woodford, born in Chicopee, Massachusetts in 1955, is a professor at Columbia University. They will each receive 6 million Swedish kronor ($598,000) in prize money. Their work “has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” noted John Hassler, the chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences. “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” he added. Rather than analyzing links between so-called “macroeconomic” variables such as inflation, production and consumption, Hall and Woodford looked to “microeconomics” to understand how the decisions of individuals and households can affect the economy. Central to their models was the insight that households and businesses are “forward-looking” when making decisions about savings or how to price products. Governments and central banks can influence this view of the future when communicating their plans for fiscal and monetary policy respectively and so “move the economy in the right direction,” the academy said. The prize, officially known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, was not instituted by Alfred Nobel. It was established by Sweden’s central bank in 1968 and is awarded in memory of Nobel. The number of individuals who have been awarded the prize now totals 101, only three of whom have been women. Fewer than half of the prizes awarded since 1969 have gone to one laureate only. The economics prize concludes this year’s Nobel awards. South African judge and human rights pioneer Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. A day prior, Canadian writer Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in literature.

cnn.com.title: Fed officials are warning of more pain. Many Americans are already feeling it
cnn.com.text: Four years ago, with inflation at multi-decade highs, then-Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell delivered a blunt message to Americans: Getting inflation under control would come at a cost. The Fed needed to act “forcefully,” Powell told attendees at a key central banker conference that August. Doing so, he cautioned, would bring “some pain” for consumers. Now, with the Fed back to raising interest rates for the first time in three years, a familiar warning about the economic fallout is resurfacing. Inflation across the country is being driven primarily by fuel prices, which have skyrocketed since the war with Iran broke out in February. The Fed has little control over oil production, but by raising interest rates, it is seeking to prevent higher energy costs from spilling over into other parts of the economy and fueling broader inflation. While this type of supply-driven inflation may be easier to bring under control than the post-pandemic demand-driven inflation, “it won’t be painless either,” Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said last month. For central bankers, the challenge is balancing two competing priorities: keeping inflation in check and preserving a healthy labor market. When price increases become too rapid, the Fed typically raises interest rates, making borrowing more expensive for consumers and businesses. That, in turn, can curb spending and cool demand, easing pressure on prices. But that slowdown can come at a cost to workers, often leading to weaker hiring, fewer job openings, and, in some cases, job losses, as businesses struggle with higher borrowing costs. “Inflation is the disease. And now the Fed comes with a cure: higher interest rates,” Beth Ann Bovino, chief economist at US Bank, said. “I don’t know which is more painful because they both hurt.” Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of US economic activity, making it a key driver of growth. If Americans pull back — either because prices are eating up more of their budgets or because higher borrowing costs force them to set aside more money for expenses such as a home purchase — the economy could slow. In a worst-case scenario, that pullback could help tip the economy into a recession, Bovino told CNN. For now, though, economic pain isn’t being felt equally. Americans with substantial investments in the stock market, which is hovering near record highs, may be doing just fine. Those who rely more heavily on their paychecks to cover everyday expenses have less of a cushion against rising prices. “Those are the people being hurt,” she said. Patience is a virtue — until it isn’t With the risks of higher interest rates in mind, a growing chorus of Fed officials have recently been advocating for a more patient approach as they tackle the issue of inflation. Rather than trying to get a head start at fighting the potential for more or broader-based inflation, several central bankers have said they’d like more time to observe how economic conditions evolve to get a better idea of how many more rate hikes, if any, are needed. “There is no need for urgency,” New York Fed President John Williams said last month. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson echoed that sentiment. “Any future adjustments in policy should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook and the balance of risks,” he said earlier this month. But waiting to act carries risks of its own. With the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge more than a percentage point above its 2% annual target, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack warned that delaying action could make the fight against inflation even more painful. “The longer inflation stays above our objective, the harder it will be for us to bring it back down, and the more pain that individuals and businesses are going to be experiencing,” Hammack said in an August CNBC interview. For the Fed, the challenge is figuring out how much pain the economy can withstand — and which risk is worse: acting too soon or waiting too long. Either way, consumers are likely to pay the price. The September Consumer Price Index report due Wednesday may give officials some valuable clues.

cnn.com.title: How the Iran war could make Trump an accidental climate president
cnn.com.text: The Iran war was supposed to be a short, sharp strike that brought down the regime within a few weeks. Instead, the US finds itself enmeshed in a conflict that’s upending the world’s energy system. As oil and gas prices soar, there have been noticeable shifts toward clean energy, and it’s raised a profoundly weird question: Could this war make President Donald Trump an accidental climate president, at least on the global stage? It would be a deep irony, if so. Trump is the climate-denier-in-chief. He has called global warming a “hoax,” clean energy a “scam,” pushed fossil fuels, and unraveled a slew of climate and environmental protections. But as the war grinds into its eighth month, it’s highlighting the immense vulnerability of fossil fuels to geopolitical instability. There are signs of global clean energy moves, even as the picture remains complex, with some countries scrambling for coal instead. The longer the war continues, some experts say, the bigger the impact it could have on undermining global oil and gas demand. “With all (Trump’s) efforts to encourage fossil fuel use, he might end up accelerating their phase down instead,” said Samantha Gross, director of the Energy Security and Climate Initiative at the Brookings Institution. The launch of the US and Israel’s war on Iran in February led to the biggest oil shock in history. Iran strangled the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that transported roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, sending the cost of a barrel of oil surging over $100. Many analysts predicted the price spike would be short-term, but it has persisted even as Iran’s chokehold over the strait has loosened. Shipping costs to get oil through the Strait of Hormuz have surged, and new fronts are opening up in the conflict, including attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi oil facilities and tankers. It’s all affecting demand. Back in January, the International Energy Agency forecast global oil demand would rise by 930,000 barrels per day in 2026. By September, the picture had changed dramatically. The IEA now forecasts a decline of 2.5 million barrels a day due to the “impasse” in negotiations between the US and Iran. Less oil means less planet-warming pollution. Global fossil fuel emissions are on track to fall around 0.5% in 2026, according to an analysis from Carbon Brief, a non-profit climate change publication. It would mark the first fall since 2020, when the Covid pandemic ground the world to a halt. It also means big shifts in transportation, where most of the world’s oil goes. People are driving and flying less, but these are likely temporary changes, said Sverre Alvik, vice president and energy transition outlook director at DNV, a Norway-based consultancy. Much more permanent are the vehicles people are buying. Global sales of electric vehicles were up 4% in the second quarter of 2026, according to the IEA, which said the Middle East crisis “has clearly reinforced the case for EVs as a way to address energy security and fuel cost concerns.” Australia and parts of Asia have seen EV booms, as has Europe, where sales hit record highs in 2026, according to a report from the non-profit advocacy group Transport & Environment. Fuel prices were a key factor, with diesel reaching particularly painful highs, up 38% since the start of the war. The US bucks the trend, however. EV sales have slumped as the Trump administration has cut support for them and effectively banned cheaper Chinese models. They’re down more than 30% this year so far, according to research firm Motor Intelligence. Then there’s natural gas. The conflict has dealt “a major supply shock” to the world’s gas markets, according to the IEA, which projects global demand will shrink by around 0.5% in 2026. Countries are seeking alternatives, with dozens implementing policies to switch from fossil fuels to clean power since the war started. Harnessing the sun and wind doesn’t rely on a few volatile chokepoints in the same way as oil and gas. “The new geopolitics of energy is driving clean energy solutions and electrification,” said Amy Myers Jaffe, director of the Global Energy, Climate, and Sustainability Lab at New York University. Investment in solar capacity in Southeast Asian countries, for example, has roughly quadrupled in the first two quarters of this year, according to data from the Rhodium Group, an independent research provider. Most of the region’s liquified natural gas comes from the Gulf, so they had to “make a quicker pivot,” said Tess Carter, an associate director for energy and climate at Rhodium. It will take time to see real evidence of an accelerating shift away from oil and gas, said Gross. A wholesale move to EVs and widespread changes in grid-scale electricity are lengthy processes. “But I do expect that it is coming,” Gross said. That said, there is a catch. The transition to alternative energy options has not just meant renewables; some countries have turned to coal, the dirtiest fossil fuel. Global coal demand is now projected to rise by 1.2% in 2026, a reversal of earlier forecasts which had projected a small decline. There is also the possibility that oil and gas demand could come swinging back — the IEA projects a recovery for oil in 2027. And we’ve been here before on big global disruptions. Some environmentalists hoped the pandemic would lead to a clean energy shift, instead, fossil fuel demand surged in 2021. How permanent the shifts are may depend on how long the conflict endures. For every month it lasts, the probability of permanent oil “demand destruction” increases, a DNV analysis found. “If the war lasts for four years, for example, then our analysis shows that oil demand will never resume to the level we had in 2025,” DNV’s Alvik said. Some are hopeful that whatever happens, more permanent changes are already ingrained. Iran has shown drones and missiles are all that’s needed to strangle a waterway — not a powerful navy. “The world cannot unsee what has happened, and oil and natural gas supply seem much more insecure than they did before the war,” said Gross of the Brookings Institution. Rob Jackson, a climate scientist at Stanford University, said the conflict “could have a sustained effect because dozens of countries are now promoting EV incentives, charging infrastructure and electrification in general.” Still, he finds the notion of Trump as an accidental climate president “ridiculous.” He may have hastened clean energy uptake overseas, but he has gutted green energy in the US and “set us back decades,” Jackson said. “The forces driving green energy around the world — cleaner, cheaper fuels — will ultimately prevail despite him.”

cnn.com.title: ‘Trump is dragging the party down’: GOP scrambles to stop steep midterm losses
cnn.com.text: The Republican Party’s midterm campaign has turned into a triage operation just three weeks out from November, as officials race to avert losses in a string of once-safe seats that they increasingly fear could cost them total control of Congress. The worsening landscape has alarmed GOP operatives across several battleground states, forcing the party to pour resources into traditionally red districts and states at the expense of their once-expansive ambitions in Democratic areas. And after months of pressing President Donald Trump to ramp up his travel on behalf of key candidates, some Republicans now worry he’s grown so unpopular that his presence on the campaign trail may in some cases be doing more harm than good. One House Republican running for re-election said of the president’s numbers: “Trump is dragging the party down.” The grim outlook gripping the GOP follows weeks of polling showing Republicans on track to lose the House amid intense voter anger over the Iran war and rising cost of living — and at grave risk of losing their once-solid majority in the Senate as well. The widening number of competitive races has complicated Republican leaders’ plans to make up ground by unleashing hundreds of millions of dollars down the stretch. Despite a massive cash advantage fueled in part by pro-Trump super PAC, MAGA Inc., the spending so far has failed to significantly shift Republicans’ fortunes as more money gets diverted toward races once counted on as comfortable wins. Already, the Senate Leadership Fund, the top GOP super PAC in Senate races, has suspended its ad reservations in North Carolina and plowed at least $10 million into Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. It also recently invested $5 million in South Carolina to boost incumbent Sen. Darline Graham amid concerns among some Republicans she’s losing ground to Democrat Annie Andrews in the deep red state. That’s on top of the more than $100 million that the Senate Leadership Fund has spent in Texas to boost Ken Paxton, who is scrambling to shore up GOP support in his race with Democrat James Talarico after a bruising primary campaign. Trump himself has now traveled to Texas three times in one month to rally voters on Paxton’s behalf. “We were all hoping the war was going to be over now, but it’s not,” said one Trump adviser. “We shouldn’t have a fight in a place like Texas, but obviously we do.” Top Republicans steering spending on the House side are also expected to narrow their focus in the coming days, doubling down on races they see as winnable while slashing their investment in candidates whose fortunes are fading, multiple people familiar with the matter said. That winnowing will mark the latest acknowledgment of the challenge facing Republicans — and an effort to concentrate resources on the select candidates capable of defending their seats, or flipping blue districts, and limiting Democrats’ encroachment overall. The Cook Political Report dealt the latest blow on Friday, moving 18 House races toward Democrats. Those contests include five toss-up seats across Iowa, Pennsylvania and Washington that the closely watched analysis projects the Democratic candidates are now more likely to win. The Senate map has also provided little reassurance for the GOP. Paxton is suffering a drip-drip of damaging audio leaks from a private fundraiser, further frustrating Republican officials who already believe he’s running a poor campaign. Democrats hold polling leads in swing states like Georgia and North Carolina, while making insurgent runs in solidly red states like Alaska and even Kansas. “I don’t know that the environment could possibly get worse than it is,” said Jason Roe, a Michigan GOP strategist advising Rep. Tom Barrett, who is in a neck-and-neck race against Democratic challenger Will Lawrence. “If we lose this, it couldn’t have been won.” Inside the White House, Trump and his top advisers are clear-eyed about the difficult odds of keeping the House and the rising threat to the Senate majority, people familiar with the matter said. But there is still optimism that Republicans can limit their losses and turn the prospect of a blue wave into little more than a ripple. Trump advisers expect the polls to tighten in swing races in the campaign’s final days, especially as more ads hit the airwaves and less-engaged Republican voters begin to tune in. “I’m not saying we are going to f***ing win, it is going to be so great. No, I am not saying that. But do we get wiped out? No, we aren’t gonna get wiped out,” said another House Republican running for re-election. Some strong GOP candidates are likely to outperform the generic ballot polling that shows Democrats favored by a healthy margin, the people familiar argued. At the same time, they’re counting on a handful of far-left Democratic candidates to underperform. And even at the current margins, they note, the difference between Republicans losing the House or expanding their majority is only a matter of a few percentage points across a handful of races. “This election is going to come down to one side saying Republicans have not cleaned their mess up fast enough, and what we are saying is, ‘We know you are struggling, but these are the things we are doing to make your life better and, by the way, they are crazy,” another Republican told CNN. For his part, Speaker Mike Johnson has vowed to do everything he can to hold the majority and is campaigning in more than 40 districts and 20 states leading up to the election. “Speaker Johnson is not slowing down and helping to get resources to every district that will decide the majority,” Johnson’s political communications director, Greg Steele, said in a statement to CNN. While Trump has largely steered clear of swing districts of late, he has shown newfound enthusiasm for the campaign trail that his advisers have rushed to take advantage of, sending him to favorable areas across the country where they believe he can help GOP turnout. They’ve shrugged off any talk of Trump needing to lay low given his sagging approval ratings, arguing that the midterms are going to be a referendum on his presidency no matter what. “The panic is unwarranted and it’s unfounded,” one White House official said of the GOP’s midterm trajectory. “It’s all going to come down to who has the ability to turn out their low-propensity voters. … That’s why we’re going where we’re going: To jazz up the base.” In a statement, White House spokesman Davis Ingle called Trump “the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party.” National Republican Congressional Committee spokesman Mike Marinella said in a statement, “House Republicans have a more favorable map, a stronger ground game, historic fundraising and spending advantages and battle-tested incumbents while Democrats are stuck dragging their unelectable socialist nominees across the finish line.” A senior Republican National Committee official argued that pollsters and strategists are writing off the GOP’s chances in the midterms too soon. “The first ones to rush and get on the phone with you all in these times are not the ones in the fight,” the official told CNN. “They would rather just say nobody knows what they are doing and everything is doomed than take an objective look at what is happening.” Trump’s rallies — which included a stop in Texas on Thursday and a trip to upstate New York on Friday to stump for gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman — have bolstered Trump’s mood and view of Republicans’ chances, the White House official and others familiar with his comments said. Nevertheless, Trump has tacitly acknowledged that his presence may not be helpful everywhere at a time when large majorities are frustrated with his economic policies and oppose the Iran war. The president has declined to rebuke GOP candidates who have broken with him on the war and tariffs out of an understanding that they “need to run a campaign,” the White House official said — though those Republicans have still typically cleared the move with the White House ahead of time. Trump has also stayed away from some races where vulnerable Republicans have tried to carve out an identity separate from him, such as Maine Sen. Susan Collins. The president isn’t currently expected to travel to Maine ahead of the midterms, people familiar with the matter said, though they cautioned his schedule fluctuates and that could change. Still, there’s little expectation that any GOP candidate can fully escape the gravitational pull that Trump has exerted on the political landscape since returning to the White House. And after nearly two years of demands for GOP unity, Trump advisers have counseled Republicans that their best hope in the final weeks is to make their own pitches for why they should get another term in Congress — and crucially, what they plan to do once they’re there to assuage voters’ frustrations. “We’re fighting it out individually now,” the Trump adviser said. “It’s ugly out there for both sides, and it’s going to be hand-to-hand combat.”

cnn.com.title: John Kennedy takes his ‘baton twirler’ act on the road for the midterms — and tests it out for 2028
cnn.com.text: After hearing Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy unload his characteristically colorful combination of homespun quips, over-the-top insults and Talladega Nights movie quotes to reporters on Friday, former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Michigan Senate GOP candidate with whom Kennedy was campaigning, knew his own words wouldn’t be getting much attention. “It’s like following the baton twirler in the talent show,” Rogers said. “You know, you’re never going to win that thing.” Kennedy has taken his act on the road, campaigning with GOP Senate nominees in several states in the closing weeks of this year’s midterm elections — including stops in Ohio on Thursday and Michigan on Friday, where he repeatedly declared that Rogers “pisses excellence.” The 74-year-old Kennedy is “tired,” he said, but still thinking about making a second trip to Alaska and a stop in Texas, both also home to key Senate races, ahead of Election Day. It’s a calendar that could serve as a prelude to a bid for national office. Kennedy says he is weighing a run for the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. He’ll have to decide soon after the midterm elections whether to seek the White House or run for a third term in the Senate. He told reporters in Michigan on Friday that as he thinks about a presidential run, his biggest concern is “the goober factor.” “If a bunch of goobers run, and I don’t think I can be effective in the Senate anymore, then I would consider it,” he said. “But right now, I’m running for reelection.” What are the differences, CNN asked, in where the so-called “goobers” want to steer the GOP and where Kennedy would like to move the party? “Let me tell you about goobers — and I’m not going to name goobers,” Kennedy said. “Being a goober is a lot like pornography. It’s hard to define, but you know it when you see it.” ‘He’ll have to change up his persona’ Later Friday night, Kennedy drew loud cheers and a number of laughs during his speech to what Rogers’ campaign said was about 900 attendees at a barn party in Highland — situated in Oakland County, an affluent and highly educated Detroit suburb that is a swing region in Michigan elections. But interviews with attendees afterward laid bare the challenge that would confront the Louisiana senator if he tries to translate what works in Washington, and in front of audiences that have never seen him in person before, onto the presidential campaign trail — where voters would demand that he prove he isn’t a “goober” himself. Even some of Kennedy’s biggest admirers at the barn party told CNN on Friday they thought his wit wouldn’t be enough to fuel a presidential campaign. Jan Dillaha, a 64-year-old manufacturing company executive in Indian River, said she loves Kennedy and reeled off some of her favorite lines from the senator. She even noted that, in his speech Friday night, Kennedy had omitted one go-to Kennedyism. “He left out ‘hobo on a ham sandwich,’ which is my personal favorite,” she said. But as for 2028, Dillaha said, Kennedy “would not be my first pick,” even though she thinks he’d do well as president. “To be honest, speaking in there, most of the stuff that he said tonight, I’ve heard before,” she said. “But, you know, you can’t do that over the course of two years and not have people get tired of it. So he’s going to have to up his game there.” James Semerad, a 70-year-old retired Navy veteran who lives in Clarkston — but once lived in Louisiana — said Kennedy “has a unique way of saying stuff” that connects with the state. “He’s got good stage presence. He’s got good charisma. And he makes issues funny, rather than just very serious,” Semerad said. “He has a way of twisting some really important points in a way that makes you think. He’s a funny guy, but he’s also a really smart guy.” What about Kennedy for president in 2028? “He’ll have to change up his persona somewhat,” Semerad said, “to look more presidential.” ‘Kale tastes like I’d rather be fat’ On Capitol Hill, Kennedy’s sharp exchanges with witnesses in congressional hearings often make news. And sometimes, he misfires. That was the case last month, when Kennedy helped Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt hold up a poster displaying text messages as Schmitt accused former special counsel Jack Smith of a conspiracy based largely on Schmitt confusing the Atlanta Hawks and the University of Iowa Hawkeyes. For all his homey, sometimes movie-inspired and occasionally crude witticisms, Kennedy is also a clear-eyed political operator. He is a former Democrat who switched parties in 2007, after the party’s massive midterm losses, when he was state treasurer. He said his own political operation has been conducting polling on key races this year. And he acknowledged to reporters that the GOP is facing intense political headwinds this fall. “The cost of living is a big issue. And it’s more than just dollars and cents. I sense it on both sides. … It’s cost of living, but it’s also people. They’re angry, and if they’re not angry, many of them feel a deep melancholy — and they just feel like, you know, these people in Washington, they don’t listen and they don’t care,” Kennedy said. “And the system no longer works for them.” Kennedy put his wit to work for Rogers on Friday, first at a joint stop at a manufacturing plant in Sterling Heights, and then at the barn party. For the second event, Kennedy had kept his blue-striped button-down shirt, navy blazer and quartz field watch on a blue and yellow nylon strap, but ditched the charcoal trousers and light brown penny loafers he’d worn earlier in favor of lighter-wash jeans and cowboy boots.
