Rina Shah has been listening with us. She is a political strategist with experience as a GOP congressional adviser. Good morning, Rina.
RINA SHAH: Hi. Good morning.
MARTIN: So Mara mentioned the president's complaints, and in some cases, moves against people like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, the media, the government of Norway. Is - does any of that motivate voters at this point, either in his base or independents?
SHAH: Well, I think it's really important to see what this really is. The diesel deal and the energy ceasefire announcement, I believe, are less about immediate relief and more about creating a permission structure for Republican candidates. The volumes are really too small to meaningfully move prices before November 3. I think most analysts are saying that plainly, and most of us kind of get that.
But the move lets candidates say that the president is trying something on cost instead of doing nothing. And that's really the narrow political utility here. The risk is that Zelenskyy's criticism and then the lack of clear details on the ceasefire turn it into another foreign policy story that down-ballot Republicans then have to explain rather than use.
MARTIN: But also it doesn't work. It doesn't seem to be working. He's saying one thing, and the facts prove to be otherwise. And to that end, you know, the president's defending - he's aggressively defended his decision to launch trade wars with much of the world, his military war with Iran. Those are both things that have raised prices for Americans. The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll indicates that independent voters favor Democrats by 19 points on the economy. So the question is, you're saying, even if it creates a permission structure, does that - is that enough?
SHAH: Well, look, let's look at the broader midterm picture here. Trump is running the same play he always has - make every race about himself and then bet that his base's intensity outweighs his approval numbers, which we know are pretty dismal. The difference this cycle is that the grievances that are driving a lot of the White House's agenda - which are media fights, the Department of Justice's action against people from the first term, his personal score-settling - those are more self-generated than they were in 2016 or '18. Back then, a larger share of what he amplified tracked the existing voter frustration.
Now more of it originates from inside the administration, and it's getting projected outward, and that really changes the utility for candidates. It motivates the core base, but it doesn't give swing voters a new reason to show up when their main concern is still the price of diesel and groceries. But I'd be remiss if I didn't mention here the practical problem for Republicans in these next three weeks, and it's that there is not a clean off-ramp for them. Candidates in really tight races would prefer a more narrow message on things like border enforcement and costs, and the White House is not structured at all to deliver that.
Trump treats the midterms as an extension of his own presidency rather than a set of local races, which is really unusual, even by our modern standards. Presidents have always campaigned, but they have rarely, rarely made themselves the constant central character this late while the party is trailing on the economy. And what that does is forces candidates to either fully nationalize their races or spend time creating distance, and neither of which is ideal with three weeks left.
MARTIN: Sure. So if the president can't or won't focus his message on what voters care about right now, and if there doesn't seem to be anybody in the president's circle who can get him to do that, is there anything that congressional candidates can do?
SHAH: Oh, that is the question du jour. Look, three weeks out, it's very hard for anyone to redirect him. He sets the agenda. The people closest to him can sometimes influence timing or emphasis on a particular issue like prices, but they rarely change his overall focus or stop him from going where he wants to go. At this point in the midterm cycle, I think the political reality of the map and the polls can sometimes force a more narrow message. But that's really different, again, from someone inside Trump world circle - they're successfully shifting him.
I would say this - look, if the polls are right and Republicans are trailing on the broad economy or the cost-of-living question, the other issues that can still drive their turnout are the border and public safety. Those have consistently been stronger for Republicans in recent cycles, and they give candidates a concrete contrast - things like enforcement, resources and results, versus what they argue has been a more permissive Democratic policy.
MARTIN: OK, before we let you go through...
SHAH: Also energy domestic production.
MARTIN: Thirty seconds left, though. Republicans...
SHAH: Sure
MARTIN: ...A big campaign bank. Republicans are outspending Democrats in these final weeks. Do they have - is that enough to erase some of these Democratic advantages that we're seeing in the polls?
SHAH: Truly, I don't believe so. I think right now, what we're looking at is a real downside because what's emanating from the White House has created that. The downside here to Trump's strategy so far is that it's locked the midterms into a pure referendum on him. And look, by inserting himself constantly and tying every race to his record and grievances, he's made it really hard for vulnerable Republicans to run as independent of Washington. And in a cycle where his approval is low and prices remain high, that nationalizes races in a way that often favors the out-party...
MARTIN: OK.
SHAH: ...Which is the Democrats.
MARTIN: That is Republican political strategist Rina Shah. Rina, thanks.
SHAH: Thank you.

theguardian.com.title: Australian politics live: Climate protester restrained after interrupting NSW parliament; Albanese says he’ll do whatever he can to stop ‘abhorrent’ US execution live stream
theguardian.com.text:
Climate protester restrained by MPs after interrupting NSW parliament
Penry Buckley
A climate protester has been restrained by NSW MPs after he climbed over a barrier to interrupt question time to protest against the approval of the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) coalmine extension by the state’s Independent Planning Commission last month.
Earlier this afternoon, question time was interrupted for several minutes by the protest, during which eight activists from environmental advocacy group Rising Tide threw pages of government and academic climate reports into the chamber, including the Net Zero Commission’s report on coalmining emissions, which said mine expansions are against the state’s legislated emissions reduction targets.
In the parliamentary livestream, MPs appeared shocked before the speaker, Greg Piper, cut the feed. Footage shared by the group Rising Tide, which organised the protest, showed two MPs, independent MP Michael Regan and Labor MP David Saliba, helping parliamentary staff restrain one protester who climbed over the barrier.
In a statement, the protester, Andrew Sneddon, said he had been driven to do so by “the Minns government’s failure to address the climate crisis”.
We need a government that listens to its own experts, stops approving new fossil fuel projects and delivers an urgent, fair transition for coal workers and communities.
As the world hurtles towards climate catastrophe, we cannot stand by in silence. If our government won’t act with the urgency this crisis demands, everyday people like myself are forced to step up.
The Minns government has been contacted for comment.
Thanks for joining us today. Here were our key headlines:
Australia engineer Robert Pether, released from an Iraqi prison after more than five years in prison over a contract dispute, has again asserted his innocence and said he was hours from death when he was finally freed.
The Northern Territory is set to legalise the use of OC Spray (also known as pepper spray), citing a 99% success rate for its trial. Availability will also be expanded, with 16 and 17-year-olds allowed to carry the spray with parental permission, the NT government said.
A climate protester was restrained by NSW MPs after he climbed over a barrier to interrupt question time to protest against the approval of the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) coalmine extension by the state’s Independent Planning Commission last month.
Liberal National MP Angie Bellwas forced to withdraw a comment on the floor of the House of Representatives that small business minister Anne Aly and prime minister Anthony Albanese should be “stoned in the square” over a tax office decision. Aly later condemned the comments.
And the eSafety commission says it “does not have powers to proactively prevent” the livestreaming of a US military execution, but says it will monitor and enforce existing standards that could obligate online platforms to block it themselves.
Thanks for joining us – we’ll be back again tomorrow morning.
'It is racist. It is misogynistic': Anne Aly responds to Coalition MP's 'stoning' comment
The Labor minister Anne Aly has responded powerfully to a “racist … misogynistic” comment on the floor of parliament after the Liberal National MP Angie Bell said Aly should be “stoned in the square” over a tax office decision.
Bell was forced to withdraw the comment, also directed at the prime minister.
Aly has also revealed the awful reality that she has received 19 death threats on social media in the past week alone.
On Instagram, Aly said:
I don’t usually comment about these sorts of things, but I feel like I have to. This past week alone, I’ve had 19 death threats on my social media. And in the past I’ve had death threats that are couched in that exact same language.
Stone her.
It’s not just something that a parliamentarian shouldn’t say in terms of advocating violence against another parliamentarian. It is something that stands against our Australian values.
We are a country that proudly stands against violence against women and against regimes that usual brutal methods like stoning against women.
This is not just something that we should just turn away from.
It is racist.
It is misogynistic.
And it is something that should never have been said.
No police action expected as NSW attorney general calls climate protester a 'ratbag'
NSW police say no further action is expected after this afternoon’s protest at state parliament against the approval of the extension of the Hunter Valley Operations mine.
In a statement, a police spokesperson said at about 12.35pm on Tuesday, a man “jumped from the public gallery onto the floor the NSW Parliament Legislative Assembly during question time”.
“He was removed from the room by NSW Police Special Constables and issued a move on direction which he complied with. No further police action is expected at this time.”
David Saliba, one of the MPs involved in restraining protester Andrew Sneddon after he jumped from the gallery, told Channel Nine that MPs were surprised by a loud noise as Sneddon landed on the chamber floor.
It was pretty bad, I think at the time because our backs were towards it. [I] heard it, [I] reacted as best I could, and to see all the other MP faces as well being a bit shocked by it all. Not the way to get your message across.
Speaking in question time after the protest, the NSW attorney general, Michael Daley, said in 21 years in parliament, he had “never seen a member of the gallery jump on to the floor of the house”, calling Sneddon a “ratbag”.
“It is completely unacceptable behaviour, this is the people’s house, it is open to the public in ways that many parliaments around Australia and the world are not and we would like to keep it that way.”
In a statement, the NSW Greens justice spokesperson, Sue Higginson, said that “non-violent protests that inconvenience people in the pursuit of global survival should be listened to and understood, and I’ve been told that the last time someone entered the NSW Parliament floor was the suffragettes fighting for the vote”.
The climate crisis is going to get worse, and people that have copped the fires and floods and droughts will rightly come to our democratic institutions for accountability and to have their voices heard.
One Nation migration cuts won’t stop skilled workers coming to Australia, Hanson says
Pauline Hanson has told an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry event at Parliament House that One Nation won’t stop skilled workers coming into the country.
Despite promising cuts to net overseas migration (Nom) of more than 750,000 people over three years, Hanson says business won’t lose out.
“We are not going to hold back any business that requires skilled labour coming to the country,” she says.
“We’re not attacking that.”
Hanson says workers coming into the country on the Pacific Island Labour Mobility Scheme, as well as working holidaymakers and other skilled workers will be allowed into Australia.
“That skilled migration program, of skills that we need. No more Uber drivers. No more tax accountants and all this rest of it that we don’t need.”
Under Hanson’s plan, released last month, temporary visa numbers would be returned to 2017 levels, under what One Nation says would represent a net-negative arrivals rate for the first three years. That would mean the net overseas migration total would be 130,000 under the One Nation plan.
Economists, immigration experts and key sectors, including universities and aged care, all say the policy will damage the economy and cause worker shortages.
Childcare paedophile confronted in court as extradition to NSW approved
One of Australia’s most notorious paedophiles has had abuse hurled at him in court after a move interstate to face 180 more charges was approved, AAP reports.
A victim supporter vented her fury at the former childcare worker Ashley Paul Griffith, 48, in Brisbane magistrates court on Tuesday, screaming: “Rot! Rot! Fire! Brimstone! Burn!”
Griffith was jailed for life with a non-parole period of 27 years in Queensland in November 2024 after pleading guilty to 307 child sexual offences.
He has also been charged in New South Wales with 180 child sexual offences allegedly committed against 23 girls at a childcare centre in Sydney between 2014 and 2017.
Magistrate Belinda Merrin was told an application had been filed on 13 July on behalf of the NSW attorney general, Michael Daley.
That followed an application on 26 June by Queensland attorney general, Deb Frecklington, who had unsuccessfully asked for the transfer to be fast-tracked.
The application was not opposed by Griffith’s barrister Matt Black.
The path for Griffith to be transferred to face the NSW charges was cleared in June after his appeal against the severity of his Queensland sentence was dismissed.
Merrin did not specify a date or time for Griffith’s transfer.
Throughout two decades of preying on children in Queensland, Griffith filmed all but one of his victims, building a vast cache of abuse he shared online.
When detectives raided his Gold Coast home in 2022, they seized more than 4,000 child abuse images and videos documenting much of his offending.
The offences related to more than 60 victims aged between one and nine, including 28 rapes of preschool-aged girls in Queensland childcare centres.
NorthernTerritory to legalise OC spray for people as young as 16
The Northern Territory is set to legalise the use of OC spray, citing a 99% success rate in its trial.
Availability will also be expanded, with 16 and 17-year-olds allowed to carry the spray with parental permission, the NT government says.
OC (oleoresin capsicum) spray is also know as pepper spray. It causes immediate inflammation and severe burning sensation in the eyes, skin and respiratory tract.
“Territorians have embraced OC spray for self-defence and made it clear they want to continue to have access and they want to see that access expanded to younger people,” says the chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro.
“During the trial, we had a lot of feedback about OC spray only being available to people aged 18 years and over, with many parents telling us that they wanted their 16 and 17-year-olds to have access as well.”
Pepper spray provides a self-defence option for young people, many of whom held down night-time jobs, Finocchiaro says.
Availability will also be extended to roles in security, hospitality, crowd control and licensed venues.
Western Australia is the only other jurisdiction in the country allowing the general sale of OC spray.
Deputy opposition leader asked about MP’s ‘stoning’ comment
Back on Afternoon Briefing on the ABC, the deputy opposition leader, Ted O’Brien, is asked about comments from the member for Moncrieff, Angie Bell, who said in parliament the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and small business minister, Anne Aly, should be “shamed and stoned in the square” over the tax office’s decision to ban credit cards being used to pay tax bills.
Bell was forced to withdraw the comments, made on the floor of the House of Reps.
“Look, Angie was the first then to hop up and withdraw her comments,” O’Brien says, before pivoting to praising Bell’s willingness to “fight” for her electorate.
However, pushed by Patricia Karvelas, O’Brien concedes “tone and language” matter in politics.
“And that is why she did the right thing by withdrawing.”
One Nation treasury spokesperson, Barnaby Joyce, has challenged Jim Chalmers to a debate on the economy.
Speaking at Parliament House in Canberra, Joyce, who defected from the Nationals last year, says he has “a rough idea” what he’s doing in the portfolio.
“I’m happy to pull myself up against Chalmers any day of the week, if you want to line it up, I’ll have a lot of fun there,” he says.
He says he is happy to debate Tim Wilson, the shadow treasurer, as well, but concedes One Nation is “not out to kill the Coalition”.
“We’re out to get rid of the socialist government. We believe it’s a socialist government. I was thinking this morning … what happens if there wasn’t One Nation who weren’t doing the job we’re doing?
“Australia would be a very depressing place because you know you’re in the status quo. You know it’s stagnant.”
Worst conditions in Australia since the depression, Hanson says
Tom McIlroy
The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, says economic conditions in Australia are the worst since the Great Depression, including for business operators, the manufacturing sector and the homeless.
“I have never seen the country as bad as this, as what I am seeing at the moment,” she has told an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry event in Canberra.
“Politics in Australia is changing. It’s changing because people have never done as tough as what they are now.
“I don’t think I remember a time, apart from the depression, that I have heard about, [with] the number of people who are homelesses in our country, the number of small businesses that have gone insolvent.”
A few more things from Anthony Albanese’s interview withPatricia Karvelas.
The prime minister confirms he will attend the Cop31 climate conference – Australia is joint host – in Turkey next month.
It’s been in my diary for some time.
I’ve been invited specifically by President Erdogan, the relationship with Turkey is a very important one.
And I think it sends a really good message that you essentially have leadership of this Cop from Turkey and Australia, two countries that are geographically very, very distant, have different economies, different cultures, but which are working together in the interests of humanity.
The PM is asked his opinion of the Trump administration considering livestreaming the execution by firing squad of former US soldier Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people in a mass shooting on a military base more than a decade ago.
Australia has had a bipartisan position of opposition to the death penalty. And I find the idea of livestreaming the death of anybody completely abhorrent. We should do whatever we can to stop that occurring.
I don’t know why anyone would want themselves to watch such an event, let alone sit back and allow potentially kids and families to get access to this.
Pauline Hanson is speaking at the same time as the PM.
The One Nation leader is attending a conference hosted by the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry at Parliament House.
She slams the Albanese government over its handling of the economy, including the Australian Taxation Office ban on credit cards and tough conditions for small business operators.
Hanson says she and One Nation’s treasury spokesperson, Barnaby Joyce, have experience running small businesses, something she says is in contrast with the Labor frontbench.
“One Nation wants Australia to be the best place in the world to do business,” Hanson says. “Not one of the best. The best.”
Hanson has called for government to get out of the way of business operators, to cut red tape and provide sustainable energy supply.
Albanese denies his government is in a ‘midterm slump’
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is appearing on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program.
He is taken to comments he made to his own caucus that the government “would be kicking with the wind in the fourth quarter” (an Australian rules reference from a rugby league-following PM).
Albanese is asked whether this is a concession his government is in a “midterm slump”.
No, what it means is that you need to make sure that we continue to be focused on the needs of Australians.
We need to make sure as well that we’re focused on, where are we at, a year ahead, 10 years ahead.
How do we set Australia up for the stronger future?
Albanese also – uninvited – reflects on the former Kooyong MP Josh Frydenberg “stalking” the opposition leader, Angus Taylor. Frydenberg has published a book, seen as an undeclared, and as yet uncommitted – but still very public – consideration of a return to politics.
Detained democracy campaigner to meet consular officials in Vietnam
The detained Australian democracy campaigner Tran Hiep will be able to meet Australian consular officials in Vietnam for the first time since his sudden arrest nearly a month ago.
The 51-year-old hasn’t been directly heard from since before he failed to board his flight from the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, on 18 September after meeting with human rights defenders.
Vietnamese authorities confirmed he had been arrested and charged with alleged terrorism and forging identity documents and it’s understood he is being held in Ho Chi Minh City’s B34 pre-trial detention centre.
Hiep’s wife, Chloe Dang, has told Guardian Australia he will soon be granted his first in-person visit with consular officials though contact with his family is still not allowed.
The Labor MP Emma Comergot booted, as did the Nationals MP Kevin Hogan, after he accused the government of running a “protection racket” around small business minister, Anne Aly.
Tony Burkewould not confirm whether the commonwealth would approve or reject a massive coalmine extension in NSW.
Some more from the NSW parliament, where the state government has introduced legislation to establish the Great Koala national park.
The member for the Blue Mountains, Trish Doyle, who introduced the bill said the state forests in the legislation would only be incorporated in the new park once the Clean Energy Regulator had formally recognised the associated carbon project.
Penny Sharpe said 13% of the 178,000 hectares would be designated regional reserve, rather than national park, to allow recreational activities such as bushwalking, trail-bike riding, camping and four-wheel driving to continue, as well as dog walking in select reserves. She said this decision followed community feedback.
The bill would allow the minister to approve motor racing events on existing regional roads in regional parks within the Great Koala national park, “recognising the long history of car rally events in the region”.
The government said it continued to support affected forestry workers, with the bill containing a provision enabling Forestry Corporation staff to be appointed to suitable roles within NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service.
NSW government introduces bill to establish Great Koala national park
The New South Wales government has introduced legislation to establish the long-promised Great Koala national park.
The new park will add more than 178,000 hectares of state forest to the national parks estate, with the government estimating it will protect 12,000 koalas, 36,000 gliders and more than 100 threatened species.
The park will go ahead after a contentious regulatory change by the Albanese government allowing state governments to earn carbon credits by storing carbon dioxide in native forests on public land.
Combined with existing national parks and reserves, it will be one of the largest parks in NSW, creating a protected area spanning more than 475,000 hectares.
The NSW environment minister, Penny Sharpe, said:
The Great Koala national park is one of the most important things we can do to save koalas in NSW. It is also about creating an area that people can explore and enjoy for generations.
State parliament will debate the bill next week and the government hopes the park will be officially gazetted and opened by the end of the year.
Government pay offer falls short, public service union says
The main public sector union says the federal government’s offer of a 9% pay rise over the next three years falls short of expectations.
The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) put a 5% pay rise each year or equal to CPI – whichever is higher – which it said had been endorsed by more than 18,000 members.
The CPSU’s newly elected national secretary, Rebecca Fawcett, said the union would speak with members once more about next steps.
CPSU members [have] been clear from the beginning of these negotiations: they want to see pay that keeps up with the cost of living, which recognises the essential work they do every day. The APS-wide pay offer that has been tabled today falls short of what our members asked for, and what public sector workers deserve. This is now in our members’ hands. They will decide whether it is good enough, and the union will continue to fight for a pay offer that respects these vital workers, and the important services they deliver to the community.
Climate protester restrained by MPs after interrupting NSW parliament
Penry Buckley
A climate protester has been restrained by NSW MPs after he climbed over a barrier to interrupt question time to protest against the approval of the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) coalmine extension by the state’s Independent Planning Commission last month.

In the parliamentary livestream, MPs appeared shocked before the speaker, Greg Piper, cut the feed. Footage shared by the group Rising Tide, which organised the protest, showed two MPs, independent MP Michael Regan and Labor MP David Saliba, helping parliamentary staff restrain one protester who climbed over the barrier.
In a statement, the protester, Andrew Sneddon, said he had been driven to do so by “the Minns government’s failure to address the climate crisis”.
We need a government that listens to its own experts, stops approving new fossil fuel projects and delivers an urgent, fair transition for coal workers and communities.
As the world hurtles towards climate catastrophe, we cannot stand by in silence. If our government won’t act with the urgency this crisis demands, everyday people like myself are forced to step up.
The Minns government has been contacted for comment.

theguardian.com.title: Shock, anger and a crackdown: why a contentious electoral revision has sparked outrage
theguardian.com.text:
Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.
Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.
The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.
“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.
The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.
While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.
The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.
The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.
Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.
Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.
As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”
On Monday, the Kerelam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”
What else we’re reading about
Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.
Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.
Climate| Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announced water cuts of at least 10% across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
32
At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check
For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”
For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.
Get in touch
Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

theguardian.com.title: RJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad, dies aged 34
theguardian.com.text:
The actor RJ Mitte, whose personal experience living with cerebral palsy informed his role as Walter White Jr in the television series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34 in Brownsville, Texas.
“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” Mitte’s representatives said in a statement. “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.”
A publicist for the actor confirmed news reports that Mitte took his own life. No further details about the circumstances were given.
The Brownsville police department said no foul play was suspected. The Cameron County justice of the peace, Cyndi Hinojosa, told the Associated Press that an autopsy would be performed.
From the age of 15, Mitte played Walter White Jr, the son of Bryan Cranston’s high school chemistry teacher turned drug kingpin, Walter White, on 56 episodes of the acclaimed AMC show, which is often cited as one of the best television series of all time.
In 2015, he spoke to the Guardian about being a disabled actor who played disabled characters. “You accept the risks and you accept these will be the parts you play. But it’s all about how you play those parts – you have to show the inner strength that people have,” he said.
Mitte’s co-stars paid tribute to him after news of his death broke, including Cranston, who wrote a lengthy tribute on Instagram. Cranston described him as “my sweet son on Breaking Bad”, a “fine actor” and a “vocal advocate for performers with disabilities”.
“It is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life,” Cranston wrote. He said he and Mitte had been texting each other a few weeks ago about possibly meeting for lunch. “I don’t know if that lunch would have changed his future,” Cranston wrote. “But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed. I’ll miss you, son.“
He said Mitte “never – ever – allowed [his disability] to be an excuse for anything” during the show’s production. “He met the demanding shooting schedule head-on with great determination.”
Aaron Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman, said in a statement: “I am at a loss. I am heartbroken over this news. RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed.”
Dean Norris, who played Walt Jr’s uncle Hank Schrader, wrote on social media: “Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can’t believe it. Thinking of him and his family.”
In addition to Breaking Bad, Mitte had roles on other series including Switched at Birth and The Guardians of Justice. Days before his death, he was promoting his new film, Talking to Strangers, billed as a “romantic tragedy”.
Earlier this month, Mitte appeared on the Joe Vulpis Podcast, speaking in depth about his time on Breaking Bad. He noted his character was based on a real-life friend of the show’s creator, Vince Gilligan. “It really felt real playing this character and getting into the groove with this character,” Mitte said.
Offscreen, Mitte was an outspoken advocate for disability representation in entertainment, and he served in various philanthropic roles, including as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and as president of the Mitte Foundation.
Born in 1992, Mitte was raised in Mississippi by adoptive parents. In a 2016 interview with the Guardian, he said he found out he was adopted when he was eight years old.
“My step-brother told me. He’d overheard my mum and my stepdad at the time talking about it, and he threw it in my face,” he said. “But I didn’t really care. It didn’t seem relevant, because I never once in my life felt unloved or like I was a burden.”
- In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

theguardian.com.title: Coastal erosion in England has claimed at least 183 homes in past 16 years
theguardian.com.text:
Seaside communities along the east coast of England have lost at least 183 homes to coastal erosion and landslides over the past 16 years, figures obtained by the Guardian reveal.
After councils judged properties across the Yorkshire and East Anglian coasts too vulnerable to remain safely occupied, the homes were proactively demolished.
The demolitions cost £1.1m, with the Environment Agency contributing about £482,000 towards clearing 61 homes at risk of collapsing and the rest paid for by councils and at times by homeowners themselves.
Coastal erosion is the gradual wearing away and retreat of the sea shoreline, which can destabilise cliffs and eventually force homes and infrastructure to be demolished before they collapse. While it is a natural process, scientists said the climate crisis was accelerating the retreat of the UK’s shores.
The Guardian requested data from nine councils noted in a House of Commons environment, food and rural affairs committee (EFRA) report as being some of the most vulnerable to coastal erosion.
East Riding of Yorkshire council, which includes vulnerable communities in Skipsea, Aldbrough and Mappleton, has demolished 66 homes since 2010 – the most of these nine local authorities.
Great Yarmouth borough council (GYBC) has demolished 64 homes since 2010, with all the houses located in the village of Hemsby. Since December 2025, the council has removed 41 properties in the seaside resort.
A GYBC spokesperson said: “Last winter, the dunes in Hemsby saw about 50% of the erosion predicted for the entirety of the next 30 years. More than 10 metres of land was lost in just over 12 months.
“Council staff continue to liaise with people to make sure residents and the public are safe and work closely with people to offer support and advice and explain the options available.”
North Norfolk council has proactively demolished 21 homes over the same period.
East Suffolk council, which only held data for the past six years, recorded a sharp rise in demolitions last year. Eight homes were demolished between 2020 and 2024, and 16 between May last year and April this year.
Most of East Suffolk’s homes demolished this year are understood to be in Thorpeness. Hilary Lightfoot’s home, in which she lived and raised a family for 20 years, was demolished this year. “I’ve lost £650,000 – that was what my flat was worth,” she said. “I’ve had to dig into my pension savings to buy a house, of which I still owe money on. I’ve borrowed money. It’s just disastrous.”
The Environment Agency estimates that 3,500 properties in England are at risk from coastal erosion by 2055, increasing to more than 10,000 properties by 2105.
More than 6 miles (10km) of major roads, 107 miles of minor roads and 3.5 miles of railway – many serving small, coastal communities – are also at risk from erosion over the next 80 years, according to the EA.
Unlike flood damage, which can be covered by the Flood Re scheme, there is no UK insurance product for coastal erosion because insurers treat coastal retreat as a “virtual certainty” for some seaside homes rather than an accidental risk, according to the EFRA committee’s report.
East Suffolk council said that although some government funding was available towards demolition, “there are currently limited mechanisms to support the wider costs of adaptation and relocation” for residents.
The authority said it had invested about £1.5m in short-term measures designed to slow erosion and give residents more time to prepare, while also testing new approaches through the government’s flood and coastal innovation programme.
Sophie Day, senior research associate at the University of East Anglia, said because the east coast was made up of “very sandy, gravelly, silty material”, it was more vulnerable to erosion.
She said wetter winters, made more likely by the climate crisis, would saturate and destabilise soft cliffs such as those on the east coast, while increased storminess and rising sea levels would worsen the impact of high tides and leave beaches with less time to recover between storms.
While councils have increased spending on sea defences over the decades, Day said these protections have created an “illusion of permanence” for what is an accelerating issue. The scale of the threat from coastal erosion meant “we are going to have to shift to more of an acceptance of not intervening any more and enabling retreat”, she added.
Day said adapting to a retreating coastline meant planning for the loss of homes and infrastructure before the next emergency, while working more closely with communities.
“Having skilled people who are able to engage, who have the time, the training, the skills, to go and sit at somebody’s kitchen table and talk to them about the fact that, in a year, even five months’ time, their home may not be livable. What are the options? How can we find ways of giving people choices and support?”
North Norfolk district council (NNDC) said: “Households in all 21 homes were supported by NNDC. Nineteen of these properties were proactively demolished before they reached the cliff edge and became an emergency.
“NNDC continues to work with the Environment Agency and Defra … to better prepare communities. A number of pilot opportunities are under development. It is hoped that through this work, more targeted support for those impacted can become part of the business as usual and supported by government for the whole coast into the future.”
A spokesperson for East Riding council said: “East Riding of Yorkshire has some of the fastest eroding coastlines in Europe, resulting in the loss of homes, businesses and roads. Through the Changing Coasts East Riding project, the council is working directly with residents, businesses and communities to find out the full economic, environmental and social impacts of these losses.”
An Environment Agency spokesperson said it was “very aware” of how erosion was affecting coastal homeowners and communities.
They said: “While local authorities are best placed to support affected residents, we’re backing them with £36m for coastal erosion adaptation pilots, slashing planning regulation red tape in vulnerable areas and offering £10,000 grants to fund the safe demolition of affected properties – with scope to go further for more complex jobs.”

theguardian.com.title: Same-sex couple sue over Slovakia’s refusal to register marriage
theguardian.com.text:
A same-sex couple are suing authorities in Slovakia for refusing to register their Austrian marriage, testing whether a landmark EU court ruling can turn recognition abroad into legal security at home.
Their fight exposes a clash between European obligations and national restrictions – and what that means for LGBTQ+ people living under Robert Fico’s populist-nationalist government.
Ivan Novotný, 31, and Metod Špaček, 51, married in Austria in 2020, but six years on, their marital status at home remains unrecognised.
There is no same-sex marriage in Slovakia, a socially conservative, predominantly Catholic country; neither is there any form of civil partnership.
But Novotný and Špaček, who are both lawyers and former diplomats, are not asking for that. They want the Slovakian authorities to recognise a marriage that was concluded legally in another EU country – something the bloc’s top court has said is mandatory for all EU members.
“I’ve said this publicly several times, and [LGBTQ+] activists in Slovakia have criticised me for it: Metod and I are not discriminated against here. We have a lovely life here in Bratislava, in Slovakia,” Novotný said. “So, we don’t actually need [recognition of marriage] for our day-to-day lives.”
For example, said Novotný, when Špaček was hospitalised during the Covid pandemic he was treated by a “lovely” doctor who recognised Novotný’s official relationship to her patient.
He added: “She put me down on the report as ‘husband’ and gave me all your [Špaček] medical information. The problem is: that was because she was nice, not because she had to do it. If someone wanted to make trouble for us, they could do it.
“That’s not how the rule of law should work.”
The couple argue they are on solid legal ground after a ruling by the EU’s highest court in November 2025 in response to a case brought by a Polish same-sex couple who had married in Berlin.
Jakub Cupriak-Trojan and Mateusz Trojan had challenged the Mazovia provincial governor’s refusal to recognise their German marriage. The court ruled that member states must recognise such marriages where couples had exercised their right to move and reside in another EU country, and created or strengthened family life there.
The European court of justice ruling does not require member states to allow same-sex weddings at home.
The Slovakian authorities explained why Novotný and Špaček’s request to register their Austrian marriage had been turned down in a letter signed by the interior minister, Matúš Šutaj Eštok.
“[The letter] says that since the constitutional definition of marriage [in Slovakia] is a bond between a man and a woman, they lack the legal basis for formally recognising the marriage certificate. That’s essentially it,” said Špaček, who served as chief of staff to the country’s liberal former president Zuzana Čaputová.
Across town, in the house his grandparents built on a hill overlooking the Danube, Marián Žáry Kukelka, 44, recalled his wedding to his partner, Ondrej, in 2023. The couple married in Hainburg an der Donau, an Austrian town visible from their terrace.
Žáry Kukelka, a radio presenter for the public broadcaster STVR, is also suing Slovakian authorities. He uses his full married name on air (Žáry is Ondrej’s surname) and is supported by his colleagues. But his official documents refer to him as Marián Kukelka. He said: “It’s a court case for love. I don’t need that surname to live my life, but for me it’s a kind of tribute to my partner, that I can carry his surname too.”.
Žáry Kukelka lives behind Bratislava Castle, not far from Zámocká street – the scene of the homophobic attack in 2022 where two people were shot dead outside the LGBTQ+ bar Tepláreň.
The anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric of many Slovakian politicians, especially in the government, was contributing to an atmosphere of increasing hostility, he said.
Last year, Fico’s government backed constitutional changes recognising only two sexes and tightening adoption restrictions. Žáry Kukelka told the Guardian that Hainburg an der Donau had been “overwhelmed” with LGBTQ+ couples from Slovakia wanting to get married since a change to Austrian legislation made it possible.
He himself had experienced little in the way of abuse as a gay man, he said, although he admitted he thought carefully before using the words “my husband”, depending on whom he was talking to.
“Two weeks ago, we were in Switzerland, and there we held hands in public for the first time in a long time,” he said. “We felt it was different there.”
Slovakia’s interior ministry said it was bound by the country’s existing constitutional and legal framework, regardless of whether a marriage was valid abroad.
It acknowledged the primacy of EU law but argued that recognition for freedom of movement purposes did not require registration as a marriage. Its administrative work “cannot replace decisions by the legislature or the constitutional legislature,” the ministry told the Guardian.

theguardian.com.title: Tuesday briefing: Could Burnham take Britain back towards the EU?
theguardian.com.text:
Good morning. After a holiday spent contracting nursery bugs from an 11-month-old, it’s good to return. Yesterday, Andy Burnham marked his first day back after party conference by calling for a closer relationship with the EU and drawing a line under a decade of “drift and division”. On Sunday, he said it was “clear” the Kremlin had been involved with the 2016 Brexit referendum vote.
Both statements mark a break, rhetorically at least, from his predecessors. Conservative governments long insisted there was no evidence of Russian interference in the Brexit vote. Keir Starmer attempted to put the entire issue of Brexit behind him, treating it as a historic event rather than a cause of economic pain.
But for all his words about a closer relationship with the EU, Burnham has kept the details pretty vague. Today’s newsletter, with the help of the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent Jennifer Rankin and our senior political correspondent Peter Walker, asks what his stance might actually amount to. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories
- UK | Andy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps were “almost certainly” behind threats to RAF Fairford, the firmest attribution of responsibility made so far by the UK after an incident late last month.
- UK politics | A close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm, the Guardian revealed.
- Ukraine | Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to respond to Russia’s continuing attacks on the Ukrainian power grid as European leaders rally around Kyiv amid a feud with Donald Trump over Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries.
- Israel | Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the documentary NAZA and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.
- US news | RJ Mitte, the young actor best known for playing Walter White Jr in the award-winning TV series Breaking Bad, died on Monday. He was 34.
In depth: What does Burnham want from Europe?
In the years after it voted to leave the European Union, Britain became something of a laughing stock among EU member states. “It was like a box set TV drama. People in Brussels would be staying up to watch votes in the House of Commons,” Jennifer Rankin, who moved to Brussels to cover the EU for the Guardian in January 2016, tells me. Civil servants in Brussels grew to regard the UK as one might regard a belligerent and ungrateful elderly relative, an impression that reached its apotheosis when the former Northern Ireland secretary Brandon Lewis admitted that the UK’s Brexit arrangements for Northern Ireland would break international law (albeit in a “very specific and limited way”.)
“From 2016 to 2020, the UK was seen as a model of how not to run your country,” Jennifer says. This impression softened after the passing of the Withdrawal Agreement Act in early 2020, and the Windsor framework deal, which amended the arrangements under the Northern Ireland protocol in 2023. “That was a turning point in drawing a line under the bad blood of the Brexit years,” Jennifer says. Keir Starmer’s government then sought to cooperate with the EU on various issues such as security, food and fishing, but the “reset” he pledged to deliver was tightly circumscribed by his red lines: no rejoining the single market, no customs union, no freedom of movement.
After his conference speech, Burnham suggested he might be open to reconsidering this when he suggested, somewhat cryptically, that the UK could go “all the way” (presumably towards full EU membership), and yesterday he called for a “longer-term discussion” about Britain’s relationship with the EU. But what might that actually mean?
Could the UK rejoin the EU?
Burnham has been “showing a lot of ankle” to remainers over the last few weeks, Peter Walker tells me. During his Labour conference speech, he promised to lay out “different options” for Britain’s long-term relationship with Europe, and acknowledged that Brexit had caused “more harm than good”.
“It’s pretty clear that a decent majority of people would like to push a switch that meant Brexit had never happened,” Peter says. Indeed, a YouGov poll in January 2025 found that just 11% of people thought Brexit had been more of a success than a failure. And as recently as last week, the Messina Group, a polling company, reported that half of voters say they would like to rejoin the EU. The economic consequences of Brexit are now well known, and research has estimated that, a decade after the referendum, UK GDP per head is between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been without Brexit. Yet reversing this decision would require another referendum, which would be politically fraught, reigniting a debate that splintered the country a decade ago, and reducing a highly complex and technical issue to a binary decision.
It’s hard to imagine Burnham – or any politician, for that matter – wanting to fight the next election while pledging something so divisive. Notably, even the Liberal Democrats, the most pro-EU of the major parties, favour rejoining the single market and customs union but describe UK membership of the EU as a “long-term goal” rather than an immediate priority.
What other options are on the table?
If a second referendum seems like a vanishingly distant prospect, other changes could take place without one. In the combustive years after Brexit, there was a short-lived hope that the UK might pursue its own version of the Norway model, allowing it to become a member of the European Economic Area. “It was the Conservatives who decided to pursue the hardest Brexit possible,” Peter reminds me.
In theory, a softer deal could mean rejoining the single market and customs union. But this would mean breaking Labour’s red lines, which Burnham has said he will stick to. And if the UK was to rejoin the single market but remain outside the EU, it would be forced to accept rules that it had no power to shape. “As soon as you look at the democratic deficit that comes with single market membership, the case for rejoining the EU becomes stronger,” Jennifer tells me.
The debate over rejoining the EU is often conducted in relatively parochial terms, as if it only concerns Britain. But the UK’s future relationship with the EU will be largely shaped by the member states of a union that has changed significantly since the referendum. Far-right parties are gaining power in France and Germany, while the mercantilist politics of China and the US have inspired the EU’s Made in Europe agenda, a series of protectionist laws designed to bolster European industry and reduce reliance on Chinese imports.
In this context, Burnham may decide it’s better to be inside the tent than outside it. The Made in Europe agenda is particularly concerning for the government, since UK industry could suffer if exports were legally classified as “non-European” goods under these new laws. But as Mujtaba Rahman wrote in an interesting opinion piece for the Guardian in July, “any serious rejoin debate must start from an honest assessment of what the EU has become”.
What happens next?
Right now, the longer term outcome is anyone’s guess. In his statement to the Commons, Burnham confirmed that the planned UK-EU summit will go ahead in November. Negotiators are expected to discuss a trade deal on food and drink, a deal on emissions trading, a plan to link the energy systems of the EU and UK and the new youth mobility scheme. These areas were all discussed at last years’ UK-EU talks, so Burnham wasn’t announcing anything we didn’t already know.
“There’s a lot of frustration in Brussels that the UK has been talking a big game on a reset with the EU, without actually changing very much,” Jennifer says. “The theme over the last ten years is that the EU has always been waiting for the UK to define what it wants. The rhetoric may be warmer, but the substance has stayed the same.”
What else we’ve been enjoying
- I have always found that TV – with its twisting plotlines, and lack of demands – is a good cure for grief. Today’s one change that worked, by writer Georgina Elliott, on how the cinema gave her some focus after the death of her brother, poignantly depicted what it’s like to muddle through such times. Poppy Noor, newsletters team
- Chloe Kerleroux’s photo essay about Atlanta’s Bill Pickett rodeo is a beautiful window into a competition which encompasses athleticism, hip-hop, fashion and the celebration of contemporary Black cowboy and cowgirl culture. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team
- Here’s a line I didn’t expect to read today: professor Devi Sridhar, chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh, is worried about the pneumonic plague (although it might not be for the reasons you suspect). Poppy
- Kiran Sidhu was touching, on considering who to pass her most prized possessions down to in her will since she doesn’t have children. Poppy
- I, too, have been had by the myth that my (small amount of) muscle will turn into fat if I don’t force myself into a few push-ups every week. Not so, according to this week’s Is it true that … column – although what does happen when you stop exercising isn’t that much more reassuring. Poppy
Sport
Cycling | Matt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain team for next week’s World Cycling Championships in Shanghai amid allegations of misconduct.
Football | Almost half of female footballers are considering leaving the sport because of financial concerns or psychological stress, and 57% have struggled with their mental health, according to a report highlighting the working conditions for players worldwide.
Sport | Manchester United have endured their worst league start in 40 years but coach Michael Carrick insists he does not feel under pressure and has said his captain, Bruno Fernandes, will rediscover his form.
The front pages
The Guardian leads with “PM: Britain’s relationship with EU ‘not good enough’”. The i has “Burnham ready to sign new EU deal next month – as he attacks Brexit ‘damage’”. The Mail says “Burnham in retreat over Russia Brexit ‘lies’”.
The Times splashes on “Cut screen time in class ‘for sake of pupil health’”. The Financial Times has “Putin breaking ‘ceasefire’ on energy targets, says Zelenskyy”. The Mirror reports on comments from Reform’s Robert Jenrick on migrants, under the headline “Horrifying”.
Today in Focus: The Latest
Trump rewards Putin and betrays Ukraine with Russia diesel deal
Donald Trump’s deal to buy Russian diesel has been met with fury from Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said it was ‘a weak decision’ and would generate ‘billions’ in extra revenue for Putin’s war effort. The Ukrainian president has also rejected US calls for an ‘energy ceasefire’, which would require Kyiv to stop striking oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end its attacks on energy infrastructure. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s senior international correspondent, Luke Harding.
Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings
The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
The Naffah family has been making church bells in the Lebanese town of Beit Chabab for three centuries. Led by master bell-maker Naffah Naffah and his two sons, their workshop is the last remaining production centre for church bells in Lebanon and the only source of church bells for much of the Middle East.
Crafted using a mix of modern and ancient tools, each bell takes about two months to make and bears the names of those who worked on it. Naffah and his sons Charbel and Youssef are determined to preserve the tradition. Charbel will succeed his father as master of the workshop and Youssef helps alongside studying medicine, but says he would take Charbel’s place if needed.
“Traditions are important to us,” he says. “We are living and breathing tradition here in this workshop.”

Bored at work?
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

theguardian.com.title: Card surcharge ban used as ‘cover’ for larger price increases by Australian businesses, experts say
theguardian.com.text:
Businesses are using the recent ban on credit card surcharges as “cover” to pass along much larger price increases to customers, experts say, as cafes and restaurants struggle to cope with climbing costs and rising interest rates.
Credit card surcharges, typically worth about 1.5% of the transaction, were banned from 1 October, as part of a Reserve Bank-led reform aimed at improving transparency for customers and, ultimately, lowering bank fees.
Small Flat White, an online coffee price tracker, has reported that 17% of cafes have increased their prices since the start of the surcharge ban.
Of those who raised coffee prices, the average increase was 50c, or more than 10%, according to the survey of more than 1,500 cafes.
That is multiples of the typical 1.5% card surcharge fee.
Stephen Wu, an economist at investment bank UBS, said resilient consumer demand and a high inflation environment “may be allowing merchants to use the change as ‘cover’ to pass through broader cost pressures”.
“Following years of above-target inflation, consumers may be more accepting of price rises,” Wu said.
“Evidence of ‘round-up’ pricing in items such as coffee suggests pass-through could exceed the surcharge itself.”
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has warned businesses that they must not “mislead consumers” by claiming a price rise is due to the surcharge ban when the increase also reflects other costs.
The ACCC has also said that businesses who try to avoid the ban by describing the surcharge as another type of fee or charge “may be engaging in misleading conduct”.
Wes Lambert, chief executive of the Australian Restaurant & Cafe Association, said business costs were rising rapidly while coffee prices in Australia were among the lowest in the world.
Lambert said businesses changed their prices for many reasons, and that the surcharge ban could have been the impetus for company owners to build up the courage to pass on costs to customers.
“Maybe this is the catalyst that has caused cafes and restaurateurs around the country to wake up.”
Lambert said restaurants were blaming the need for price rises on higher produce costs, steep rents and recent adjustments to junior pay rates and awards.
Many business owners are also affected by the four interest rate rises in 2026, which have driven up repayments on variable-rate loans and equipment financing.
“It should be no surprise that in a high inflation, high interest rate environment that businesses are going to raise their prices,” he said.
Despite being telegraphed well in advance, the surcharge ban has triggered a furious response from small business groups.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, was forced to intervene after the Australian Taxation Office announced it would no longer accept credit card payments for tax owing.
Chalmers said the government would provide additional funding to the ATO to cover the cost of the surcharge until the middle of next year.
Despite the furore, Morgan Campbell, the head of policy at consumer advocate group Choice, said: “I don’t think there’s any shock in the way this is working”.
“There was always an acknowledgement that some businesses would put up their prices. But consumers are better off knowing the price up front,” Campbell said.
He said it was too early for Choice to begin its own research on how the surcharge ban was working.
“Some of this will take some time to wash through the system,” he said, noting the RBA expected businesses to put more effort into finding lower cost bank providers.
If some businesses are putting up their prices by much more than the surcharge, Campbell suggested it was up to customers to decide how to respond.

theguardian.com.title: Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel kill five people on Mexico’s Pacific coast
theguardian.com.text:
At least five people have died after Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel pummelled Mexico’s Pacific coast, causing flooding that downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and inundated homes.
Simon claimed the life of a 71-year-old man who died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo in the southern state of Guerrero, governor Evelyn Salgado said at a press conference.
The storm also damaged infrastructure and homes in the state’s coastal towns, including the major seaport of Acapulco, she said.
Tropical Storm Rachel is blamed for the deaths of four members of one family, including two children, whose bodies were found on the outskirts of the city of Ensenada in Baja California, the state’s prosecutor’s office reported.
Five more people remained missing, while security forces used helicopters to rescue 32 people, prosecutors said. Baja governor Marina del Pilar said officials were helping more than 50 people in temporary shelters.
Simon did not make landfall and, after weakening to category two on the five-point Saffir-Simpson scale, was moving away from the coast, authorities said. A rain alert remained in place.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said heavy rainfall associated with Simon in west-central Mexico over the next few days might still produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Officials warned waves of up to five metres high were still expected in some coastal areas. Flooding and landslides had already hit communities close to rivers and streams in the states of Michoacan and Colima.
The El Niño phenomenon, characterised by rising water temperatures in the Pacific, is fuelling a more intense hurricanes this season in the region.
Meteorologists say the 2026-27 El Niño, which causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions, is certain to be the biggest ever recorded. Scientists now also think human-caused global heating is making El Niños more intense.
With Agence France-Presse and Associated Press

theguardian.com.title: Death on Six Flags rollercoaster in US triggers ride closures across six states
theguardian.com.text:
Theme park company Six Flags temporarily closed nine rollercoasters across six amusement parks on Monday after one person died and several others were injured in an incident involving a coaster in Georgia.
A spokesperson for the park said they closed similar attractions across their parks “out of an abundance of caution” after the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24km) north-west of Atlanta.
Officials did not confirm how the person died, nor how the others were injured or their conditions.
Cobb County police department’s major crimes unit has launched an investigation.
Witnesses who spoke to NBC affiliate WXIA of Atlanta said they saw a man fall from the Goliath rollercoaster. “He fell and hit the car three different times,” one witness told the station.
A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said, adding that they are providing support to the guests and team members impacted.
Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the rollercoaster. However, local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster.
The rollercoaster, which was opened in 2006, reaches top speeds of 70mph (about 113 kph) and heights of 200 feet (61 meters), the park’s website reports. During about 3 1/2 minutes, riders “navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills”, according to the website.
“I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one,” Lisa Cupid, the Cobb County board of commissioners chair, said in a statement. She added that next of kin have been notified.
The amusement park is a major part of the county’s tourism and brings in visitors from across the south-east, Cupid said.
“We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories,” she said.
The incident comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain, in Southern California, announced that it is retiring its famous X2 rollercoaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride.
The park had settled one wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022.
Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed rollercoaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries and his death was ruled accidental.

theguardian.com.title: Bedbug infestation forces Qantas to ground plane in Rome
theguardian.com.text:
Qantas has been forced to ground a plane in Rome after bedbugs were discovered on the aircraft on its way from Perth.
The parasitic insects were found in the front of the economy section of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner as it made its way from Perth to Rome for the QF5 flight on 9 October, a source with knowledge of the incident confirmed on Tuesday.
Bedbugs are small insects that feed on the blood of some mammals, including humans, which can be hard to eradicate.
As first reported by the SMH, the aircraft had to be taken out of service for cleaning after its arrival in the Italian capital, resulting in the cancellation of the Qantas Rome to Perth service on 10 October.
A Qantas spokesperson said the flight was cancelled to allow its engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after “an issue identified on a small number of economy seats”.
They said the airline wanted to “sincerely apologise” to customers for the disruption.
Affected passengers were given accommodation and rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, Qantas said.
The airline said its aircraft cabins were cleaned regularly and to an extremely high standard and treated with disinfectant every 50 days as a standard precautionary cleaning measure.
Prof Michelle Power, a parasitologist at Macquarie University, said the bedbugs had “more than likely” been brought on to the plane in someone’s luggage or on a passenger’s clothes and then escaped into the cabin.
“They’re associated with travel. People may go to a hotel that’s infested and because they like dark spaces and are attracted to the smell of human clothes, they make their way into someone’s luggage.”
“They’re a flightless insect, without planes,” she said.
Power said bedbugs were not dangerous, even though their bites could be itchy and irritating, but they were very difficult to get rid of and could hide in bedsheets and crevices for a long time without needing to feed.
She said there were “two sides to bedbugs”: on the one hand, wealthier people who travelled a lot got them and subsequently moved them around, whereas people already experiencing health inequities may not be able to afford pesticides or potentially heat water to the 55C required to kill them.

theguardian.com.title: ‘Universal appeal’: Celebrity Traitors producer reveals secrets to its success
theguardian.com.text:
For the celebrities chosen as traitors in the BBC’s juggernaut reality show, the task is simple – kill off fellow contestants without getting caught.
Yet with the new series of Celebrity Traitors once again attracting huge audiences, its UK producers are delighting in one of the show’s more wholesome qualities – its popularity is staving off the death of television’s ability to unite the nation.
“It’s very difficult to get people to watch programmes, and there is a huge joy coming up with something that a very large amount of people watch,” Stephen Lambert, head of the Celebrity Traitors producer Studio Lambert, told the Radio Times.
“The show has universal appeal … It has established itself as ‘appointment-to-view TV’,” he added.
Despite its appeal, however, Lambert may still struggle to attract the man he revealed to be his dream contestant: Tom Cruise.
More than 10 million people have tuned in to watch some episodes, well in excess of half the viewers watching TV during the show’s time slot. It is also pulling younger viewers away from other devices and on to the sofa, with 1.6 million people aged between 16 and 34 tuning in for this series’ premiere.
In doing so, it has bucked a long-running trend that has seen mass TV audiences become increasingly rare. The arrival of streamers, digital platforms and smartphones have ensured such viewing figures have become the preserve of the Olympics, England World Cup matches and the odd breakthrough hit.
The success of The Traitors has inevitably spawned similar formats based on deceit and questionable detective skills, as producers attempt to replicate its allure. Lambert said that whether it was the celebrity edition or the regular series of The Traitors, the secret to its success came down to two words: “Dramatic irony.”
“It’s the engine of The Traitors,” he said. “It’s about the pleasure that we know more than the protagonists – we know who is lying. And it’s fun to try and watch people work out who the liars are.”
When it comes to the celebrity edition, he said viewers delighted in seeing famous faces uncomfortable as they “have so little control” over events. “It’s such an immersive game that people get caught up in it, and show how they really are,” he said.
Lambert confirmed that casting for Celebrity Traitors was not difficult because its popularity meant that the names who agreed to go into the traitors’ castle were also fans. Producers have previously noted the show does not face the usual challenges of attracting names to formats that ask them to eat bugs or train for weeks on end.
Not only would Cruise be a tough man to pin down, Lambert also said securing sports stars continues to be a perennial problem for casting directors. Sports men and women not only have gruelling schedules, but their media activities are guarded closely by personal agents and their clubs.
When asked about dream contestants, Lambert said: “Tom Cruise, maybe? And we would like to have a big sports star. But if they are an active one, they have commitments.”
