Towards the end of the week, the system will continue eastwards, bringing showers to parts of Crete, which was hit by severe flooding a week earlier. Those storms swept some cars and trees into the sea.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, a category 4 storm, is moving close to Mexico’s Pacific coast, near the state of Jalisco. It is the latest of 21 named storms in the Pacific this season, 11 of which have reached hurricane strength.
At the time of writing, Simon has a central pressure of 933mb and maximum sustained winds of nearly 150mph (241km/h). However, the hurricane is expected to weaken rapidly if its core moves onshore, cutting it off from the warm ocean waters that fuel it.
Heavy rainfall is affecting south-western Mexico, where totals could reach 300-400mm across a wide area, rising to 400-500mm in the wettest locations.

theguardian.com.title: Pakistan detains hundreds of politicians from Imran Khan’s PTI party
theguardian.com.text:
Politicians from the party of the former Pakistani prime minister Imran Khan have been detained after the suspension of a provincial government now under emergency rule.
Pakistan’s president declared a state of emergency and suspended the government in north-western Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, led by Khan’s ally Sohail Afridi, on Sunday.
Asif Ali Zardari’s federal government said the emergency rule was invoked after the provincial government failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province, which borders Afghanistan.
Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party rejected that assertion, saying it was enforced to deter his supporters from marching to Islamabad, the capital, to pressure the government for his release.
The imposition of emergency rule and suspension of the provincial government have sharply escalated confrontation between the 74-year-old former cricket star and the country’s powerful military.
The emergency rule came a week after Khan’s supporters had rallied for days in the province, intending to march to Islamabad to demand his release and provide medical treatment.
“Yes, I can confirm that the chief minister and some of his cabinet members have been taken into preventive custody,” the government minister Talal Chaudhry told Reuters.
If any were found to have cases to be tried against them, they would be charged and tried, he said, but the others would be released. He said the detentions occurred on Sunday at the provincial chief minister’s house in the city of Peshawar in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Witnesses and officials said the chief minister’s house and other important facilities in the vicinity had been cordoned off with a heavy police presence, paramilitary forces and shipping containers.
Shaukat Yousafzai, an aide of Khan, condemned the detentions and demanded the politicians’ release.
Khan’s three sisters and hundreds of his supporters were also detained before the planned march.
The party’s last large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes with security forces, and Khan’s 2023 arrest prompted nationwide riots that led his supporters to attack military installations.
Pakistan’s constitution allows the government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency.
The minister of law, Azam Nazeer Tarar, said a provincial governor would take charge in the province after the president declared the state of emergency. The province has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months.
The federal government and the military accuse Khan’s PTI of failing to curb the violence, a charge the party denies.
Zardari’s administration and the PTI held several rounds of talks since the call for the march was made last month.
The government was ready to accept all of the PTI’s demands, including a go-ahead for the march, Tarar said, adding: “We asked for just one thing, that the party should publicly condemn the militancy and join our hands in the fight against militants.”
They did not agree and that is why the talks broke down, he said.

theintercept.com.title: ICE Raid on Ilhan Omar Shows How Dangerous Two Years of Flailing Trump Could Get
theintercept.com.text:
In the mode of historic fascist regimes, President Donald Trump’s administration sent federal agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to raid the home of a political opponent, singled out for her race and religion, in a transparent effort to strip her of her citizenship.
On Monday, agents with Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing, conducted a search of the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., with federal officials describing the incursion as part of “an ongoing federal criminal investigation.”
HSI was previously known for targeting human traffickers, drug smugglers, and war criminals. But under the second Trump administration, the unit has been increasingly focused on investigating protesters and immigration fraud.
That latter category is exactly what Trump administration officials have been prejudiciously applying to Omar for months. In March, Vice President JD Vance said, “We actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.”
And, last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that “something is going to happen” on the Omar case, with immigration czar Tom Homan confirming an investigation.
The ICE raid against Omar, however, is an extremist escalation in Trump’s long-running threats to denaturalize the member of Congress, who was born in Somalia but came to the U.S. as a refugee when she was a young child. Omar, who has denied the repeated allegations of immigration fraud, is on the ballot for reelection in November.
Not only does the raid send a chill to all naturalized citizens who, like Omar, oppose the Trump regime, it is also one of the most ominous signs to date of how dangerous Trump and his acolytes can get in the next two years.
With his popularity tanking and his grip on power growing tenuous, Trump is becoming a flailing tyrant. Meanwhile, he has been granted extraordinary executive power by a loyalist Supreme Court and has purged the federal government of practically all checks and balances. It’s a recipe for immense harm.
A Nakedly Fascist Move
Debates about whether the Trump regime qualifies as fascist are old, tired, and not worth retreading here.
There can be little doubt, though, that targeting a racialized political opponent for deportation three weeks before an election is a nakedly fascist move — especially in the context of the far right’s evermore vitriolic attacks on Somali communities nationwide.
“Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post last week. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back!”
It was nothing short of an exhortation to a race war.
As his popular support continues to wane, we can be sure that the president and his white supremacist Cabinet will marshal the force of the federal government in even more fascistic ways.
Many means of stopping Trump have been defanged, as the raid itself makes clear.
We cannot rely on the courts. The warrant to search Omar’s home, for instance, was signed by a judge.
The judicial system, indeed, has permitted vast swaths of Trump’s anti-immigrant excesses. Courts have also sent activists to prison for decades for attending protests against the federal government. And, while some federal judges and even the Supreme Court have pushed back on some of Trump’s agenda, it is also the courts that have covered the president with impunity. We know, too, that this administration routinely disregards court orders in the knowledge that it will not face consequences.
There is little more optimism to be had on the congressional front. Even if Democrats take back Congress in November, they must reckon with an embattled authoritarian executive with a fully funded standing militia — namely, ICE.
Democrats should unite to stop Trump’s efforts to lawlessly deport a colleague based on a racist political witch hunt, but we can expect little congressional action beyond condemnatory statements. Indeed, all too many centrist Democrats have been happy to throw left-wing colleagues, particularly Muslims like Omar and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., to the wolves.
Elected leaders, from the national to municipal level, should be strategizing about how to protect their constituents from Trump’s worst extremes in the knowledge that he and his allies will escalate further. Impeachment should be a priority, yes, but so too should passing laws to dismantle and defund ICE, among other measures — just the sorts of things mainstream Democrats have refused to countenance.
If not the courts or elected leaders, what then? The answer is clear: Trump’s desperate authoritarianism must also be met by mass popular and militant opposition.
It is not enough to vote in November, then cross our fingers for two more years. Organizers on the front lines defending immigrant neighbors against ICE are exhausted and need numbers and support.
Activists facing trial or already sentenced to decades in prison for resisting Trump’s regime need ongoing legal support and funding. Readiness is all.
This is not to suggest that we must live in a state of paralyzing fear of an evermore delusional tyrant. The point, rather, is to recognize the danger and go on.
Resistance to Trump, to the border regime, and to racist state violence already exists; it must be supported, expanded, and the subject of an escalation of our own.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

theintercept.com.title: Susan Collins-Aligned Super PAC Buys Attack Ads in Portland... Oregon
theintercept.com.text:
A Republican-affiliated super PAC is having a little trouble finding Maine on a map.
The Defending Main Street super PAC spent thousands of dollars on an attack ad to audiences thousands of miles away from the Maine Senate race it was targeting.
The ad hit Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson on the issue of taxes and cost of living in the state.
“Maine can’t afford Troy Jackson and all his taxes,” the ad said.
The group, which describes itself as the “most effective independent expenditure organization supporting the governing wing of the Republican Party,” paid for the ad to attack Jackson, who’s mounting a challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins. Both candidates have made cost of living a central plank of their campaigns in the run-up to the midterm election on November 3.
The only problem with the ad in question: The group paid for the video ad to show more than 1 million times in the wrong Portland.
Rather than being delivered to audiences in Portland, Maine, the state’s largest city, the ad was shown to digital audiences more than 3,000 miles and three time zones away in Portland, Oregon, according to data from Google.
The mix-up may be embarrassing for the super PAC, which is oriented around electing so-called moderate Republicans like Collins, but likely spared voters in Maine from the latest wave in a deluge of ad spending in the state, according to Andy O’Brien, a political operative who supports Jackson.
“We have billionaires with no connection to Maine spending millions of dollars to buy Susan Collins the election, so it’s pretty hilarious to see them throwing money at the wrong Portland,” O’Brien told The Intercept. “It’s clear these people don’t know anything about Maine, because they’re directing their ads to the wrong Portland.”
“I’m glad they’re wasting their money in Oregon and not continuing to waste it in Maine.”
Representatives of the Jackson’s and Collins’s campaigns and a spokesperson for Defending Main Street did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The group is affiliated with Republican Main Street Partnership, a nonprofit group that counts Collins among its nine members in the Senate. Republican Main Street Partnership was initially aimed at supporting moderate Republicans that has, along with much of the rest of the GOP, moved to the right in recent years.
Busy Maine Street
The race between Collins and Jackson — a longtime Maine politico who stepped in to replace Graham Platner after Platner dropped out amid allegations of sexual assault — has become one of the most high-profile races in the country in the run-up to the midterms.
The campaign has helped make Maine one of the top locations for political spending this cycle, according to the Portland Press Herald.
The Defending Main Street ad, however, did not have the impact its sponsors might have hoped. The ad buy first came to light after an X user reported seeing multiple anti-Troy Jackson ads in Portland, Oregon.
“I’ve gotten 5 anti-Troy Jackson ads in the last 24 hours. I choose to believe they mixed up Portlands,” wrote the user, who goes by the name Lillian Belle and posts about progressive politics in Oregon. “Hearing I’m not alone lol.”
That suspicion appears to be borne out by data from Google Ads Transparency Center, which shows Defending Main Street dropped between $20,000 and $25,000 to place the 30-second ad in hundreds of ZIP codes across Oregon and the state of Washington between October 8 and October 11.
O’Brien, the Maine political operative, said, “At least now Portland, Oregon, residents can enjoy some of the crap we’ve been seeing every single day.”

theintercept.com.title: Pentagon Finally Counts an Iran War Death — Six Months Late
theintercept.com.text:
The Pentagon quietly acknowledged additional Iran war deaths on Friday evening after The Intercept repeatedly demanded an explanation for inaccurate statistics on a War Department website tracking U.S. casualties from the conflict.
Almost 900 U.S. troops have been wounded or killed in the war with Iran, according to the official Pentagon count, including the two deaths added on Friday. This raises the Pentagon’s total to 21 dead.
The additional war dead include Maj. Sorffly Davius, a signals and communication officer with the New York Army National Guard who was assigned to the headquarters of the 42nd Infantry Division and died while on duty in Camp Buehring, Kuwait, on March 6. For more than six months, The Intercept has raised Davius’s case in dozens of emails and phone conversations with Pentagon officials and publicly in 10 articles.
The Pentagon recently revamped the website of the Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS — which provides official counts of dead and wounded for Congress and the White House — to include more detailed casualty category tables. But it initially listed no “non-hostile” illness or injury fatalities, despite the Pentagon announcing in March that Davius died “as a result of a non-combat related incident.”
At first, the military claimed that Davius was involved in another operation instead of Epic Fury — the original designation of the Iran war. Two weeks ago, however, The Intercept revealed that a recent National Guard news release admitted that when “President Donald Trump made the decision to attack Iran and launched Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28, the [42nd Infantry] division headquarters began conducting combat operations.” The 42nd served as the primary headquarters leading what became, according to Maj. Gen. Jack James, the division commander, the “largest and first long-range precision fires campaign in the history of the United States Army.” James specifically saluted Davius, whom the Guard admitted was “conducting operations” when he died.
Last week, The Intercept pointed the Pentagon to the non-hostile illness or injury casualty count for Epic Fury on the website, and emphasized its tally showing zero deaths was not possible.
“I will check within,” Patricia Kreuzberger, a Pentagon spokesperson said on Tuesday. “Let me reach out to leadership.”
Three days later, and after repeated follow-up messages on Friday, the tally was updated, to 1.
In addition to Davius, the DCAS death count now also includes an unidentified Navy suicide that occurred last month, according to a U.S. official who spoke on the condition of anonymity. DCAS currently lists this death as “pending,” despite the recent addition of a “self-inflicted” category to the website.
A “War Department official” told The Intercept by email on Sunday that “the Department is introducing a ‘Pending Adjudication’ category to track the status of active duty casualties pending final categorization and reporting in DCAS.” She added: “This new category will allow the Department to minimize reporting delays while ensuring data consistency between the DoW and Joint Staff.”
The “pending” designation, however, isn’t new. The Pentagon re-introduced it to DCAS in mid-July, and major discrepancies have continued in the tally since.
Many casualties remain uncounted in DCAS, including a sailor who suffered a non-combat-related injury aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln as it was involved in “strike missions in support of Operation Epic Fury” on March 25.
Most Iran war casualties in the official count — 454 personnel as of Friday — have occurred since July 7, after the Trump administration claimed the conflict ended. At that time, the Pentagon switched from counting casualties under Epic Fury to the anodyne moniker “Overseas Operations.”
The most recent casualties are three Army personnel wounded in action this month. The latest known Iran war fatality is Capt. Bianca Wilkerson, 37, of Norfolk, Virginia, who died on September 18 from a “coronary issue,” according to her brother. He said she returned from Saudi Arabia on September 10 and was headed back but died on the return flight, according to reporting by the Virginian-Pilot. A U.S. official told The Intercept that Wilkerson died “as a result of a non-combat-related incident,” but after nearly a month, DCAS still lists no non-hostile illness or injury deaths.
“There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude,” Reps. Chrissy Houlahan, D-Pa., and Adam Smith, D-Wash., said in a joint statement on Friday after the House Armed Services Committee discovered “a discrepancy in the Pentagon’s reporting of casualty numbers” and brought it to “the Trump Administration’s attention.” They continued: “The failure of Secretary Hegseth to immediately take ownership of the problem also does a grave disservice to the men and women putting their lives on the line in service to our country.”
For six months, The Intercept has reported on anomalies in official counts offered on DCAS. When the first ceasefire was struck between the Trump administration and Iran on April 7, the tally of U.S. casualties was 385. Despite a pause in hostilities, the number slowly rose to 428, according to Pentagon statistics. But on April 21, the number of wounded-in-action troops declined by 15 without public acknowledgment by the War Department. Despite repeated questions for months, the Pentagon has not explained the adjustment.
Other discrepancies have also gone unjustified for months. An Army “illness/injury” death appeared on or about May 26 but disappeared by June 1. On July 20, the Pentagon repeatedly altered DCAS, adding 100 casualties to the war’s tally without explanation; the total number of wounded cited by DCAS on that date included counts of 413, 427, and 447. Three days later, the Pentagon dropped the Iran war death toll from 18 to 14. On July 22, DCAS added 10 recent casualties to the Epic Fury count. By July 25, those wounded personnel were dropped from the tally. They may have been added to the Overseas Operations casualty toll, but the Pentagon has failed to offer any explanations.
Prior reporting by The Intercept also found that the Pentagon’s official tally of dead and wounded personnel is a gross undercount, stemming from what one U.S. government official called, in April, a “casualty cover-up.” When the Washington Post also suggested last month that the Pentagon had suppressed the casualty numbers, self-styled War Secretary Pete Hegseth called the report “DISGUSTING and FAKE.”
When asked by The Intercept about the Pentagon’s continued peddling of bogus statistics, Kreuzberger did not offer an explanation. An email from a nameless “War Department official” said: “We have nothing to provide beyond the Defense Casualty Analysis System website.”

theintercept.com.title: Trump Wanted Minneapolis 15 Case to Be Another Prairieland. Instead, Twin Cities Rallied Behind Anti-ICE Activists.
theintercept.com.text:
As the Trump administration unveiled an indictment earlier this year against 15 anti-ICE activists, many of whom identify as radicals, for purportedly tormenting federal agents last winter, a top U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement official took the podium.
There were two types of protests, said Homeland Security Investigations special agent in charge Michael McCarthy, who oversaw the ICE agents in a St. Paul, Minnesota, field office who conducted the investigation.
“Peaceful protest is a protected right, and a cornerstone of our democracy,” said McCarthy. “When protest turns into rioting, violence or criminal activity, it becomes unlawful and it will not be tolerated.”
McCarthy’s comments stood in stark contrast with ICE’s record in Minneapolis, where a federal judge had been forced to issue an injunction to stop federal agents from pepper-spraying and arresting peaceful protesters during their enforcement blitz, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
Legal experts, too, had criticisms of the indictment: The Justice Department, one pointed out, had concocted a federal conspiracy out of what would normally be misdemeanor charges.
In the months since, criticisms of the case have only grown louder. Court filings revealed that McCarthy’s agents secretly infiltrated groups that preach nonviolence, including labor unions and nonprofits. They also wielded subpoenas in a fruitless hunt for financiers of “domestic terrorism,” taking a cue from President Donald Trump’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-7 labeling swaths of the far left as terrorists.
The Trump administration has won some success in going after left-wing protesters under NSPM-7, but the Minneapolis case is proving to be more challenging.
In other prosecutions targeting activists, like the Prairieland case in Texas, mainstream groups have shied away from supporting the defendants. In Minnesota, though, groups once wary of being associated with the 15 defendants, many of whom are self-described anarchists, have rallied to their side.
Powerful labor unions that make up the backbone of the state’s progressive movement have raised funds on behalf of the defendants, incensed at the infiltration from federal undercover agents. Rather than dividing and conquering the left, the case has united it.
Supporters of the defendants, who have collectively come to be known as the Minneapolis 15, recently packed a bowling alley for a fundraiser. On October 3, hundreds of labor union members marched through downtown Minneapolis, demanding that the charges against the activists be dropped.
Meanwhile, the defendants themselves have so far mounted a unified, joint defense; none of them have taken a plea deal.
“They’re trying to split the movement and absolutely failing,” said Emmett James Doyle, a defendant in the case. “There’s been just complete solidarity behind us from basically every sector of Twin Cities life.”
“Can’t Indict 100,000 People”
Doyle’s ruddy face and wild beard would have been at home in Big Bill Haywood’s Industrial Workers of the World a century ago. By day he’s a union carpenter, by night he plucks a banjo and sings songs about America’s radical past.
Federal prosecutors allege that he brought those songs to life on the streets of Minneapolis.
In a 94-page indictment, prosecutors claim that Doyle and the other 14 defendants were members or associates of a group called Direct Action Minnesota that “infiltrated and exploited lawful protests” to target ICE.
Prosecutors painted a dark picture of DAMN. Their tactics allegedly included blocking access to a federal building used by ICE with disabled cars or trailers, bringing shields and gas masks to protests, and, in one instance, following an ICE agent across state lines to his home in Wisconsin.
Government attorneys also leaned heavily on the defendants’ comments to each other in private messages about their frustration with more mainstream protesters and the need for “militant” action.
Despite the prosecutors’ claims about rioting and violence at the June press conference, however, the top federal prosecutor in Minnesota, U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen, was unable to identify injuries to federal officers when reporters pressed him.
There are committed anarchists among the defendants charged in the indictment, several defendants told The Intercept, but there was little difference between what they did and what thousands of Minneapolis residents did during the federal immigration crackdown.
Ordinary Minnesotans walked frigid streets with whistles dangling from their necks to alert their neighbors about ICE raids. They sent license plate numbers of federal vehicles to Signal group chats. Members of rapid-response networks trailed suspected agents in their cars.
The indictment is replete with examples of protesters trailing agents in vehicles, a tactic known as “commuting.” Yet that was a tactic so widely employed by rapid-response groups in Minneapolis that it was even adopted by a congressional candidate in a suburban district who recently won his Democratic primary.
“I think there are people in the government who really do believe that there is like a small cabal of people who are fomenting all the dissent, and if you get rid of them, that everyone will be quiet,” Doyle said. “And that’s fundamentally wrong.”
Doyle, like the four other defendants interviewed by The Intercept, declined to discuss the specific allegations in the indictment, citing advice from his attorney.
Still, another defendant, Treasure Thoreson, was adamant that none of the defendants ever used violence. Thoreson is a special education teacher whose elementary school’s lanyard was still dangling from her neck during a recent interview. She believes the group was targeted because of its radical views.
“They clearly had people that they had identified as problematic in some way and have been trying to tie these people to leading the resistance,” Thoreson said. “They can’t indict 100,000 people, so really, they’re just trying to find people to make examples of.”
“Attack on the Movement’
Thoreson said she has received steady support from her teachers union since the indictment.
She and many other defendants believe the charges against them are a way of attacking Minnesota’s powerful labor movement. By the count of defendants who spoke to The Intercept, at least 11 of the 15 have been involved in union organizing.
The internal Homeland Security Investigations files unearthed by the defense team lend credibility to this theory. Undercover agents attended an organizing meeting at the United Labor Centre, a building that houses multiple unions. HSI, the investigative wing of ICE, also subpoenaed the financial records of the SEIU and the Communications Workers of America as part of an overlapping probe into “domestic terror financing.”
Several defendants interviewed by The Intercept were amused at the idea that they were receiving funding from mainstream organizations. They have long lobbed critiques at the labor movement’s institutional core from its fringes.
After some initial hesitance, unions and nonprofit groups responded in force to the case. Days after the indictment, some labor groups signed onto a joint statement denouncing the charges. After a court filing from the defendants revealed the subpoenas of the unions’ financing, more labor organizations raised their voices.
“Generally speaking, the labor movement is awfully conservative — too conservative — on issues like this, and can sometimes be scared out of solidarity with people who are fighting back,” said Kieran Knutson, the president of CWA Local 7250 in Minneapolis.
More unions rallied, Knutson said, as it became clear that prosecutors could not point to examples of physical harm, as union locals pressured statewide organizations, and as the defendants themselves articulated why the case was important.
“These are active people in the labor movement, and I think in many ways people see them as an expression of the movement as a whole,” Knutson said. “And these charges were an attack on the movement as a whole.”
Knutson said he knows the value of solidarity: In 1993, he was charged with assaulting a man wearing neo-Nazi patches during an antiracist demonstration on the University of Minnesota campus, according to news reports from the time. He was acquitted with the help of attorney Keith Ellison, who later went on to win election as the state’s attorney general.
“I know what it’s like to have the weight of the charges just hanging over you,” Knutson said.
The leading candidate in the Hennepin County Attorney race, state Rep. Cedrick Frazier, who also works as a lawyer for labor union Education Minnesota, told The Intercept in a recent interview that the charges should be dismissed.
“I think they’re trying to, for lack of a better word, ‘Trump’ up some charges to continue his pursuit of retribution against Minnesota,” said Frazier. “I mean, look, they don’t like labor groups.”
A broad coalition of labor groups including the state AFL-CIO endorsed an October 3 rally and march in support of the defendants, another sign that skepticism of the case has gone mainstream.
Hundreds of janitors, teachers, public employees, and hospitality workers joined the march, said Isaac Sant, a defendant and longtime labor organizer. He said seeing them on the streets was “humbling.”
Sant recently joined defendants from other cases with political overtones, including Prairieland, to form what they are dubbing the NSPM-7 Defendants Union.
“I can only speak for myself, but I don’t have any problem linking my case to the Prairieland cases. I think what happened to them was a travesty and a miscarriage of justice,” Sant said. “I think it’s very important that we stand in solidarity with people who are in that position, and especially with people who are getting railroaded even worse than we are.”

lemonde.fr/en.title: France braces for fresh nationwide student demonstrations
lemonde.fr/en.text:
France readied on Tuesday, October 13, for fresh nationwide demonstrations supporting students who have been protesting poor classroom conditions for weeks, with authorities and participants wary of further violence. The mobilization, backed by unions and the hard-left opposition La France Insoumise party, was to include a march through Paris starting in the afternoon, along with marches in other cities. It follows demonstrations on Thursday that saw more than 70,000 people take to the streets across France, with about 500 people arrested.
French authorities had been hoping that the student protest movement that started in late September was starting to ease, days ahead of half-term holidays. The protests have seen students pile up dumpsters and other obstacles to block access to high schools, with clashes occasionally breaking out with police.
On Monday, only 130 of France's 3,700 lycées were closed, according to the Education Ministry, though it stated that, while "the number of school closures is falling (...) the violence is intensifying." The Education Ministry said eight members of teaching staff were injured on Monday, mostly in the Paris region and cities of Bordeaux and Lyon, in relation to the protests.
In an incident seemingly unrelated to the protests, and not included in the ministry's tally, police arrested a 14-year-old on Monday near Marseille after a middle school headmaster and a teacher were shot with a hunting rifle, wounding both.
'Aren't being heard'
While most of the protests have been peaceful, students say they are determined to press the government to address the problems of too many absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded class schedules and other grievances.
"Students aren't being heard enough (...) not their proposals to authorities and elected officials," a 19-year-old graphic design student in Paris, Leo, said. He added that the protesters – many of whom were minors – were "disturbed by the level of repression never before seen for a student movement".
One young protester lost a hand from a police stun grenade earlier in the protests, another lost many of his teeth from a tear-gas canister fired in his face at close range, and another lost an eye. Rights groups and students have accused the police of a disproportionate use of force.
Several police officers and teachers have also been hurt, and on Monday authorities said fireworks fired through a tube injured two school workers in Reims, one school worker in a Paris suburb and a police officer outside a school in Marseille.
Tuesday's demonstrations supporting the students were to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living.
President Emmanuel Macron, speaking to reporters on Monday, said the pupils' grievances would take time to address and urged restraint from protesters. "These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect," Macron said.
More than 6,800 people – largely minors – have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests, according to the Justice Ministry. Police have opened internal investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators.
After last week's nationwide demonstrations, the government promised some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools. A government spokeswoman on Monday said they had started to be assigned. But the national students' union has dismissed the government's move as "crumbs" and is demanding a €10 billion boost for lycées.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Cairo residents outraged over felling of their trees
lemonde.fr/en.text:
LETTER FROM CAIRO
Avenue 250 is a dark green line cutting through Cairo. Some of its trees are more than 100 years old. Ficus trees of every size, flame trees ablaze with red flowers in May and enormous rubber trees have grown along an old railway line, forming a tunnel through which slow-moving trains pass, sounding whistles as powerful as foghorns.
Alongside this accidental green corridor, countless plant sellers, flowerpot vendors and gardening tool merchants set up shop in the shade, selling their wares at high prices to the residents of Maadi – an oasis of greenery in Africa's most populous city, with more than 23 million inhabitants.
In June 2021, the Egyptian government announced plans to raze the entire area to create a new thoroughfare, the Axis of Algeria, designed to run across southern Cairo. The plant sellers were ordered to evacuate. Nothing seemed capable of stopping the new regime, led by autocratic Abdel Fattah el-Sissi since 2013, from carrying out this project. Yet a local protest, backed by Egyptian celebrities, halted the bulldozers. Since then, the project has been suspended, though not officially abandoned.

lemonde.fr/en.title: On the slopes of Besançon, an aggressive chamois attacks joggers, and the prefect authorizes its killing
lemonde.fr/en.text:
"I didn't hear it coming. I only had time to see its head 10 centimeters from me, and then, nothing, total blackout..." Despite her misfortune, Milena, 30, who prefers not to give her last name, considered herself "lucky." While she was running in the hills around Besançon on October 1, the experienced jogger was violently attacked by a chamois, which literally knocked her out. The charge happened on a paved downhill stretch, just a few hundred meters from the city limits.
"I was unconscious for about five minutes. On the GPS, you can see I zigzagged: I must have tumbled. When I came to, I was disoriented and covered in blood. I tried to get home, but after 100 meters, I realized it wasn't possible." A passerby found her sitting on the ground, crying and confused, and helped her call the fire department. "A nurse who was also passing by applied pressure to my wounds while waiting for help. My instinct was that if I was going to die, I should at least call my father," Milena recalled. She was treated in the emergency room for serious injuries: ten stitches in her shoulder, pierced by a horn, and 18 staples in her scalp.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Why Ceuta and Melilla remain a point of contention between Spain and Morocco
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Just a few kilometers from Andalusia, on the African shore of the Strait of Gibraltar, Ceuta serves as a gateway to Europe. This Spanish autonomous city, long claimed by Morocco, has become a flashpoint in tensions between the two countries. Though Spain considers its sovereignty over Ceuta non-negotiable, it nonetheless relies on cooperation from Morocco to control migration flows. On July 30 and 31, the arrival in Ceuta of around 72,000 people from Morocco sharply heightened these divisions. In this city of about 83,500 residents, reception facilities were quickly overwhelmed. According to the Spanish government, the vast majority of migrants had left within days, but thousands remained, some in overcrowded centers and makeshift camps, others left to fend for themselves on the streets and beaches.
The crisis quickly took on a national dimension. On September 2, during the Dia de Ceuta, the territory's annual celebration, thousands of protesters took to the streets of Madrid, Seville, Valencia, Malaga, and other cities across the country in support of Spanish control over Ceuta. Some of the crowds chanted, "Ceuta is not for sale," "United Ceuta will never be defeated," and "Spain yes! Morocco no!" Vox, the far-right party, called on its supporters to mobilize under the slogan: "No to the invasion. Defend Ceuta. Defend Spain."
On September 23, before the United Nations General Assembly, Spain's socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called on people not to "give in to fear," not to "make the migrant an enemy," and not to "violate the law." Three days later, the ultraconservative platform Sociedad Civil Española organized a "march for dignity" in Madrid to defend Ceuta and Melilla – the other autonomous Spanish city in North Africa – and to request early elections, publishing a manifesto calling for the "militarization" of Ceuta and the expulsion "to Morocco of all the invaders." The protest brought together thousands of demonstrators – 20,000 according to the authorities, 180,000 according to the organizers. The right and the far right have accused the three successive governments led by Sanchez since 2018 of having weakened border controls. On October 5, after his housing proposals were rejected, the prime minister announced early elections for November 29. The crisis in Ceuta has now become an election topic.

lemonde.fr/en.title: A disastrous day for French supermarkets after massive cyberattack targets refrigeration systems
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Charles Dezon, owner of the Intermarché supermarket in Gradignan, southwestern France, had never imagined that one day he would have to throw away nearly an entire dumpster's worth of frozen food because of a cyberattack. His store and around 300 others in the same group – which also includes the Netto brand, as well as about 100 Coopérative U stores, 80 Carrefour stores, several members of the E.Leclerc network and around 30 Monoprix stores – were hit by a large-scale cyberattack targeting refrigeration systems overnight from October 11 to October 12, first reported by BFM-TV.
"The attack was probably launched around 11 pm, but we only realized it at 4 in the morning when our delivery driver saw the storeroom was flooded. The temperature had reached 50°C in the cold room, which set off a sprinkler," Dezon told Le Monde.
In addition to raising the temperature of the defrosting system in freezers and cold-storage rooms to 50°C, the hackers extended the defrost cycle from one hour to eight hours so that alarms would go off later. The method delayed intervention and increased the damage. According to a Facebook post by the Intermarché store in La Haye, Normandy, some of the store's equipment melted as temperatures climbed to 80°C.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'Breaking Bad' actor RJ Mitte dies at 34
lemonde.fr/en.text:
RJ Mitte, the young actor best known for playing Walter White Jr. in the award-winning TV series, Breaking Bad, has died, his representatives told Agence France-Presse (AFP) on Monday, October 12. He was 34. The cause of death for the actor, who lived with cerebral palsy, was not immediately revealed. "It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," said a statement issued by Sean Reilly.
A teenage Mitte first appeared in Breaking Bad in 2008 as the son of chemistry-teacher-turned-drug-kingpin Walter White, a role that won Bryan Cranston global acclaim. "Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," Reilly said.
That campaigning evolved into working as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and for Shriners Children's, a nonprofit hospital network. "He also served as president of The Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, while using his platform to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities," Reilly added.
Breaking Bad, which ran for five seasons between 2008 and 2013, is routinely acclaimed as groundbreaking television, and was recently named by the New York Times as the best TV show of the 21st century.
'You will be missed'
Co-stars rushed to pay tribute to the performer, with Cranston recalling how Mitte was 14 when the show began and "met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination." "That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor," Cranston wrote in an Instagram post.
Aaron Paul – who played Jesse Pinkman, White's young partner in crime – saying he was "at a loss" over the news. "RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed," he said, according to the Hollywood Reporter. "And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that."
Dean Norris, who starred in the series as Mitte's on-screen uncle, a special agent with the Drug Enforcement Agency, said he was "heartbroken" by the news of the young man's death. "Though RJ didn't play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set," Norris wrote on social media. "He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can't believe it. Thinking of him and his family."
Fellow actor and disability campaigner Marlee Matlin, who appeared with Mitte in Cinemability: The Art of Inclusion, a documentary that examined the history of disability portrayals in US film and television, said her heart was "shattered."
"There will never be another like RJ Mitte. You will always have a place in my heart. RIP," wrote Matlin, who became the first deaf actress to win an Oscar when she scooped the top honor for Children of a Lesser God.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 911 calls reveal emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed after failed execution
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials following her failed lethal injection last month, according to 911 dispatch recordings reviewed by The Associated Press. The recordings show that precious minutes elapsed as officials and responders tried to figure out whether a request for emergency help in the execution chamber was legitimate. The first call came in at 8:40 p.m. on Sept. 30, and it was more than half an hour before prison officials affirmed it was legitimate.
“Per supervisors here .... we have been informed it is a false call,” one unidentified person says at 9:03 p.m. “There is no medical assistance needed at Riverbend Prison.”
Four minutes later, a responder reported: “Somebody is outside the gate at the prison telling us that it’s real and demanding us to go in. They say they are some sort of state official. I need somebody to get out to the gate and talk to those people.”
It wasn’t until 9:11 p.m. that prison officials affirmed the call for help was legitimate, the calls show. Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. At one point, Pike was on a ventilator and her attorneys did not expect her to survive. However, they said Pike woke up and began talking and walking with assistance, and she has since been discharged and is back at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years.

lemonde.fr/en.title: For NATO's top commander, 'the Alliance is unlikely to be caught by surprise'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
In a relatively unprecedented move, US General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, publicly unveiled what he called his "theory of victory" on Monday, October 12, during a major international security forum in Warsaw. His speech was as much intended to reassure European public opinion about the military capabilities of the Atlantic Alliance as it was to send a clear deterrent message to Russia against any escalation in its hybrid operations targeting the continent.
"I think our populations around the alliance are a bit nervous," General Grynkewich acknowledged. "What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it," he added. "Still, no one should mistake our defensive nature for weakness or lack of resolve (...). Through our collective strength, we aim to deter and keep the peace. But if someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight(...). We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those may be. We will, in short, ensure any attack against any ally proves utterly futile," he emphasized at the outset.

lemonde.fr/en.title: DR Congo's former president Joseph Kabila forms new force with M23 armed group
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Former DR Congo president Joseph Kabila on Monday, October 12, joined forces with the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group to head a new outfit, taking a more direct role in the insurgency ravaging the country's volatile east.
The tie-up was presented at a joint press conference at Kabila's residence in Goma, the major city in mineral-rich eastern Congo that the M23 has controlled since January 2025.
The new group – known as the Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN) – was presented as a "politico-military" outfit that will "pool their strengths, resources and means" with the aim of "putting an end to tyranny by any means, including force." It will be headed by Kabila and rebel leaders will serve as deputies.
Kabila was condemned to death in absentia a year ago for "complicity" with the M23. The 55-year-old Kabila, who ruled from 2001 to 2019, is accused by Congolese authorities of being one of the initiators of the Congo River Alliance (AFC), the now dissolved political wing of the M23. Kabila has denied the allegation.
The announcement of Kabila's new alliance comes amid an uncertain political climate in the Democratic Republic of Congo. President Felix Tshisekedi, 63, Kabila's successor, will reach the end of his second five-year term in 2028. The Congolese constitution sets a limit of two five-year terms. Yet for several months, the presidential majority has been preparing public opinion on amending the text.
Decades of conflict
Kabila has rarely been seen in public since he stepped down after elections in 2018. He had steered the vast country since January 16, 2001 when his father Laurent Kabila, a former rebel leader-turned-head-of-state, was murdered by a bodyguard.
In 2006, Joseph Kabila was elected president in the country's first free elections since independence from Belgium.
In 2011, Kabila was re-elected in a vote marred by violence and fraud. A year later, the M23 – a mainly ethnic Tutsi rebel group – began an uprising in the eastern Kivu region. The United Nations and Western governments accuse Rwanda of backing M23 but Kigali denies supporting the insurgency.
Eastern DRC has been plagued by violence for over 30 years with several attempts at mediation having failed so far. A deal signed in December by Kinshasa and Kigali, under the auspices of Washington, has had no tangible effect on the ground. Meanwhile, in July 2025, Kinshasa and the M23 committed, as part of a Qatari-mediated process, to a ceasefire that is not being respected.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Pope Leo XIV to be hospitalized in Rome on Tuesday for a lung operation
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Pope Leo XIV will be admitted to hospital on Tuesday morning, October 13, for an operation to remove a lump from his lung, the Vatican said. The 71-year-old Leo announced on Sunday that he would undergo an operation "in the coming days." The surgery to remove a pulmonary nodule, a small growth of tissue in the lung, will mark the pope's first hospitalization since he became head of the 1.4 billion Catholics on May 8, 2025.
Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni told Agence France-Presse on Monday that the pontiff would be admitted on "Tuesday, late morning." The recovery time could be about a week, the Vatican said. Leo's audiences have been canceled until October 20. The operation is expected to take place at Rome's Gemelli hospital, which has a dedicated papal suite.
In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told assembled crowds in St Peter's Square that doctors had discovered the nodule "at a very early stage" during recent medical checks. "The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it," he said.
Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is believed to generally be in good health, enjoying sports, especially playing tennis. He is expected to recover from the operation in time for a planned visit to Latin America next month. The 11-day official trip from November 6-17 will see him visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Economics Nobel Prize awarded to Americans Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, who rebuilt the macroeconomic analytical framework
lemonde.fr/en.text:
The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, commonly referred to as the Nobel Prize in Economics, was awarded on Monday, October 12, to two Americans for providing "microeconomic foundations for macroeconomic stabilization": Robert Hall, 83, professor at Stanford University in California, and Michael Woodford, 71, professor at Columbia University in New York.
The two men, who will share 12 million Swedish kronor (about €1.07 million), did not work directly together, but both developed new macroeconomic models based on the actual behavior of households and businesses. This made stabilization policies – against inflation and recessions – more effective. According to Timo Boppart, a member of the prize committee and professor at Stockholm University, the analytical framework prior to their research was "a black, unreliable box." Hall and Woodford made it possible to see under the hood.
Until the 1970s, macroeconomic stabilization was understood mainly through the work of John Maynard Keynes, with a focus on government intervention. When recession loomed, it was necessary to stimulate the economy through budget deficits or by creating money. Conversely, if inflation threatened, the economy needed to be slowed by reducing deficits and tightening credit. For a long time, Keynesian solutions worked.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Ukraine's EU accession bid advances with new chapter
lemonde.fr/en.text:
The European Union will on Tuesday, October 13, open new negotiation chapters with Ukraine, an essential step in Kyiv's long path to join the bloc. Ukrainian lawmakers on Monday passed legislation protecting the rights of national minorities, which removes a major hurdle in Kyiv's bid for membership.
The status of the Hungarian-speaking minority in western Ukraine had long caused tensions with Budapest, and Hungary had blocked Ukraine's EU membership bid, officially submitted days after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. European Council President Antonio Costa on Monday said he welcomed "today's decision by EU Member States to open two further negotiation clusters with Ukraine and Moldova."
"We look forward to opening all remaining clusters as soon as possible," he said, adding: "Your future lies in the EU. Let's keep up the momentum!"
Aspiring members will have to carry out sweeping reforms in their countries to comply with EU norms ranging from environmental policy to agriculture. Thirty-five negotiation chapters have to be completed and then a unanimous decision by the 27 member states to accept a new member is necessary to join the bloc.
The ratification by each member state can be through parliamentary approval or a referendum.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Why the Trump-Putin fuel agreement benefits Russia
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Donald Trump boasts. Vladimir Putin remains silent. True to form, the Russian president did not utter a word for three days after his American counterpart announced on Friday, October 9, a "deal" on diesel, followed by an announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire agreement between Kyiv and Moscow.
Between these two statements, Trump openly expressed what Putin thinks: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky "chose not to" end the war, declared the US president on Saturday, who "suggested" that Ukrainians elect "a new leader who can make a deal." In effect, that's what Moscow wants: an end to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries and the replacement of Zelensky with a more accommodating leader.
But Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire doesn't align with Putin's plans. For over a year, the Kremlin had stalled negotiations by refusing any temporary end to fighting, arguing that a pause would allow the Ukrainian army to regroup. Moscow demanded a comprehensive peace agreement to "eliminate the root causes" of the conflict – in other words, an agreement on Moscow's terms. Trump, therefore, has once again sowed confusion, surprising Kyiv and prompting silence in Moscow.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Federal agents search home of Trump critic Ilhan Omar
lemonde.fr/en.text:
US federal agents searched the Washington home of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar on Monday, October 12, as part of a criminal investigation, officials said, marking a dramatic escalation in President Donald Trump's confrontation with the outspoken lawmaker. The search was conducted by agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of US immigration enforcement, according to Fox News, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The operation, just three weeks before Omar seeks re-election in the November 3 midterms, raised concerns about longstanding Justice Department practices intended to prevent law enforcement actions from influencing elections. The cable network reported that the operation was linked to a criminal fraud investigation concerning immigration paperwork submitted on behalf of the Somali-born congresswoman by her late father when she was a child.
Trump's border enforcement chief Tom Homan told Fox News he was unwilling to give details ahead of any official announcement but confirmed that an "investigation was ongoing for a while" and that "there was a warrant executed this morning."
US media quoted the Justice Department confirming that agents had carried out a court-authorized search in the Washington area, but officials did not identify Omar or disclose the nature of the investigation. The search reportedly began around 6 am. Video footage apparently taken by a member of the public and posted to X showed several agents wearing HSI jackets outside Omar's Washington residence.
Omar said she will "not be silenced" and called the search of her home the "latest escalation" in President Donald Trump's "intimidation" campaign. Omar, 44, is a leftist Democrat and fierce critic of Trump, particularly his administration's sweeping crackdown on immigration. The Republican president has repeatedly clashed with Omar, who came to the United States from Somalia as a child and has frequently been the target of his political attacks.
Rare offense
In September, Homan said that Omar was the subject of an ongoing criminal investigation, but again declined to provide details. Omar said at the time that Homeland Security officials had not contacted her about any investigation, dismissing the allegations against her as politically motivated attacks. There was no immediate public response from Omar to Monday's search.
Omar was first elected to Congress in 2018 and represents a district including Minneapolis, home to one of the largest Somali communities in the United States. She is a member of the group of left-wing Democratic lawmakers known as "The Squad," who have been among Trump's most vocal opponents in Congress. No charges against Omar were announced in connection with Monday's search.
Trump and his Republican allies have for years argued that non-citizens vote in significant numbers in US elections, a criminal offense punishable by imprisonment and deportation. But studies consistently find non-citizen voting to be too rare an offense to have affected the outcome of any federal election.

lemonde.fr/en.title: OpenAI's latest blow to mathematicians: 'They have annihilated my field of research'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
"Tuesday night, I cried and it woke up my daughter," confessed mathematician Hugo Duminil-Copin, the recipient of the 2022 Fields Medal, during a videoconference organized by the Société Mathématique de France on Thursday, October 8. The reason for his tears? The American artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI posted more than 719 manuscripts, grouped into 372 families, claiming to solve many open mathematical problems. No fewer than 16 of these questions were directly related to the French researcher's work.
"They have annihilated my field of research," he calmly explained. He shared a slide, generated by AI, that depicted a rabbit being crushed by several trucks. "They wanted to prove they could massacre us," he added, before referring in the question-and-answer session to "a dismantling of our activity."
The mathematics community has been living a nightmare for the past month. On September 8, OpenAI posted evidence that its programs had solved a problem with a million-dollar prize since 2000 (the Navier-Stokes problem). It was a shock. This was already the third such blow for Duminil-Copin, who had realized the potential of these AIs as early as April. Along with a colleague, he discovered that an AI developed by Anthropic, a competitor of OpenAI, was able to solve a difficult problem, providing elegant and concise proof.

lemonde.fr/en.title: French high school students plan third day of protests Tuesday
lemonde.fr/en.text:
France's high school students begin a new stage of their campaign for improved conditions on Monday, October 12, hoping to maintain the momentum with a fresh wave of demonstrations. Last Thursday's demonstrations mobilized tens of thousands of people across France: 71,500 according to interior ministry figures. Nearly 256,000 took part in last Tuesday's day of action.
The new protests, scheduled for Tuesday, could be a turning point in the movement, launched in mid-September, which the government hopes is already winding down. On Friday, the government noted a dramatic drop in the number of blockades and meetings outside the country's high schools, where students – most between 15 and 18 – complete their high school education. More than 96% were opening on Friday, said the Education Ministry.
The authorities are all the more keen to see the student protests end given that online activists have called for demonstrations to protest the cost of living next Saturday. For President Emmanuel Macron's administration, that brings back troubling memories of the grassroots Yellow Vest movement. Their protests, launched in 2018 over a planned fuel tax rise, saw massive demonstrations and clashes between police and protesters that shook the presidency during Macron's first term in office.
Alleged cases of police misconduct
On Friday, the justice ministry said more than 6,800 people had been detained since the demonstrations started, 86% of them minors. After clashes between some protesters and riot police left some students severely injured, sparking criticism of police tactics, the government suspended the use of stun grenades that cost one student his hand. Police are investigating 18 alleged cases of misconduct within their ranks.
Last week, the government came up with concrete proposals to try to address the students' demands. Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced, late on Thursday, that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Sunday promised to make changes to the 2027 budget bill to respond to some demands expressed through an online platform the government set up to gather students' views.
The student organizations behind the protests are yet to be convinced, however. The Union of High School students described the initial announcements last week as "crumbs." They are maintaining their demand for an extra €10 million to be invested in the country's high schools.
France's 10,000 medical students are meanwhile beginning to express concern at the effect any continued school blockades could have on exams that start on Monday, which help determine their eventual speciality. They do not want to see the students' action disrupt such a crucial stage of their education.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Oldest covered market in Paris 'completely destroyed' in overnight fire
lemonde.fr/en.text:
A fire has destroyed the French capital's oldest covered food market, a popular street food venue named after red-clad orphans, authorities said on Monday, October 12.
The Marché Couvert des Enfants Rouges in the Marais neighborhood has existed since 1615, and draws its name from the red outfits orphans wore at a hospital near the venue until 1772. Food & Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year, after other eating spots in London, Bangkok, the French city of Lyon and Mexico City.
"The market was completely destroyed" overnight from Sunday to Monday, Lieutenant Colonel Pierre de Bouvier told reporters on site in the early hours of the morning. "Nothing remains of the covered market," he said, adding that its metal structure had "partially collapsed" inside.
Authorities said the fire broke out at 3:00 am, but the fire brigade did not receive a call until 4:15 am.
The mayor of the central Paris district, Ariel Weil, said he was relieved the fire was under control and would not spread further. He said that 17 businesses inside the market had been destroyed. "The worst has been avoided," he said. "No neighboring buildings have been affected."
Weil told Le Monde that firefighters chose to prevent the blaze from spreading to other buildings by letting it burn in the middle of the market. He added that although the market is the oldest in Paris, "what burned doesn't have any patrimonial value, so to speak, but were mostly lightweight stalls."
On Monday morning, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire visited the site of the fire. He later said the capital would work on relocating vendors to another area "so they can resume their activities as quickly as possible."

welt.de.text:

welt.de.title: „Putin will mehr als Selenskyj einen Deal“ – Trump legt gegen ukrainischen Präsidenten nach
welt.de.text: US-Präsident Donald Trump will ungeachtet der Kritik an seinem jüngsten Vorgehen im Ukraine-Krieg den Aggressor Russland nicht stärker in die Pflicht nehmen und sieht vor allem die Ukraine unter Zugzwang. Auf die Frage einer Reporterin, was er dazu sage, dass Russland die von ihm selbst verkündete Energie-Waffenruhe verletzt habe, sagte Trump: „Nun, ich müsste mir das erst einmal ansehen, denn es gab Verstöße auf beiden Seiten.“ Auf Nachfrage, wie er Russlands Präsidenten Wladimir Putin dazu bewegen wolle, sich an die Waffenruhe zu halten, sagte Trump, er glaube, dass Putin eine Einigung erzielen wolle – und man den ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj dazu bringen müsse, das ebenfalls zu wollen. Auch eine weitere Reporterfrage, wo er bei Putin die Bereitschaft für eine Einigung sehe, wenn dieser die Ukraine angreife, bügelte Trump ohne ein Wort der Kritik am Kreml ab: „Ich glaube, sie werden eine Einigung erzielen. Ich glaube tatsächlich, dass Putin mehr als Selenskyj daran interessiert ist, einen Deal zu machen.“ Selenskyj hatte die USA zuvor aufgefordert, Russland zur Einhaltung der von Trump verkündeten und auf den Energiesektor begrenzten Waffenruhe anzuhalten. „Wir warten darauf, welche konkreten Schritte die Amerikaner bereit sind zu unternehmen“, sagte Selenskyj in einer per Videoschalte auf dem Warschauer Sicherheitsforum übertragenen Rede. Man sei am Sonntag sehr überrascht worden von Trumps Ankündigung in sozialen Medien, dass im Ukraine-Krieg alle Angriffe auf Energieanlagen sofort gestoppt würden, sagte Selenskyj weiter. „Und direkt nach der Veröffentlichung des Beitrags führte Russland einen gezielten Angriff auf ein Kraftwerk in Charkiw durch, wodurch unser Energiesystem weiteren Schaden davontrug.“ Selenskyj betonte, die Ukraine sei mit einem Stopp von Angriffen auf Energieanlagen einverstanden, wenn Russland dies auch respektiere. Man habe deshalb auch in der vergangenen Nacht darauf verzichtet, russische Ölraffinerien anzugreifen. Trump hatte die Ukraine in den vergangenen Tagen gleich mehrfach vor den Kopf gestoßen: So verlangte er nach einem Telefongespräch mit Putin die Ablösung Selenskyjs und verkündete eine Vereinbarung zur Lieferung von Hunderttausenden Tonnen Diesel aus Russland. Bei europäischen Verbündeten wie auch im eigenen Land gab es daran starke Kritik. Mehrere US-Senatoren – auch aus den Reihen seiner Republikaner – kritisierten den Diesel-Deal als rechtswidrig, weil der Kongress im Jahr 2022 die Einfuhr russischer Energieträger untersagt habe, damit die USA nicht Russlands Krieg finanzieren. Donald Trump verteidigt das Diesel-Abkommen gegen parteiübergreifende Kritik. Die Vereinbarung werde amerikanischen Landwirten helfen und die hohen Kraftstoffpreise senken. Das Geschäft soll US-Regierungskreisen zufolge Moskau jedoch eigentlich für Friedensgespräche öffnen. Die US-Gesandten Jared Kushner und Steve Witkoff hatten ukrainischen Vertretern am Freitag in Miami mitgeteilt, das Abkommen solle die russische Haltung aufweichen und Präsident Wladimir Putin an den Verhandlungstisch zurückholen, sagten drei mit dem Vorgang vertraute Personen der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters. Der russische Vize-Ministerpräsident Alexander Nowak kündigte unterdessen an, Russland könne seine Diesel-Exporte auf das Vorkrisenniveau von mehr als drei Millionen Tonnen pro Monat steigern. Die Vereinbarung entlaste den Weltmarkt bereits, sagte Nowak im russischen Staatsfernsehsender Rossija-24. Russlands Dieselexporte sind aufgrund ukrainischer Angriffe auf Ölraffinerien und selbst auferlegter Beschränkungen für den Verkauf ins Ausland eingebrochen.

welt.de.title: Wie Putin von seinen eigenen Generälen mit Fake News betrogen wird

welt.de.title: Trump spricht erneut von Einwanderern, die „Haustiere ihrer Nachbarn essen“
welt.de.text: US-Präsident Donald Trump hat erneut seine unbelegte Behauptung verteidigt, haitianische Einwanderer in Springfield im Bundesstaat Ohio würden Haustiere von Einwohnern essen. „Wie sich herausstellt, hatte ich recht“, sagte Trump, ohne seine Vorwürfe näher auszuführen. „Erinnert ihr euch, dass ich während der Debatte einige der Dinge angesprochen habe, die sie getan haben?“, sagte er. Er wolle nicht ins Detail gehen, aber er habe recht gehabt. Belege für seine Behauptung legte er nicht vor. Bei der Präsidentschaftsdebatte im September 2024 hatte Trump behauptet, haitianische Einwanderer würden „die Haustiere der Menschen essen, die dort leben“. Die Frau, die das Gerücht zuvor auf Facebook verbreitet hatte, löschte ihren Beitrag später, räumte ein, keine Belege dafür zu haben, und entschuldigte sich. Trump äußerte auch seine Freude darüber, dass unter seiner Regierung viele Haitianer ihren legalen Aufenthaltsstatus verlieren. „Sie bekommen ihre Stadt zurück“, sagte er mit Blick auf die Einwohner von Springfield. Anspielungen auf dritte Amtszeit Bei derselben Wahlkampfveranstaltung in Youngstown machte Trump erneut Anspielungen auf eine dritte Amtszeit. Er versprach, dass der wirtschaftliche Erfolg des Landes im Falle eines Sieges der Republikaner bei den Zwischenwahlen im November ein Ausmaß erreichen werde, „wie wir es noch nie zuvor gesehen haben“. Daraufhin riefen Zuschauer: „Vier weitere Jahre!“ Und Trump antwortete: „Das würde ich sehr gerne machen.“ Eine dritte Amtszeit ist ihm durch die US-Verfassung jedoch untersagt.

welt.de.title: Elon Musk unterstützt Republikaner im Wahlkampf mit 276 Millionen Dollar
welt.de.text: Der Tech-Milliardär Elon Musk hat US-Medienberichten zufolge im Vorfeld der Kongresswahlen 276 Millionen Dollar (247 Millionen Euro) an Organisationen gespendet, die die Wahlkampagnen republikanischer Kandidaten unterstützen. Mit dieser seit Juli gespendeten Summe ist Musk der „New York Times“ vom Montag zufolge der größte Einzelspender für die Wahl am 3. November. Unter Berücksichtigung insbesondere der Vorwahlen steigt der Gesamtbetrag auf 366 Millionen Dollar. Der größte Empfänger der Mittel war der Senate Leadership Fund der Republikaner, der 158 Millionen Dollar erhielt, um die Kontrolle der Partei über den Senat zu sichern. Schon 290 Mio. für Trumps Wahl gespendet Der Chef von SpaceX und Tesla hatte 2024 bereits 290 Millionen Dollar gespendet, um US-Präsident Donald Trump zum Wiedereinzug ins Weiße Haus zu verhelfen. Musk stand Trump zu Beginn seiner zweiten Amtszeit als Berater zur Seite und strich im Auftrag des Präsidenten tausende Stellen im Staatsapparat und bei Ministerien. Im Mai 2025 schied Musk bei der Regierungsabteilung für staatliche Effizienz (Doge) jedoch wegen eines Zerwürfnisses mit Trump über die massiv steigenden Staatsschulden aus. Inzwischen haben sie sich versöhnt. Zwar sind einzelne Wahlkampfspenden in den USA auf 3300 Dollar pro Person begrenzt. Schlupflöcher im Wahlkampffinanzierungssystem ermöglichen es politischen Großspendern aber, Beiträge an sogenannte Political Action Committees zu leisten, die wiederum Kandidaten unterstützen. Bei den Kongresswahlen am 3. November droht Trumps Republikanern eine Niederlage. Laut Umfragen dürften sie ihre knappen Mehrheiten im Repräsentantenhaus und womöglich auch im Senat verlieren. Bei einem Wahlsieg könnten die Demokraten in der zweiten Hälfte von Trumps Amtszeit zahlreiche Vorhaben des Präsidenten verhindern.

welt.de.title: „Rekrutierungsinstrument für Terroristen“ – Kritik an geplanter Live-Hinrichtung
welt.de.text: Der Vorsitzende des US-Repräsentantenhauses, Mike Johnson, hat Vorbehalte gegenüber der geplanten Liveübertragung einer Hinrichtung in den USA geäußert. Verteidigungsminister Pete Hegseth hatte angekündigt, die Hinrichtung des verurteilten Attentäters Nidal Hasan durch ein militärisches Erschießungskommando live zu übertragen. „Die Sorge wäre, dass man ein Video produzieren würde, das als Rekrutierungsinstrument für zukünftige Terroristen dienen könnte“, sagte Johnson am Montag CBS News. „Wir müssen die politischen Auswirkungen all dessen gründlich durchdenken.“ Der Republikaner sagte, er werde sich die Hinrichtung auf keinen Fall ansehen, sollte sie live übertragen werden. Es gäbe auch andere Kollegen, die Bedenken hätten, sagte Johnson noch. Hasan war 2013 zum Tode verurteilt worden, weil er auf dem Militärstützpunkt Fort Hood im US-Bundesstaat Texas 13 Menschen erschossen und rund 30 weitere verletzt hatte. Hasan wäre der erste Mensch seit Ende des Zweiten Weltkrieges, der durch ein Erschießungskommando des US-Militärs hingerichtet wird. Die Ankündigung der Liveübertragung löste international sowie bei Demokraten wie Republikanern in den USA Empörung aus. Selbst Präsident Donald Trump, ein vehementer Verfechter der Todesstrafe, stellte die Liveübertragung am Freitag in Frage.

welt.de.title: Britische Beziehungen zur EU „nicht gut genug“ – Burnham rudert zurück
welt.de.text: Der britische Premierminister Andy Burnham hofft bei dem in wenigen Wochen anstehenden EU-UK-Gipfel auf den Abschluss diverser Abkommen mit der Europäischen Union. Es brauche in vielen Bereichen eine „engere Zusammenarbeit“, sagte der Regierungschef vor den Abgeordneten im britischen Unterhaus. Es reiche nicht aus, am Status quo festzuhalten, dieser sei „nicht gut genug“. „Schlimmer noch, es wäre eine schwere Pflichtverletzung, sich abzuwenden.“ Der EU-UK-Gipfel findet am 20. November in Brüssel statt. Bei dem Treffen sollen laut Burnham eine Reihe von bereits geplanten Abkommen vorangebracht werden, darunter etwa Vereinbarungen zum Handel mit Lebensmitteln und Getränken sowie zum Emissionshandel. Auch im Bereich der Migration – für Burnham eines der zentralen Themen des Gipfels – wolle man die Zusammenarbeit vertiefen, so der Premier. Burnham hatte zuletzt als erster britischer Regierungschef seit dem Brexit konkret von der Möglichkeit zur Rückkehr in die EU gesprochen, der Weg dahin wäre aber auch bei einer Entscheidung für entsprechende Gespräche weit. Großbritannien war im Januar 2020 aus der EU ausgetreten. Beim Gipfeltreffen wolle man zunächst „ein erfolgreiches Ergebnis“ erzielen, sagte Burnham. Anschließend könnten beide Seiten „einen ernsthaften Dialog über die verschiedenen Optionen auf lange Sicht“ führen. Zu jedem Zeitpunkt habe dabei jedoch „die britische Öffentlichkeit das Sagen“.

welt.de.title: „Trotz der Räumung der großen Lager kann man nicht sagen, dass das Problem jetzt weg ist“
welt.de.text:
Kurz vor dem Besuch des spanischen Königspaares in Ceuta haben die Behörden das Flüchtlingslager komplett geräumt. „Man versucht ein Bild von Recht und Ordnung herzustellen. Militär und Polizei patrouillieren“, so WELT-Reporterin Diana Pieper aus Ceuta.
